2027-06-06.title: Tenth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers
With the Lord there is steadfast love, and with him is great power to redeem
So we do not lose heart … our inner nature is being renewed day by day
Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother
2027-06-06.alt: Sunday. Year B. Ordinary Time resumes its Sundays after the great feasts of Pentecost, the Trinity and Corpus Christi (kept in India on 30 May). Gloria and Creed. The memorial of St Norbert, bishop, is omitted this year because it falls on a Sunday. In Kerala the schools have reopened and the monsoon has arrived. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-06.verse: And looking at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.”
theo: After weeks of great feasts the Church returns to the green Sundays of Ordinary Time, the season of growth, and today's readings go back to the very beginning, to the garden. Adam and the woman have eaten from the forbidden tree. They have hidden among the trees. And God comes looking: “But the Lord God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” It is the first question God asks in the Bible, and it is not the question of a policeman but of a father looking for a lost child. God knows where Adam is; Adam needs to know where he is. Adam answers with the first confession of human fear: “I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.” Sin has made the friend of God afraid of God. Then comes the chain of excuses: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate.” The man blames the woman and, quietly, God who gave her; the woman blames the serpent: “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.” Nobody says: I did it. Sin divides; it turns people against each other and against God. But God does not abandon them. To the serpent he speaks a curse and, hidden inside it, the first promise of salvation: “I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel.” The Church calls this verse the Protoevangelium, the first Gospel (Catechism 410–411). The war will not last for ever; a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent's head, though he himself will be wounded. Christians have seen in that offspring Christ, wounded on the Cross and victorious, and in the woman, Mary, the new Eve. The Psalm is the cry of everyone who has hidden from God and now calls to him: “Out of the depths I cry to you, O Lord … If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who could stand? But there is forgiveness with you.”

St Paul, in the second reading, speaks from the depths of his own sufferings. He has been afflicted, perplexed, persecuted, struck down. Yet he keeps preaching, because he believes: “just as we have the same spirit of faith that is in accordance with scripture, ‘I believed, and so I spoke,’ we also believe, and so we speak, because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus.” Faith in the Resurrection gives him courage: “So we do not lose heart. Even though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day.” Every ache of growing older, every illness, every loss is the outer tent wearing out, while within, God is building something new. “For this slight momentary affliction is preparing us for an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, because we look not at what can be seen but at what cannot be seen.” And then the great hope: “For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.” Adam lost the garden; Christ prepares for us a house that will never be lost.

The Gospel shows Jesus surrounded by opposition from two sides. Such crowds gather at the house that “they could not even eat.” His relatives hear what people are saying, “He has gone out of his mind,” and come to take charge of him. The scribes from Jerusalem go much further: “He has Beelzebul, and by the ruler of the demons he casts out demons.” Jesus answers with clear logic: “How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.” Then a short parable: “no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his property without first tying up the strong man.” Satan is the strong man who has held humanity captive since the garden; Jesus is the stronger one who has come to bind him and set his prisoners loose. That is the promise of Genesis 3:15 coming true before their eyes. Then a solemn warning: all sins and blasphemies can be forgiven, “but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit can never have forgiveness.” This is not a single careless word but a hardened refusal to recognise God's saving work, calling the Holy Spirit's work the devil's; whoever refuses mercy to the end shuts the door from the inside (Catechism 1864). Finally his mother and his brothers arrive and stand outside. In the language of the time “brothers” meant close relatives; the Church has always taught that Mary remained ever a virgin and that these were cousins or kinsmen (Catechism 500). Jesus looks at those seated around him and says: “Here are my mother and my brothers! Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.” He does not reject his mother; he reveals what makes her truly great. No one ever did the will of God more perfectly than Mary, who said, “Here am I, the servant of the Lord” (Luke 1:38). She is his mother twice over, by flesh and by faith. And the door is opened to us: whoever does the will of God belongs to the family of Jesus. Adam hid; the new family of Jesus sits around him, listening.
conn: “Where are you?”
The first question God asks in the Bible (Genesis 3:9). It is the question of a seeking love; Jesus came “to seek out and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).
The chain of blame.
The man blames the woman and God; the woman blames the serpent. Sin breaks the communion of man and woman and of humanity with God (Catechism 400).
The Protoevangelium.
Genesis 3:15, “the first Gospel”: the first announcement of the Messiah and Redeemer, of a battle between the serpent and the Woman, and of the final victory of a descendant of hers (Catechism 410).
The Woman.

The Fathers saw Mary as the new Eve: where Eve listened to the serpent, Mary believed the angel (St Irenaeus, in substance). The Woman returns in Revelation 12, clothed with the sun, at war with the dragon.
“I believed, and so I spoke.”
Paul quotes Psalm 116:10 in its Greek form. Faith that is real cannot keep silent.
The earthly tent.
Paul, a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3), compares the body to a tent and our resurrection life to a building from God, eternal in the heavens.
“He has gone out of his mind.”
Jesus' own relatives (Greek: “those from beside him”) misunderstood him. Even those closest to Jesus had to grow in faith.
Beelzebul.
A name for the prince of demons, perhaps from a Philistine god (2 Kings 1:2). The scribes cannot deny the exorcisms, so they slander their source.
The strong man and the stronger one.
An echo of Isaiah 49:24–25: “the captives of a tyrant will be rescued.” Luke 11:22 calls Jesus “one stronger” who overpowers the strong man.
Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
To refuse deliberately to accept God's mercy by repenting; such hardness of heart can lead to final impenitence and eternal loss (Catechism 1864).
“His mother and his brothers.”
In Hebrew and Aramaic usage “brothers” includes cousins and kinsmen; James and Joses, called “brothers of Jesus,” are sons of another Mary (Mark 15:40; Catechism 500).
altar: God asked Adam, “Where are you?” At every Mass Christ, the stronger one who has bound the strong man, gathers his new family around the altar. The penitential act at the beginning of Mass is our answer to God's question: Here I am, Lord, I have sinned, have mercy on me.

In the Eucharist we receive the victory promised in Genesis 3:15: the Body that was wounded in the heel, the Blood that crushed the serpent's head. Those who eat this Bread and do the will of God become the brothers and sisters and mother of Jesus, his true family.
outline: Opening
Tell of a child who hides after breaking something precious, and the parent who calls, not angrily, “Where are you?”
Point 1 · Where are you?
God seeks the one who hides; sin makes us afraid and quick to blame.
Point 2 · The first Gospel
Enmity between the serpent and the Woman, and the victory of her offspring.
Point 3 · The stronger one
Jesus binds the strong man; only a heart that refuses mercy remains unforgiven.
Point 4 · My mother and my brothers
Doing the will of God makes us the family of Jesus, as Mary was first of all.
Closing image
A crowded room in Capernaum: Jesus looking round at the faces seated on the floor, smiling, and saying, “Here are my mother and my brothers!”
Take-home line
“Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.”
live: Answer the question
Tonight, in silence, let God ask you: Where are you? Answer him honestly, without excuses, and go to confession soon if you have been hiding.
Stop the blame
This week, when something goes wrong at home or at work, be the first to say: I was wrong, I am sorry.
Do his will
Each morning pray: Lord, what is your will for me today? And each night: Did I do it?
Do not lose heart
Visit or call someone who is old or sick, whose “outer nature is wasting away,” and remind them of the house God is preparing.
fathers: St Irenaeus (in substance)
The knot of Eve's disobedience was untied by the obedience of Mary. What the virgin Eve bound by unbelief, the Virgin Mary loosed by faith (Against Heresies III, 22, 4).
St Augustine (in substance)

Mary did the will of the Father, and so it is a greater thing for her to have been Christ's disciple than to have been his mother. She is blessed because she heard the word of God and kept it; she carried the Truth in her mind more happily than the flesh in her womb (Sermon 72A).
St Augustine (in substance)
The blasphemy that is not forgiven is the impenitence of a heart that, to the end of life, refuses the forgiveness offered in the Church by the Holy Spirit (Sermon 71).
magis: Catechism 397
Man, tempted by the devil, let his trust in his Creator die in his heart and, abusing his liberty, disobeyed God's command. This is what the first sin consisted of.
Catechism 410–411
After the fall God did not abandon man: Genesis 3:15 is called the Protoevangelium, the first announcement of the Messiah and of the Woman; many Fathers see in her the Mother of Christ, the new Eve.
Catechism 500

The brothers and sisters of Jesus are close relations, according to an expression found in the Old Testament; the Church has always understood these passages as not referring to other children of the Virgin Mary.
Catechism 1864
There are no limits to the mercy of God, but anyone who deliberately refuses to accept his mercy by repenting rejects the forgiveness of his sins and the salvation offered by the Holy Spirit.
Lumen Gentium 58
In the course of her Son's preaching Mary received his words when he praised those who hear and keep the word of God, as she herself was faithfully doing.
saints: St Norbert (c. 1080–1134)

His memorial (6 June) is omitted this year because it falls on a Sunday. A worldly cleric at the imperial court, he was thrown from his horse in a thunderstorm in 1115 and changed his life. He became a priest and preacher of penance, founded the Canons Regular of Prémontré (the Norbertines or Premonstratensians) in 1120, and became archbishop of Magdeburg in 1126. He was known for his love of the Eucharist.
This week

9 Jun: St Ephrem, deacon and doctor (optional). 11 Jun: St Barnabas, apostle. 13 Jun: Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time (St Antony of Padua). The weekday readings: the Second Letter to the Corinthians and the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5).
2027-06-06.prayer: O God, from whom all good things come, grant that we, who call on you in our need, may at your prompting discern what is right, and by your guidance do it. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord God, you came looking for Adam when he hid; you still ask each of us, Where are you? Give us the courage to come out of hiding and to answer without excuses. Lord Jesus, stronger than the strong man, set us loose from every bondage of sin. Make us your true family, doing the will of the Father as your Mother did, and keep us from losing heart until we reach the house not made with hands. Amen.

2027-06-20.title: Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stopped
Give thanks to the Lord, his love is everlasting (or: Alleluia)
If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation
Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?
2027-06-20.alt: Year B. Liturgical colour: green. This week: St Aloysius Gonzaga (memorial, Monday 21), the optional memorials of St Paulinus of Nola and of Sts John Fisher and Thomas More (Tuesday 22), and the solemnity of the Nativity of St John the Baptist (Thursday 24). In India and many other countries the third Sunday of June is also kept as Father's Day: a good day to pray for fathers, living and dead.
2027-06-20.verse: He woke up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” Then the wind ceased, and there was a dead calm.
theo: Few readers in Kerala need to be told what a storm at sea means. In these weeks of the monsoon the waves come high on the beaches of Vizhinjam, Chellanam and Ponnani, the small boats are pulled up on the sand, and fishing families watch the sky. Today's readings are full of that same sea. The first comes from the end of the Book of Job. For thirty-seven chapters Job has suffered, argued with his friends and demanded an answer from God. Now at last “the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind.” But God does not explain Job's suffering. He asks Job to look at creation, and in the verses we hear today he speaks of the sea: “Or who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb?” The sea in the Bible is the image of all that is wild, dark and threatening, the chaos that God tamed at creation. And God speaks of it as a mother speaks of a newborn child: “when I made the clouds its garment, and thick darkness its swaddling band.” The terrifying ocean is, to God, an infant in swaddling clothes. Then he sets its limits: “and prescribed bounds for it, and set bars and doors, and said, ‘Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stopped.’” Job is not answered with an argument; he is answered with a Presence greater than his storm. The Psalm tells the story of sailors caught in such a storm: “They mounted up to heaven, they went down to the depths; their courage melted away in their calamity.” Then “they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he brought them out from their distress; he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed.”

Mark's Gospel takes us onto the Sea of Galilee at evening. Jesus has spent the day teaching the crowds in parables from a boat. Now he says, “Let us go across to the other side,” to the Gentile shore. The disciples take him “just as he was,” tired from the day. A sudden windstorm comes down on the lake, as often happens there, and “the waves beat into the boat, so that the boat was already being swamped.” Several of these men were fishermen who knew this lake; they are terrified. And Jesus? “He was in the stern, asleep on the cushion.” Only Mark gives us that small detail, the cushion, the kind of thing an eyewitness remembers; the ancient tradition says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching. They wake him with a cry that is half prayer, half reproach: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” Many of us have prayed that prayer. Jesus rises. “He woke up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’ Then the wind ceased, and there was a dead calm.” He speaks to the storm as he spoke to the unclean spirit in the synagogue of Capernaum, with a word of command. Then he turns to his disciples: “Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?” And they are filled with a new and greater fear, the awe that falls on people in the presence of God: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” Every Jew who knew Job 38 and Psalm 107 knew the answer. Only the Lord shuts in the sea with doors; only the Lord makes the storm be still. The man asleep on the cushion is the Creator of the sea. Mark does not write the answer; he leaves it for us to say.

St Paul gives us the answer in the second reading, and shows us what follows from it. “For the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all; therefore all have died. And he died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them.” The one who calmed the sea is the one who went down into the deepest storm of all, death itself, and rose. He did it for all. So Paul can say: “From now on, therefore, we regard no one from a human point of view.” We can no longer look at anyone only by caste, wealth, language or religion; each one is a person for whom Christ died. “So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!” The God who in the beginning set bounds to the sea is making all things new in Christ. The early Christians loved to see the Church in the boat on the lake: tossed by the waves of history, often afraid, sometimes feeling that the Lord is asleep, but never alone, because he is in the boat. Pope Francis preached on this Gospel on the evening of 27 March 2020, alone in a rain-soaked St Peter's Square during the pandemic, and said that we had discovered that we are all in the same boat. Jesus does not promise us a sea without storms. He promises that he is in the boat, and that the storm has a limit: thus far, and no farther.
conn: “Out of the whirlwind.”
God answers Job not with an explanation of suffering but with his own presence (Job 38:1). The same God who speaks from the storm will one day sleep in a boat in the storm.
The sea in the Bible.
For Israel, a people of shepherds and farmers, the sea was the image of chaos and danger (Genesis 1:2; Psalm 89:9; Revelation 21:1, “the sea was no more”). Only God rules it.
Swaddling band.
Job 38:9 pictures the newborn sea wrapped in cloud like a baby. In Luke 2:7 the Creator himself is wrapped in swaddling clothes.
Storms on the lake.
The Sea of Galilee lies about two hundred metres below sea level, ringed by hills; cool winds can rush down the valleys and raise sudden, violent storms.
The cushion in the stern.
A detail found only in Mark, the kind an eyewitness remembers. Early tradition (Papias, quoted by Eusebius) says Mark wrote down the preaching of Peter.
“Peace! Be still!”
The Greek verb Jesus uses for the sea (literally “be muzzled”) is the one he used to silence an unclean spirit in Mark 1:25. Jesus confronts the storm as a power hostile to life.
“He woke up.”
Mark uses the verb that later describes the Resurrection (Mark 16:6). The Lord who rises from sleep to save his disciples will rise from death to save the world.
A first-century boat.

In 1986, during a drought, a fishing boat from about the time of Jesus was found in the mud near Ginosar on the Sea of Galilee. It is about eight metres long: a boat of this kind could have carried Jesus and the Twelve.
“A new creation.”
Paul's phrase in 2 Corinthians 5:17 links Baptism with the first creation: the God who separated the waters in Genesis 1 makes a new creature in the waters of Baptism (Catechism 1265).
altar: At every Mass, after the Our Father, the priest asks the Lord to deliver us from every evil, to grant peace in our days, and by the help of his mercy to keep us from sin and safe from all distress. In that prayer the Church cries out like the disciples in the boat, and the Lord answers, as on the lake, with peace: the peace of the Lord be with you always.

The Christ who rebuked the wind is the Christ who comes to us in the Eucharist, Body and Blood, soul and divinity. The one who died for all gives himself to each one of us, so that we who live may live no longer for ourselves, but for him.
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever been in a real storm, at sea, on the road, or in the hospital corridor, and felt that God was asleep?
Point 1 · Thus far and no farther
God sets bounds to the sea: every storm has a limit.
Point 2 · Asleep on the cushion
The disciples' cry: do you not care that we are perishing?
Point 3 · Peace! Be still!
The word of the Creator, and the question: who then is this?
Point 4 · The love of Christ urges us on
One died for all; in him we are a new creation.
Closing image
A small fishing boat pulled up on a Kerala beach in the monsoon rain, with a cross painted on its bow.
Take-home line
“Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?”
live: Name your storm (Mark 4:38)
Tell Jesus plainly in prayer this week about the storm you are in, even with the disciples' words: Lord, do you not care? He can bear our honest prayer.
Pray for those at sea
Pray this week for fishermen, sailors and seafarers, many of them from our coasts, especially those away from their families during the monsoon months.
Honour your father
On this Father's Day, thank your father in person or by phone, or pray for him by name if he has died; ask God to make fathers steady in the storms of family life.
See as Christ sees (2 Corinthians 5:16)
Choose one person you usually judge from a human point of view, and pray for him or her as someone for whom Christ died.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

When you are insulted and want to strike back, you are being tossed by the waves, and your boat is in danger because Christ is asleep in you: you have forgotten him. Wake Christ, remember his word, and the storm in your heart will grow calm.
Pope St Leo the Great (in substance)

In his letter to Flavian (449) he teaches that to hunger, to thirst, to be weary and to sleep belong to the true humanity of Christ, while to rebuke the storm and still the waves belongs to his divinity: one and the same Son of God both slept and commanded the sea.
Tertullian (in substance)

The little boat on the lake was a figure of the Church, which is tossed in the sea of this world by the waves of persecution and temptation, while the Lord seems to sleep, until he is roused by the prayers of the saints and calms the sea.
magis: Catechism 302–303
Divine providence: God guides his creation toward its perfection, and his care is concrete and immediate, from the least things to the great events of history.
Catechism 548
The signs worked by Jesus attest that the Father has sent him and invite belief in him.
Catechism 616
It is love to the end that gives Christ's sacrifice its value: “the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all” (2 Corinthians 5:14).
Catechism 1265
Baptism makes the neophyte a new creature (2 Corinthians 5:17), an adopted son of God and a partaker of the divine nature.
Pope Francis, Extraordinary Moment of Prayer, 27 March 2020

Preaching on Mark 4:35–41 in an empty St Peter's Square: in the storm we find that we are all in the same boat, all fragile and all needing one another, and the Lord asks us: why are you afraid? Have you no faith?
saints: This week

21 Jun: St Aloysius Gonzaga, religious (memorial), patron of young people and students. 22 Jun: St Paulinus of Nola, bishop; Sts John Fisher, bishop, and Thomas More, martyrs (optional memorials). 23 Jun: in the evening, the Vigil Mass of the Nativity of St John the Baptist. 24 Jun: the Nativity of St John the Baptist (solemnity). 27 Jun: Thirteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-20.prayer: Grant, O Lord, that we may always revere and love your holy name, for you never deprive of your guidance those you set firm on the foundation of your love. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you slept in the boat and rose to rebuke the wind. When the waves beat into our homes and our hearts, and we cry out that you do not care, wake in us the faith that you are with us in the boat. Say to our storms: Peace! Be still! Protect fishermen and all who travel on the sea, bless our fathers, and let your love urge us on, so that we live no longer for ourselves but for you, who died and were raised for us. Amen.

2027-06-27.title: Thirteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living
I will praise you, Lord, for you have rescued me
Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor
Talitha cum … Little girl, get up!
2027-06-27.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The memorial of St Cyril of Alexandria, bishop and doctor of the Church, is omitted this year because it falls on a Sunday. In many places the collection called Peter's Pence is taken up today, the Sunday nearest the solemnity of Sts Peter and Paul, for the charitable works of the Holy Father (verify the date locally). Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-27.verse: He took her by the hand and said to her, “Talitha cum,” which means, “Little girl, get up!” And immediately the girl got up and began to walk about
theo: Today's readings stand face to face with the oldest enemy of the human race: death. The first reading comes from the Book of Wisdom, written in Greek by a devout Jew, probably in Alexandria in Egypt, in the last century before Christ. Around him were philosophies that said death is simply the end, so eat and drink while you can. The sacred author answers with a bold sentence: “God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living. For he created all things so that they might exist.” Creation is not a trap; “the generative forces of the world are wholesome, and there is no destructive poison in them.” Then he tells us where we come from and where death comes from: “for God created us for incorruption, and made us in the image of his own eternity, but through the devil's envy death entered the world, and those who belong to his company experience it.” Here, reading Genesis 3, Scripture names for the first time the serpent of Eden as the devil, and the Catechism quotes these very lines (Catechism 391, 413). Death is real, but it was not God's plan; it is an intruder. And God is on the side of life. The Psalm is the song of someone who has been to the edge of the grave and come back: “O LORD, you brought up my soul from Sheol, restored me to life from among those gone down to the Pit.” It contains one of the most consoling lines in the whole Psalter: “Weeping may linger for the night, but joy comes with the morning.” And its last word is pure Easter: “You have turned my mourning into dancing.”

In the second reading St Paul is organising a collection. The Christians of Jerusalem are poor, and Paul asks the Gentile churches of Greece to help them. He does not shame the Corinthians or order them; he reminds them of Christ: “For you know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.” The Greek word for “generous act” is charis, grace. All Christian giving begins there: we give because the Son of God gave himself. Then Paul speaks of “a fair balance”: your abundance now supplies their need, and one day their abundance may supply yours. He quotes the story of the manna in the desert: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little” (Exodus 16:18). In the Church nobody should be crushed by want while others have more than they need. It is fitting that on this Sunday many dioceses take up Peter's Pence, the collection through which the successor of Peter helps the poor and the suffering Churches of the world in our name.

The Gospel is one of the great stories of St Mark, and he tells it in his favourite way, one story wrapped inside another. Jairus, “one of the leaders of the synagogue,” a respected man, falls at Jesus' feet: “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well, and live.” Jesus goes with him, and the crowd presses in. In that crowd is a woman with no name and no standing. For twelve years she has suffered from bleeding; she “had endured much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had; and she was no better, but rather grew worse.” Her illness made her ritually unclean (Leviticus 15:25), so she should not even be there. She thinks, “If I but touch his clothes, I will be made well,” and she touches, and is healed. Jesus stops: “Who touched my clothes?” The disciples find the question absurd; everyone is touching him. But there is a difference between pressing against Jesus and touching him with faith. Jesus wants to meet her face to face. She comes trembling and tells “the whole truth,” and he gives her more than health: he calls her “Daughter,” the only time in Mark that he calls anyone so, and says, “your faith has made you well; go in peace.” Meanwhile the worst news arrives for Jairus: “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any further?” Jesus overhears and says the words this Gospel was written for: “Do not fear, only believe.” At the house the mourners are already wailing; when Jesus says, “The child is not dead but sleeping,” they laugh at him. Then, with only the parents and Peter, James and John, he takes the girl by the hand and speaks in Aramaic, words Mark keeps exactly as Jesus said them: “Talitha cum,” “Little girl, get up!” She gets up and walks; she is twelve years old, as old as the woman's suffering. And Jesus, practical and tender, tells them to give her something to eat. In one afternoon Jesus touches the two things that made a person unclean, blood and death, and they do not defile him; his life overcomes them. What Wisdom said, God did not make death, Jesus shows. He has not yet abolished death; that will happen on Easter morning. But he shows that for him death is like sleep, from which he can wake us with a word. This is why Christians call their burial ground a cemetery, from the Greek for “sleeping place.”
conn: “God did not make death.”
Wisdom 1:13 and 2:24 are quoted by the Catechism (413) to teach that death entered the world through sin, at the devil's prompting; God created us for incorruption.
“Through the devil's envy.”
The first place in Scripture where the serpent of Genesis 3 is identified with the devil. Jesus calls the devil “a murderer from the beginning” (John 8:44; Catechism 391).
“The generous act.”
In Greek charis, grace. Paul's motive for almsgiving is the self-emptying of Christ, who was rich and became poor (compare Philippians 2:6–8).
“A fair balance.”

Paul quotes Exodus 16:18: in the desert everyone gathered manna, and no one had too much or too little. The Church's teaching on the universal destination of goods rests on this (Catechism 2402–2406).
“A leader of the synagogue.”
A layman who took care of the synagogue and its Sabbath services. Jairus, an important person, kneels in public before Jesus.
Twelve years.
The woman has suffered for twelve years; the girl is twelve years old. Twelve is also the number of Israel's tribes: Jesus restores daughters of Israel to life and to the community.
“Who touched my clothes?”
Her flow of blood made her ritually unclean (Leviticus 15:25–27). Jesus does not scold her for touching him; he heals her, calls her “Daughter” and sends her away in peace.
“Talitha cum.”
Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke at home. Mark keeps a few of Jesus' own Aramaic words, like Ephphatha (7:34) and Abba (14:36).
“Not dead but sleeping.”
Christians speak of the dead as those who have fallen asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13); the word cemetery comes from the Greek koimeterion, a place of sleeping, awaiting the resurrection.
altar: The woman reached out to touch the hem of his cloak. At Holy Communion we are given far more: the Lord himself, Body and Blood, soul and divinity, comes into us. St Ignatius of Antioch called the Eucharist the medicine of immortality, the remedy against death. When we receive him with faith, the same power that went out from him in the crowd goes out to heal us.

Before receiving him we say: Lord, I am not worthy. And Jesus answers us as he answered the trembling woman: Daughter, son, go in peace. In the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, the Church continues to take the sick by the hand in his name, praying that the Lord will raise them up (James 5:14–15).
outline: Opening
Ask: what do you do when the news is bad and everyone says there is no point in praying any more?
Point 1 · God did not make death
God created us for incorruption; death is an intruder, and God is on the side of life.
Point 2 · The touch of faith
Many press against Jesus; one woman touches him with faith and is called Daughter.
Point 3 · Do not fear, only believe
Talitha cum: for Jesus, death is like sleep.
Point 4 · Rich, he became poor
The grace of Christ makes us generous: a fair balance in the Church.
Closing image
A small hand held in the hand of Jesus, and a father and mother watching their daughter stand up.
Take-home line
“Do not fear, only believe.”
live: Touch him with faith
At Communion today, do not simply go forward with the crowd. Make one act of faith as you receive: Lord, I believe you can heal me.
Visit the sick
This week visit or call someone who is ill, and if they are seriously ill, help them ask for the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick.
Pray for a family in grief
Name one family that has lost a child or a young person, and pray for them every day this week: Do not fear, only believe.
Give with grace
Give generously to the Peter's Pence collection or to a poor family, remembering that Christ became poor for you.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)
The crowd presses upon him, but faith touches him. Many throng around Christ in the Church; few touch him. Let us not only press against him, but touch him by believing.
St Ignatius of Antioch (Letter to the Ephesians 20, in substance)
We break one bread, which is the medicine of immortality, the antidote that keeps us from dying and makes us live for ever in Jesus Christ.
St Athanasius (On the Incarnation, in substance)
The Word, who could not die, took a body that could die, so that by offering it in death for all he might destroy death and raise us to incorruption.
magis: Catechism 413
“God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living”: death entered the world through the devil's envy and human sin.
Catechism 1006–1009
The meaning of death: a consequence of sin, transformed by Christ, who died and rose again.
Catechism 994
Jesus raised some of the dead, the daughter of Jairus among them, as signs of his own resurrection and ours.
Catechism 1503–1505
Christ the physician: the sick seek to touch him, and his compassion toward the sick is a sign that God has visited his people.
Catechism 2443–2446
Love for the poor: Christ, who became poor for us, will recognise his chosen ones by what they have done for the poor.
saints: St Cyril of Alexandria (omitted this year)

Bishop of Alexandria (d. 444) and doctor of the Church. At the Council of Ephesus (431) he defended the faith that Jesus is one Person, true God and true man, and that Mary is therefore truly Theotokos, Mother of God. His memorial, 27 June, gives way to the Sunday this year.
This week

28 Jun: St Irenaeus, bishop, martyr and doctor (memorial). 29 Jun: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles (solemnity). 30 Jun: the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church (optional memorial). 3 Jul: St Thomas the Apostle, the Apostle of India.
2027-06-27.prayer: O God, who through the grace of adoption chose us to be children of light, grant, we pray, that we may not be wrapped in the darkness of error but always be seen to stand in the bright light of truth. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you did not make death, and you came to destroy it. Take by the hand all who lie sick today, all children in danger, all parents waiting at a bedside. When the news is bad and others laugh at our hope, say to us: Do not fear, only believe. You became poor to make us rich; make us generous to the poor. And at the last, call us by name from the sleep of death: Little one, get up. Amen.

2027-06-29.title: Saints Peter and Paul, Apostles
readings: Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me
The angel of the Lord will rescue those who fear him
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith
You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church
2027-06-29.alt: Solemnity. Mass during the Day. Gloria and Creed. The Vigil Mass, with its own readings (Acts 3:1–10; Psalm 19; Galatians 1:11–20; John 21:15–19), was celebrated yesterday evening. In Rome the Holy Father blesses the pallia for the metropolitan archbishops appointed during the past year. A day to pray especially for Pope Leo XIV. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-06-29.verse: He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
theo: Today the Church honours together the two apostles on whom, under Christ, she was built: Peter the fisherman of Galilee, to whom Jesus gave the keys, and Paul the scholar of Tarsus, who carried the Gospel to the nations. They were very different men, and they once disagreed openly at Antioch (Galatians 2:11). But they confessed the same Lord, served the same Church, and according to the ancient tradition of the Church of Rome both gave their lives for Christ in that city under the emperor Nero, in the mid-60s of the first century: Peter crucified, tradition says head downwards, near the Vatican Hill, and Paul beheaded outside the walls on the road to Ostia. Their tombs have been venerated there ever since, and over them stand St Peter's Basilica and the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls. That is why they share one feast. The first reading shows Peter in chains. King Herod Agrippa I, wanting to win favour, has already “had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword,” the first of the Twelve to die for Christ, and now he arrests Peter during the Passover festival, guarded by “four squads of soldiers.” The future looks clear: Peter will be next. But Luke tells us what the Church was doing: “While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him.” And on the very night before his trial, Peter is “sleeping between two soldiers,” bound with two chains. He sleeps, because he has put his life in the Lord's hands. Then the cell fills with light; an angel taps him: “Get up quickly.” The chains fall off, the iron gate opens “of its own accord,” and Peter, who thought he was dreaming, finds himself in the street and says: “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me.” Peter's deliverance is also a picture of Easter: the night, the command to rise, the gate that opens. The Psalm is Peter's song: “I sought the LORD, and he answered me, and delivered me from all my fears,” and “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.”

The second reading is Paul's farewell. Writing from prison in Rome to his beloved Timothy, he knows that the end has come: “As for me, I am already being poured out as a libation, and the time of my departure has come.” A libation was wine poured out on the altar over a sacrifice; Paul sees his coming death as an offering poured out for Christ. Then he looks back over his life with three images, from the army, the stadium and the treasury: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” He does not boast; he gives thanks, and he waits for “the crown of righteousness” that the Lord will give “not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing.” He knows what it is to be abandoned by friends, but adds: “the Lord stood by me and gave me strength, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it.” Peter was rescued from prison; Paul says, “I was rescued from the lion's mouth,” and is sure that the Lord will rescue him “from every evil attack and save me for his heavenly kingdom.” For both apostles the final rescue was not escape from death but passage through death into the kingdom. Paul's last word is not about himself: “To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.”

The Gospel takes us north to Caesarea Philippi, a city built by Herod's son Philip near a great rock cliff with a shrine to the pagan god Pan. There, far from Jerusalem, among the gods of the nations, Jesus asks two questions. The first is easy: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” The disciples report the opinions: John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, a prophet. The second cannot be answered by reporting what others say: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon speaks for all: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.” Jesus calls him blessed, and tells him that this confession is not human cleverness: “flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.” Then Jesus gives him a new name and a mission. In Aramaic the word play is exact: “you are Kepha, and on this kepha I will build my church”: you are Rock, and on this rock. A rock is what does not move when the storm comes. Jesus promises that “the gates of Hades,” the power of death, “will not prevail against” his Church. And he gives Peter “the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” Every Jew knew the words of Isaiah about the chief steward of the king's house: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open, and no one shall shut” (Isaiah 22:22). The steward governs the household in the king's name. To “bind” and “loose” means to forbid and permit, to exclude and to reconcile, with authority that heaven confirms. The Catholic Church believes that this ministry of Peter did not end with Peter, because the Church still needs a rock and a steward until the Lord returns. The Bishop of Rome, the successor of Peter, is “the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful” (Lumen Gentium 23; Catechism 882). And Peter's weakness did not cancel his mission: the same man would deny Jesus three times, and be asked three times by the risen Lord, “Do you love me?” and told, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17). The Church is founded not on Peter's strength, but on Christ's prayer for him: “I have prayed for you that your own faith may not fail; and you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Today we thank God for Peter and Paul, for the faith we received through them, and for Pope Leo XIV, who sits today in Peter's chair.
conn: Caesarea Philippi.

A city at the foot of Mount Hermon, at the sources of the Jordan, rebuilt by Herod's son Philip and named after Caesar. A rock cliff there held a shrine to the god Pan. Jesus asks his question among the gods of the nations.
“Son of the living God.”
Peter's confession goes beyond calling Jesus the Messiah: he is the Son of the living God. The Catechism sees here the faith on which the Church is built (Catechism 424, 442).
Peter, Kepha.
Jesus gives Simon the name Kepha, Aramaic for “rock,” translated into Greek as Petros (John 1:42). Paul usually calls him Cephas (Galatians 1:18).
“My church.”
The Greek ekklesia translates the Hebrew qahal, the assembly of God's people at Sinai. Jesus speaks of “my” Church: he builds it, and it belongs to him.
“The gates of Hades.”
Hades is the realm of the dead; its “gates” are the power of death. Christ promises that death will not overcome his Church.
The keys.
Isaiah 22:22: the master of the palace receives the key of the house of David. Keys mean authority to govern the house in the king's name (Catechism 553).
“Bind and loose.”

Rabbinic terms for forbidding and permitting, and for excluding from and readmitting to the community. Peter receives this authority personally; the apostles share it with him (Matthew 18:18; Catechism 553, 1444).
Herod Agrippa I.
Grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea from AD 41 to 44. He executed James, son of Zebedee, around AD 44 (Acts 12:2).
“Poured out as a libation.”
A drink offering poured over a sacrifice (Numbers 28:7). Paul uses the same image in Philippians 2:17.
The pallium.

A narrow band of white wool marked with black crosses, worn over the shoulders by the Pope and by metropolitan archbishops as a sign of their communion with the successor of Peter and of the shepherd who carries the sheep. The pallia are blessed by the Pope on this solemnity.
altar: At every Mass we pray by name for our Pope and our bishop. This is not a formality: the Eucharist is the sacrament of the Church's unity, and the communion of each altar with the bishop, and of every bishop with the successor of Peter, is the sign that we share the one faith of the apostles. Peter and Paul are named in the Roman Canon among the apostles whose merits and prayers we ask.

Paul spoke of his life as poured out like a libation over the sacrifice. At the altar the one sacrifice of Christ is made present, and our lives, like those of the apostles, are poured out with his. Peter, who was told to feed the Lord's sheep, fed them with the Word and with the Bread of Life; that same food is given to us today.
outline: Opening
Ask: if Jesus turned to you today and asked, “But who do you say that I am?”, what would you answer, not from a book but from your heart?
Point 1 · Who do you say that I am?
Peter's confession, revealed by the Father, is the faith of the Church.
Point 2 · On this rock, the keys
Christ builds his Church on Peter and gives him the keys: the ministry of the successor of Peter today.
Point 3 · The Church prayed fervently
Peter in chains, the praying Church, and the angel who opens the gate.
Point 4 · I have kept the faith
Paul's farewell: a life poured out, a race finished, a crown waiting.
Closing image
Two tombs in Rome, a fisherman's and a tentmaker's, with great basilicas built over them, and pilgrims from every nation praying the same Creed.
Take-home line
“You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
live: Pray for the Pope
Pray today, and every day this week, for Pope Leo XIV: an Our Father, a Hail Mary and a Glory Be, or the prayer: Lord, guard him, give him life, make him blessed on earth.
Answer the question
Write down in one sentence your own answer to Jesus' question: Who do you say that I am? Keep it in your Bible.
Keep the faith
Name one area where you are tempted to give up, in prayer, in marriage, in work, in the fight against a sin, and ask St Paul's help to finish the race.
Learn the faith of the apostles
Read slowly this week the Apostles' Creed, one article each day, and ask what each article means for your life.
fathers: St Augustine (Sermon on the feast, in substance)

One day is kept for the passion of two apostles, but these two were one. Though they suffered on different days, they were one. Peter went first, Paul followed. Let us keep this feast, made holy for us by the blood of the apostles; let us love their faith, their life, their labours, their sufferings.
St Leo the Great (Sermon 82, in substance)
These are the men through whom the light of Christ's Gospel shone on you, O Rome. They are your holy fathers and true shepherds, who founded you far better than those who built your walls.
St Ambrose (in substance)
Where Peter is, there is the Church; where the Church is, there death is not, but life eternal.
magis: Catechism 552–553
Peter's confession and the keys of the kingdom: the authority to govern the house of God, to bind and to loose.
Catechism 881–882
The Lord made Simon alone the rock of his Church; the Roman Pontiff, as successor of Peter, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of unity.
Lumen Gentium 18 and 22
Vatican II: Christ set Peter over the other apostles; the college of bishops has authority only together with its head, the Roman Pontiff.
Catechism 765
The Lord gave his Church a structure that will remain until the Kingdom is fully achieved: the Twelve with Peter as their head.
Catechism 1444
In giving Peter the power to bind and loose, Christ gave the apostles' ministry the authority to reconcile sinners with the Church.
saints: Sts Peter and Paul in history

Simon Peter, a fisherman of Bethsaida and Capernaum, head of the Twelve, preached in Jerusalem, Antioch and Rome; his two letters are in the New Testament. Paul, a Pharisee of Tarsus, converted on the road to Damascus, made at least three great missionary journeys and wrote letters that form much of the New Testament. Both were martyred in Rome under Nero (c. 64–67). The Church of Rome has kept their feast together on 29 June since ancient times; it already appears in a Roman calendar of the year 354.
This week
30 Jun: the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church (optional memorial), the Christians killed in Nero's persecution. 3 Jul: St Thomas the Apostle, the Apostle of India.
2027-06-29.prayer: O God, who on the Solemnity of the Apostles Peter and Paul give us the noble and holy joys of this day, grant, we pray, that your Church may in all things follow the teaching of those through whom she received the beginnings of right religion. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you asked your disciples: Who do you say that I am? With Peter we answer: you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Keep your Church built on the rock, and let the gates of Hades never prevail against her. Strengthen Pope Leo XIV, the successor of Peter, and all the bishops in communion with him. Give us Paul's courage to fight the good fight, finish the race and keep the faith, and bring us at last, with your apostles, to your heavenly kingdom. Amen.

2027-06-13.title: Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time
readings: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar … and become a noble cedar
Lord, it is good to give thanks to you
We walk by faith, not by sight
It is like a mustard seed, the smallest of all the seeds on earth
2027-06-13.alt: Year B. Gloria and Creed. The Sundays after Pentecost and Corpus Christi resume the green Sundays of Ordinary Time. St Antony of Padua (13 June) falls on the Sunday this year and is not celebrated at Mass, though popular devotions to him may still be held outside Mass. The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary 92:2–3, 13–14, 15–16 = NRSV 92:1–2, 12–13, 14–15). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-13.verse: The kingdom of God is as if someone would scatter seed on the ground, and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.
theo: The green Sundays have returned. After the great feasts of Easter, Pentecost, the Trinity and Corpus Christi, the Church puts on the colour of growing things, and today's readings are almost all about growth: a sprig of cedar, a palm tree, seed scattered on the ground, a mustard bush full of birds. The first reading comes from Ezekiel, a priest who was taken to Babylon with the first exiles in 597 before Christ. In chapter 17 he tells a riddle about two great eagles and a cedar of Lebanon: the kings of the nations break off the top of Israel's royal tree and carry it away. The house of David looks finished. Then God himself speaks: “Thus says the Lord God: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar; I will set it out. I will break off a tender one from the topmost of its young twigs; I myself will plant it on a high and lofty mountain.” Notice the word “I myself,” repeated. What the great powers could only break, God alone can plant. And the tender sprig will become something no one expected: “On the mountain height of Israel I will plant it, in order that it may produce boughs and bear fruit, and become a noble cedar. Under it every kind of bird will live; in the shade of its branches will nest winged creatures of every kind.” Then comes the law of God's way of working: “I bring low the high tree, I make high the low tree; I dry up the green tree and make the dry tree flourish. I the Lord have spoken; I will accomplish it.” The Church has always heard in this tender shoot a promise of the Messiah from David's line, and in the birds of every kind the nations who will find shelter in his kingdom.

The Psalm takes up the same picture and gives it to every faithful person: “The righteous flourish like the palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the Lord; they flourish in the courts of our God. In old age they still produce fruit; they are always green and full of sap.” Here is a beautiful promise for the elderly in our parishes: age is not the end of fruitfulness. The grandmother who prays the rosary for her scattered children, the old man who still comes to the first Mass every morning, are “always green.” And the Psalm begins where all growth must begin, with thanksgiving: “It is good to give thanks to the Lord, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night.”

St Paul, in the Second Letter to the Corinthians, speaks of a growth we cannot see: the hidden ripening of our lives towards God. “So we are always confident; even though we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.” Paul does not despise this life in the body, but he knows it is not the whole story: “we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.” So whatever happens, near or far, “we make it our aim to please him.” And then a sober line: “For all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive recompense for what has been done in the body, whether good or evil.” A seed is judged by its harvest. What we sow in the body, in our families, our work and our prayer, will one day be gathered in.

In the Gospel Jesus tells two short parables, found together only in Mark. The first is the seed that grows by itself: a farmer scatters seed, “and would sleep and rise night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how. The earth produces of itself, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head.” The farmer does his part: he sows, and at harvest he goes in “with his sickle.” But the growing is not his work. Every farmer in Kerala who has sown paddy with the first monsoon rains knows this patience: you cannot pull the shoots up to make them grow faster. The kingdom of God works like that in a parish, in a family, in a soul: quietly, by night as well as by day, by a power that is not ours. The second parable is the mustard seed, “the smallest of all the seeds on earth,” which grows into “the greatest of all shrubs, and puts forth large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” Jesus is echoing Ezekiel's cedar, but he chooses a humble garden plant instead of a mighty tree. The kingdom begins small: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve fishermen and tax collectors, a few women who followed him, a handful of bread on an altar. Mark adds that Jesus spoke “the word to them, as they were able to hear it,” and explained everything in private to his disciples. God does not force growth; he sows, waits and explains, patiently, as we are able to hear.
conn: Ezekiel 17.

The chapter is an allegory. The first “great eagle” is Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who in 597 before Christ took King Jehoiachin, “the top of the cedar,” into exile (17:3–4, 12); the second eagle is Egypt, to which King Zedekiah turned for help. The closing oracle (17:22–24) moves from politics to promise: God himself will replant the royal line.
The cedar of Lebanon.

The great cedars of the Lebanon mountains were the finest timber of the ancient world; Solomon used them for the Temple (1 Kings 5:6). In the prophets the cedar is an image of kings and empires, sometimes proud and cut down (Isaiah 2:13), sometimes, as here, a sign of God's own planting.
Birds in the branches.

In the Old Testament a great tree sheltering birds is a picture of a kingdom that gives shelter to the nations: Ezekiel 31:6 (“All the birds of the air made their nests in its boughs”) and Daniel 4:12 use the same image. When Jesus says the birds nest in the shade of the mustard plant, his hearers would have caught the echo: the nations will find a home in God's kingdom.
The mustard seed.

The black mustard that grows around the Lake of Galilee has a tiny seed, about one millimetre across, yet in a season the plant can grow taller than a man. In Jewish speech “small as a mustard seed” was a proverb for the very smallest thing.
“Of itself.”

Mark 4:28 uses the Greek word automatē, from which our word “automatic” comes. It does not mean that the kingdom grows without God; it means that it grows without the farmer's control. The power of growth is in the seed and the soil God has made.
The sickle.

“At once he goes in with his sickle, because the harvest has come” (Mark 4:29) recalls Joel 3:13: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.” In the prophets the harvest is an image of God's final judgment, which Paul also names in today's second reading.
Mark 4.

This chapter is Mark's collection of parables: the sower (4:1–20), the lamp (4:21–25), the seed growing secretly (4:26–29, found only in Mark) and the mustard seed (4:30–32). It ends with the storm on the lake (4:35–41), next Sunday's Gospel.
The judgment seat.

Paul's word in 2 Corinthians 5:10 is bēma, the raised platform from which a magistrate gave judgment. The Corinthians knew one well: in the forum of their own city Paul had stood before the bēma of the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12).
St Antony of Padua.

Born in Lisbon about 1195, he became a Franciscan after seeing the bodies of the first Franciscan martyrs brought back from Morocco. A great preacher, he died near Padua on 13 June 1231 and was canonised within a year; Pope Pius XII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1946.
altar: At the presentation of the gifts the priest says over the bread: “Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation, for through your goodness we have received the bread we offer you: fruit of the earth and work of human hands.” The grain that grew “he does not know how” is laid on the altar. By the power of the Holy Spirit and the words of Christ it becomes truly the Body of Christ, the seed of eternal life planted in us.

The Eucharist is the mustard seed of the kingdom: a small piece of bread, a little wine, and yet the whole Christ, Body, Blood, soul and divinity, under these humble signs. From this small beginning the Church grows, and under its shade the nations find their home.
outline: Opening
Hold up a mustard seed, or any small seed, and ask: how much of a tree can you see in this?
Point 1 · I myself will plant it
God replants the broken cedar of David; what the powers break, God alone can plant.
Point 2 · He does not know how
The seed grows by itself, night and day; our part is to sow and wait.
Point 3 · The smallest of all the seeds
The kingdom begins small and gives shelter to all.
Point 4 · We walk by faith
Growth we cannot see, and a harvest before the judgment seat of Christ.
Closing image
A farmer in the monsoon rain, sowing and then going home to sleep, trusting the earth and the sky.
Take-home line
“The seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how.”
live: Sow one seed
This week say one word of faith, one kind word, or one invitation to prayer, and leave the growth to God.
Trust the slow growth
Name a person you have prayed for a long time without seeing change. Keep praying, and thank God for the growth you cannot see.
Honour the elderly
Visit or call an elderly person this week: “in old age they still produce fruit.” Ask them to pray for you.
Examine your sowing
Each night this week ask: what did I sow today in my family, my work and my prayer?
fathers: St Ambrose (in substance)

Christ himself is the mustard seed. He seemed small and despised when he was buried in the earth like a grain; but when he rose he grew into a tree whose branches cover the world, and the souls of the faithful rest in his shade like birds (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke, Book 7).
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

With the mustard seed the Lord encouraged his disciples. They were few and poor and weak; he showed them that the preaching would spread over the whole earth, and that what began in a few would grow beyond all expectation (Homilies on Matthew, 46).
St Gregory the Great (in substance)

A man casts seed on the ground when he places a good intention in his heart; he sleeps when he rests in the hope that comes from a good work; he rises night and day as he advances through good times and bad. The seed sprouts and grows while he does not know how, for even when he cannot measure his growth, the virtue once conceived goes on to maturity (Homilies on Ezekiel, Book 2, Homily 3).
St Augustine (in substance)

Let us sing here in hope, so that we may sing there in possession. Here we walk by faith, there we shall see; sing now as travellers sing, to lighten the toil, and keep walking (Sermon 256, on the Alleluia).
magis: Lumen Gentium 5

The Word of the Lord is compared to a seed sown in a field; those who hear it with faith and are numbered among the little flock of Christ have received the kingdom itself. Then, by its own power, the seed sprouts and grows until the harvest. The Church is on earth the seed and the beginning of that kingdom.
Catechism 546

Jesus' invitation to enter his kingdom comes in the form of parables, a characteristic feature of his teaching. Through them he calls people to the feast of the kingdom, but also asks for a radical choice: words are not enough, deeds are required.
Catechism 1021–1022

Death puts an end to human life as the time open to accepting or rejecting the grace of God manifested in Christ. Each person receives an eternal retribution in his immortal soul at the very moment of death, in a particular judgment that refers his life to Christ.
Benedict XVI, Angelus, 17 June 2012 (in substance)

Commenting on these two parables, the Pope said that the kingdom of God, though it requires our cooperation, is first of all the gift of the Lord. Our small work, which seems so little before the problems of the world, when placed in God's hands does not fear difficulties: the victory of the Lord is certain.
saints: St Antony of Padua

Today is the feast day of St Antony, so dear to Catholics all over India, but this year it falls on a Sunday and gives way to the Lord's Day. The Tuesday devotions, the novenas of the thirteen Tuesdays and St Antony's bread for the poor may go on as usual, outside the Mass.
This week
14–18 June: weekdays of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time (no memorials in the General Calendar). 19 June: St Romuald, abbot (optional). Next Sunday, 20 June: the Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-13.prayer: Lord God, you take the tender sprig and plant it on the mountain, you bring low the high tree and make the low tree flourish. We thank you for the seed of your word sown in our hearts, and for the growth you give by night and by day, when we do not know how. Lord Jesus, your kingdom is like a mustard seed: make our small faith grow, so that our families and our parish may be a shelter for the poor, the lonely and the stranger. Holy Spirit, keep us green and full of sap even in old age, and help us to walk by faith, not by sight, making it our aim to please you, until we stand before the judgment seat of Christ and are gathered into the harvest of your kingdom. Mary, Mother of the Church, who kept the seed of the Word in your heart, pray for us. Amen.

2027-06-01.title: Saint Justin, Martyr
readings: Where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds?
Their hearts are firm, secure in the Lord
Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's
2027-06-01.alt: Memorial. Tuesday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I). The weekday readings are given here; the proper readings of the memorial, 1 Corinthians 1:18–25 (“we proclaim Christ crucified”) and Matthew 5:13–19 (“You are the light of the world”), may be used instead. St Justin, philosopher and martyr, was beheaded in Rome about the year 165. June, the month of the Sacred Heart, begins today. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-06-01.verse: Jesus said to them, “Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's.” And they were utterly amazed at him.
theo: For the first days of June the Church reads the Book of Tobit, a family story told among the Jews scattered in exile. Tobit is a good man living in Nineveh, far from Jerusalem. He gives alms, shares his bread with the hungry and, at the risk of his life, buries the bodies of fellow Israelites left in the street. Today's passage begins after one such burial. Tobit sleeps outside by the courtyard wall, and a stupid accident changes his life: “I did not know that there were sparrows on the wall; their fresh droppings fell into my eyes and produced white films.” The physicians only make it worse, “until I became completely blind.” A rich man becomes a dependent. His wife Anna goes out to work: “my wife Anna earned money at women's work.” One day her employers pay her wages and add a young goat as a gift. Tobit hears it bleat and suspects the worst: “Where did you get this goat? It is surely not stolen, is it? Return it to the owners.” He will not believe her. And Anna, hurt, answers with words that cut deep: “Where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds? These things are known about you!” It is a painfully honest scene. A good man, humiliated by blindness and dependence, becomes suspicious and hard at home. His goodness in the street has not yet reached his own courtyard. The book does not hide this; it lets us see a holy man in his weakness, so that we may see how God will heal him. The Psalm describes the just man as Tobit wanted to be and will become again: “Happy are those who fear the Lord, who greatly delight in his commandments … They are not afraid of evil tidings; their hearts are firm, secure in the Lord.”

In the Gospel the enemies of Jesus come with a trap wrapped in flattery. Pharisees and Herodians, who normally disliked each other, unite: “Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and show deference to no one … Is it lawful to pay taxes to the emperor, or not?” If Jesus says yes, he betrays the people who hate the Roman tax; if he says no, he is a rebel against Rome. Jesus asks for a coin. “Whose head is this, and whose title?” “The emperor's.” Then comes the answer that has echoed through history: “Give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's.” The coin bears the image of Caesar, so it may go back to Caesar. But the human person bears the image of God (Genesis 1:27), so the whole person belongs to God. Caesar may have taxes; he may not have our worship. St Justin, whom we remember today, lived this answer to the end. Born of pagan parents at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, he searched for truth among the philosophers, until an old man showed him the prophets and Christ. He wrote to the emperor Antoninus Pius that Christians pay their taxes more readily than anyone, because Christ taught them to give to Caesar what is Caesar's, but that they worship God alone (First Apology 17, in substance). When the prefect Rusticus ordered him to sacrifice to the gods, he refused, and was beheaded with six companions. He gave Caesar his obedience in all things lawful, and gave God his life.
outline: Opening
Hold up a coin and ask: whose picture is on this? Then ask: whose picture is on you?
Point 1 · A good man in the dark
Tobit's blindness and his harsh suspicion at home.
Point 2 · The coin and the image
Caesar's image on the coin, God's image on the person.
Point 3 · St Justin, philosopher and martyr
He gave Caesar his taxes and God his whole life.
Take-home line
“Give … to God the things that are God's.”
live: Goodness at home (Tobit 2:14)
Ask yourself honestly whether the people at home see the same kindness that others see in you outside. Do one act of trust and kindness at home today.
Give God what bears his image (Mark 12:17)
Pay what you owe honestly, and then offer God the first minutes of your day in prayer, because you belong to him.
saints: St Justin (c. 100–c. 165)

Born of pagan parents at Flavia Neapolis (Nablus) in Samaria, he studied with Stoic, Peripatetic, Pythagorean and Platonist teachers in search of God. By his own account, an old man he met by the sea told him of the prophets, and “a fire was kindled” in his soul; he became a Christian about 130. Keeping the philosopher's cloak, he taught in Ephesus and Rome. His First Apology, addressed to the emperor Antoninus Pius, gives the earliest full description of the Sunday Eucharist (chapters 65–67); his Dialogue with Trypho is a respectful debate with a Jewish teacher about the Scriptures. He taught that “seeds of the Word” are scattered in all that is true. About 165, under the prefect Junius Rusticus, he and six companions refused to sacrifice to the gods and were beheaded. The Acts of their martyrdom survive. He is the patron of philosophers.
2027-06-01.prayer: O God, who through the folly of the Cross wondrously taught Saint Justin the Martyr the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ, grant us, through his intercession, that, having rejected deception, we may become steadfast in the faith. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Lord, we bear your image; take our whole selves, our minds, our work and our homes. Heal what is blind and hard in us, as you healed Tobit, and make our hearts firm and secure in you. Amen.
altar: St Justin wrote down, about the year 155, what Christians did on Sunday: the reading of the apostles and prophets, the homily, the prayers of the faithful, the bringing of bread and wine, the great thanksgiving to which all answer Amen, and Communion, which he says is not common bread but the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus. Eighteen centuries later the shape of our Mass is the same. At this altar we give to God what is God's: ourselves, offered with Christ.

2027-06-02.title: Wednesday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time · Sts Marcellinus and Peter
readings: At that very moment, the prayers of both of them were heard in the glorious presence of God
To you, O Lord, I lift up my soul
He is God not of the dead, but of the living
2027-06-02.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 9 (Year I). Optional memorial of Sts Marcellinus and Peter, martyrs of Rome under Diocletian (c. 304), whose names are said in the Roman Canon. Liturgical colour: green (red if the memorial is kept).
2027-06-02.verse: He is God not of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong.
theo: Yesterday we left Tobit blind and quarrelling with his wife. Today the Book of Tobit shows us two people, far apart, reaching the bottom on the same day. First Tobit: “with much grief and anguish of heart I wept, and with groaning began to pray.” His prayer begins with praise, not complaint: “You are righteous, O Lord, and all your deeds are just; all your ways are mercy and truth.” He confesses his sins and the sins of his people, and then asks something frightening: “command my spirit to be taken from me … For it is better for me to die than to live, because I have had to listen to undeserved insults.” Then the scene moves hundreds of kilometres east, to Ecbatana in Media, where a young woman named Sarah has been married seven times, and each husband died on the wedding night, killed by the demon Asmodeus. A maid taunts her cruelly: “You are the one who kills your husbands!” Sarah goes up to her father's upper room meaning to hang herself. But she thinks of her father: people would mock him, saying his only beloved daughter hanged herself. So instead she prays, “with hands outstretched toward the window”: “Blessed are you, merciful God! Blessed is your name forever.” Two broken people, two honest prayers, both asking to die. And then the most beautiful sentence of the chapter: “At that very moment, the prayers of both of them were heard in the glorious presence of God. So Raphael was sent to heal both of them.” God does not give them what they asked; he gives them what they needed. The answer to both prayers is already on its way, and it will bring the two of them together. The Psalm is their prayer and ours: “To you, O Lord, I lift up my soul … Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths.”

In the Gospel, curiously, we meet another woman with seven husbands. The Sadducees, priestly aristocrats who accepted only the books of Moses and denied the resurrection, bring Jesus a case designed to make the resurrection look absurd: seven brothers marry the same woman one after another, each dying without children. “In the resurrection whose wife will she be?” Jesus answers in two steps. First, they misunderstand the life to come: “when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.” Risen life is not this life continued with the same arrangements; it is transformed. Second, they misread their own Scriptures. At the burning bush God said to Moses, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:6), not “I was.” Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were long dead in Moses' time, yet God still calls himself their God. And God does not bind himself in covenant to corpses: “He is God not of the dead, but of the living; you are quite wrong.” The faithfulness of God is stronger than death. Tobit and Sarah asked to die; God answered with life. Sts Marcellinus and Peter, a priest and an exorcist of Rome, were beheaded under Diocletian about 304, in a wood outside the city. Their executioner, who later became a Christian, told the story to a boy who grew up to be Pope Damasus, and he wrote their epitaph. Their names are still read in the first Eucharistic Prayer, because the God of the living keeps them alive.
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever prayed a prayer that you are now glad God did not answer the way you asked?
Point 1 · Two prayers from the bottom
Tobit in Nineveh and Sarah in Ecbatana pray on the same day.
Point 2 · Heard at that very moment
God sends Raphael to heal both, and gives life where they asked for death.
Point 3 · The God of the living
Jesus answers the Sadducees: God is faithful beyond the grave.
Take-home line
“He is God not of the dead, but of the living.”
live: Pray honestly (Tobit 3:1–2)
When you are low, do not stop praying. Begin with praise, as Tobit did, then tell God the truth about how you feel.
Remember our dead, alive to God (Mark 12:27)
Pray today for one person of your family who has died, by name, believing that God is their God still.
saints: Sts Marcellinus and Peter (d. c. 304)

Marcellinus, a priest, and Peter, an exorcist, served the Church of Rome during the persecution of Diocletian. Tradition says they were imprisoned, continued to strengthen the faith of their fellow prisoners, and were beheaded in a wood outside Rome. Pope Damasus (366–384) wrote that as a boy he had heard the story from their executioner himself, and he composed their epitaph. They were buried in the catacomb on the Via Labicana, where Constantine later built a basilica. Their names are said in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I).
2027-06-02.prayer: Lord God, you hear the prayer of the broken-hearted at the very moment they pray. To you we lift up our souls: make us know your ways and teach us your paths. When we are tempted to despair, send us your help as you sent Raphael to Tobit and Sarah. You are the God of the living; keep in your life all our beloved dead, and through the prayers of Sts Marcellinus and Peter make us faithful witnesses to the resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: In the Roman Canon, after the consecration, the priest names Marcellinus and Peter among the martyrs with whom we ask a share in heaven. At every Mass the Church on earth prays with the Church in heaven, because the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is the God of the living. The Bread of Life we receive is the pledge of our own resurrection.

2027-06-03.title: Saints Charles Lwanga and Companions, Martyrs
readings: Grant that she and I may find mercy and that we may grow old together
Happy is everyone who fears the Lord, who walks in his ways
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart … You shall love your neighbor as yourself
2027-06-03.alt: Memorial. Thursday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I). The weekday readings are given here (first reading in NRSV numbering); the proper readings of the memorial, 2 Maccabees 7:1–2, 9–14 (the seven brothers) and Matthew 5:1–12a (the Beatitudes), may be used instead. St Charles Lwanga and twenty-one companions, the Catholic martyrs of Uganda, died between 1885 and 1887, most of them burned at Namugongo on 3 June 1886. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-06-03.verse: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.
theo: The Book of Tobit now reaches its love story. Young Tobias has set out on a long journey for his blind father, with a companion who calls himself Azariah but is really the angel Raphael. As they approach Ecbatana, Raphael tells him about Sarah, the daughter of their kinsman Raguel: “the girl is sensible, brave, and very beautiful, and her father is a good man.” Tobias is afraid, and with reason: seven husbands have died on their wedding night. But Raphael says: “Do not be afraid, for she was set apart for you before the world was made.” At Raguel's house there are tears of recognition and a warm welcome. Raguel is honest about the danger, yet he gives his daughter in marriage with a blessing: “May the Lord of heaven, my child, guide and prosper you both this night and grant you mercy and peace.” A marriage contract is written. Then comes the wedding night. Before anything else, Tobias rises and says to Sarah: “Sister, get up, and let us pray and implore our Lord that he grant us mercy and safety.” Their prayer is one of the most beautiful in the Bible on marriage. It begins with praise: “Blessed are you, O God of our ancestors, and blessed is your name in all generations forever.” It remembers creation: “You made Adam, and for him you made his wife Eve as a helper and support.” And it offers an honest heart: “I now am taking this kinswoman of mine, not because of lust, but with sincerity. Grant that she and I may find mercy and that we may grow old together.” And together they say: “Amen, Amen.” A marriage that begins on its knees is protected from evil.
