The Psalm blesses such a home: “Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table.”

In the Gospel a scribe, impressed by Jesus' answers, asks a sincere question: “Which commandment is the first of all?” Jesus answers with the Shema, the prayer every devout Jew says morning and evening: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.” And he joins to it a second commandment from Leviticus 19:18: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” The scribe agrees warmly and adds that this love is “much more important than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” Jesus looks at him and says: “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” Here a Jewish teacher and Jesus stand together on the foundation of Israel's faith, the love of the one God and of neighbour. Tobias and Sarah lived this double love on their wedding night: love of God first, in prayer, and then a love for each other that is sincere and pure. The martyrs of Uganda lived it to the point of fire. Charles Lwanga, head of the royal pages at the court of Kabaka Mwanga II, protected the boys in his care from the king's sinful demands and taught them the faith. When the persecution broke out, he baptised several catechumens the night before their arrest. On 3 June 1886, at Namugongo, he and many companions were burned alive, praying for their persecutors. Charles is said to have told the executioner that it was as if he were pouring water on him. Some of the pages were barely fourteen. With them died Anglican Christians too, witnesses to the same Lord. St Paul VI canonised the twenty-two Catholic martyrs in 1964, and today the Church of Africa, rich in faith, is their harvest.
outline: Opening
Ask: what was the first thing you did together on the most important day of your life?
Point 1 · A marriage that begins on its knees
Tobias and Sarah pray before anything else.
Point 2 · Not because of lust, but with sincerity
Pure love that wants to grow old together.
Point 3 · The first commandment
Love God with all you are, and your neighbour as yourself.
Point 4 · The martyrs of Uganda
Young men who loved God more than life, and kept their purity.
Take-home line
“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.”
live: Pray together (Tobit 8:4–5)
If you are married, pray one short prayer with your spouse tonight; if you are not, pray tonight for one married couple you know.
Love with your whole self (Mark 12:30)
Choose one area, heart, soul, mind or strength, that you give God least, and offer it to him today.
saints: St Charles Lwanga and companions (d. 1885–1887)

The Missionaries of Africa (White Fathers) reached the Kingdom of Buganda in 1879, and the faith spread quickly among young men at the royal court. Kabaka Mwanga II turned against the Christians, angered by their refusal of his immoral demands and by their loyalty to Christ above the king. Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe, who had rebuked the king, was beheaded on 15 November 1885. Charles Lwanga, who succeeded him as head of the royal pages, protected the boys and instructed them; on the night before their arrest in May 1886 he baptised several of them. On 3 June 1886 (Ascension Day) Charles and many others were burned alive at Namugongo. Twenty-two Catholic martyrs, the youngest, Kizito, about fourteen, were beatified in 1920 and canonised by St Paul VI on 18 October 1964. Anglican Christians also died in the same persecution. Namugongo is today a great place of pilgrimage on 3 June.
2027-06-03.prayer: O God, who have made the blood of martyrs the seed of Christians, mercifully grant that the field which is your Church, watered by the blood shed by Saints Charles Lwanga and his companions, may be fertile and always yield you an abundant harvest. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Lord, bless all married couples with the prayer of Tobias and Sarah, give our young people pure and brave hearts, and teach us to love you with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Amen.
altar: The scribe said that love of God and neighbour is worth more than all burnt offerings and sacrifices. At this altar we offer the one sacrifice that is pure love: Christ, who loved the Father with all his heart and loved us to the end. The martyrs of Uganda joined their lives to that offering. When we receive him, we receive the strength to love as he loved.

2027-06-04.title: The Most Sacred Heart of Jesus
readings: My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender
With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation
to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge
one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out
2027-06-04.alt: Solemnity. Year B. Friday after the Second Sunday after Pentecost (in India, the Friday after Corpus Christi). Gloria and Creed. It is the World Day of Prayer for the Sanctification of Priests, and the First Friday of June, the month of the Sacred Heart. Because it is a solemnity, the Friday abstinence does not apply today. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-06-04.verse: Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.
theo: Today the Church contemplates the love of God made visible in a human heart: the Heart of Jesus, pierced on the Cross. The readings of Year B begin not on Calvary but in the house of a father. Through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century before Christ, God speaks of Israel as a little child: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.” Then come some of the most tender words in the Old Testament: “Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk, I took them up in my arms; but they did not know that I healed them. I led them with cords of human kindness, with bands of love. I was to them like those who lift infants to their cheeks. I bent down to them and fed them.” God is pictured as a parent stooping to a toddler, holding its hands as it learns to walk, lifting it to his cheek. The child grows up and walks away to other gods. Justice would demand punishment. But God's heart does something unexpected: “My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my fierce anger … for I am God and no mortal, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not come in wrath.” The Hebrew says that God's heart is overturned within him, the same word used for the overthrow of Sodom. God's anger is overthrown by his own mercy. God is holy precisely because he does not react like a wounded human being. The responsorial song is from Isaiah: “Surely God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid … With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.” In Latin that verse begins Haurietis aquas, and Pope Pius XII took it as the title of his great encyclical on the Sacred Heart in 1956.

St Paul, in prison, writes to the Ephesians in amazement at his own vocation: “Although I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given to me to bring to the Gentiles the news of the boundless riches of Christ.” The plan of God, hidden for ages, is now revealed: all peoples are called into one Church. Then Paul kneels: “For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth takes its name.” His prayer for the Christians of Ephesus is a prayer for us on this feast: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love. I pray that you may have the power to comprehend, with all the saints, what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.” The love of Christ has dimensions. Christians have long seen in them the shape of the Cross: its arms stretched wide to embrace all, its beam reaching down to the lowest and up to heaven. We can never measure that love, but we can know it, the way a child knows its mother's love, by being held in it.

The Gospel takes us to Golgotha on the afternoon of Good Friday. It is the day of Preparation before a great sabbath, and the Law of Moses did not allow a body to remain hanging overnight (Deuteronomy 21:23), so the authorities ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken to hasten their death. The soldiers break the legs of the two others, “But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out.” John, the beloved disciple who stood beneath the Cross with the Mother of Jesus, solemnly insists: “He who saw this has testified so that you also may believe.” He sees two Scriptures fulfilled. “None of his bones shall be broken”: Jesus is the true Passover lamb, whose bones were not to be broken (Exodus 12:46), dying at the hour when the lambs were slaughtered in the Temple. “They will look on the one whom they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10): the whole world will look at this wound and be drawn to repentance and love. From the opened side flow blood and water. The Fathers saw in them the sacraments of the Church, the water of Baptism and the blood of the Eucharist, and they saw the Church herself born from the side of the new Adam, as Eve was formed from the side of the first Adam while he slept (Catechism 766). This is the Sacred Heart: not a sentimental picture, but the physical heart of the incarnate Son, pierced for us, the sign and the source of the love that Hosea foretold. Jesus said, “learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11:29). In the visions given to St Margaret Mary Alacoque at Paray-le-Monial (1673–1675), he showed his Heart burning with love and asked for reparation, Holy Communion on the First Fridays, and this feast. Today the Church kneels, as Paul knelt, before the Father, and looks on the one whom we have pierced.
conn: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”
Hosea 11:1 speaks of Israel; Matthew 2:15 sees it fulfilled in the child Jesus returning from Egypt. The Son in whom Israel's story is fulfilled is the one whose Heart we honour today.
“Cords of human kindness.”
God does not drag his people with ropes like oxen but leads them “with bands of love” (Hosea 11:4). Love, not force, is God's way of drawing us.
“My heart recoils within me.”
The Hebrew word for God's heart being overturned is the one used for the overthrow of the cities of the plain (Genesis 19:25). In God, mercy overturns anger.
“The wells of salvation.”

Isaiah 12:3 in Latin reads Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris; Pius XII named his 1956 encyclical on the Sacred Heart from these words. Jesus invites the thirsty to come to him and drink (John 7:37).
“Every family … takes its name.”
In Greek “Father” is pater and “family” is patria: every family on earth reflects the fatherhood of God (Ephesians 3:15).
Breadth, length, height and depth.
Paul's four dimensions of the love of Christ (Ephesians 3:18) have often been read as the shape of the Cross, which embraces the whole world.
“None of his bones shall be broken.”
The law of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12). John presents Jesus as the true Lamb, dying at the hour of the Passover sacrifice.
“They will look on the one whom they have pierced.”
Zechariah 12:10, where God promises a spirit of compassion and supplication, so that people mourn over the pierced one as over an only child.
Blood and water.
The Fathers saw in them Baptism and the Eucharist, and the Church born from the side of Christ as Eve from the side of Adam (Catechism 766, 1225).
The feast.

St John Eudes celebrated a liturgical feast of the Heart of Jesus in 1672. After the revelations to St Margaret Mary, Blessed Pius IX extended the feast to the whole Church in 1856, and Leo XIII consecrated the human race to the Sacred Heart in 1899.
altar: At every Mass the pierced Heart of Jesus is opened to us again. The water mixed into the wine at the offertory and the blood of the new covenant on the altar recall what flowed from his side. In the Eucharist we do not receive a memory of his love but the living Heart of Jesus himself, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.

Today the Church prays especially for priests; St John Vianney called the priesthood the love of the Heart of Jesus. Through their hands the sacrifice of Calvary is made present and the waters of salvation are poured out in Baptism and Confession. Pray for the priest who stands at this altar.
outline: Opening
Show a picture of the Sacred Heart, the kind that hangs in so many Kerala homes with a small lamp before it, and ask: what is this picture really telling us?
Point 1 · A father teaching his child to walk
In Hosea God bends down, lifts us to his cheek, and his heart recoils from anger.
Point 2 · The wells of salvation
Isaiah's joy, Paul's prayer: to know the love that surpasses knowledge.
Point 3 · The pierced side
Blood and water: the Lamb, the sacraments, the Church born from his Heart.
Point 4 · Learn from my Heart
Reparation, First Fridays, prayer for priests, and a heart gentle and humble like his.
Closing image
A soldier's spear, a wound opened, and from it a stream that reaches every baptismal font and every altar in the world.
Take-home line
“They will look on the one whom they have pierced.”
live: Enthrone or renew
If your home has a picture of the Sacred Heart, gather the family before it tonight and renew your consecration; if not, consider enthroning one this month.
First Fridays
Begin, or continue, the nine First Fridays: Mass, Holy Communion and, if possible, confession, in reparation and love.
Pray for priests
Today is the World Day of Prayer for the Sanctification of Priests. Pray by name for your parish priest and for the priest who baptised you, and send one of them a word of thanks.
Learn gentleness
Choose one person who irritates you and treat him or her today with the gentleness and humility of the Heart of Jesus.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The evangelist chose his word with care: he did not say that the soldier struck or wounded the side, but that he opened it, so that there the door of life might be thrown open, from which flowed the sacraments of the Church, without which no one enters the true life (Tractates on John 120).
St John Chrysostom (in substance)

The water and the blood are signs of Baptism and of the Holy Mysteries. From these the Church is born. As God formed Eve from the side of the sleeping Adam, so Christ gave us water and blood from his side and built the Church (Baptismal Catecheses 3).
St Bonaventure (in substance)
His side was pierced so that through the visible wound we might see the invisible wound of love. Let us enter through the open door into the Heart of Jesus and find rest there (The Mystical Vine).
magis: Catechism 478

Jesus knew and loved us each and all during his life, his agony and his Passion, and gave himself up for each one of us; his Sacred Heart, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is the chief sign and symbol of that love.
Catechism 766
The Church is born primarily of Christ's total self-giving for our salvation, signified by the blood and water from the open side of the crucified Jesus.
Catechism 2669
The prayer of the Church venerates and honours the Heart of Jesus, just as it invokes his most holy name.
Pius XII, Haurietis Aquas (1956)
The worship of the Sacred Heart is the worship of the love with which God loved us through Jesus, and the practice of our love for God and neighbour.
Pope Francis, Dilexit Nos (2024)
In the Heart of Christ we find the whole Gospel; from it the Church learns to love the world and to make reparation by building a civilisation of love.
saints: St Margaret Mary Alacoque (1647–1690)

A Visitation nun at Paray-le-Monial in France. Between 1673 and 1675 Jesus showed her his Heart, burning with love and wounded by indifference, and asked for Communion of reparation on the First Fridays, a Holy Hour on Thursday nights, and a feast of his Heart. Her confessor, St Claude La Colombière, a Jesuit, supported her. She was canonised in 1920.
This week

World Day of Prayer for the Sanctification of Priests (today). 5 Jun: the Immaculate Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary; St Boniface. 6 Jun: Tenth Sunday in Ordinary Time. 9 Jun: St Ephrem. 11 Jun: St Barnabas, apostle.
2027-06-04.prayer: Grant, we pray, almighty God, that we, who glory in the Heart of your beloved Son and recall the wonders of his love for us, may be made worthy to receive an overflowing measure of grace from that fount of heavenly gifts. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, pierced for us, we adore you and we trust in you. You taught us to walk and lifted us to your cheek; you bent down and fed us. Forgive our coldness and ingratitude, and accept our love in reparation. Make our hearts like yours, gentle and humble. Bless our homes, our children, and all the priests of your Church. Amen.

2027-06-05.title: The Immaculate Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary · St Boniface
readings: I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my whole being shall exult in my God
My heart exults in the Lord
His mother treasured all these things in her heart
2027-06-05.alt: Saturday of the Ninth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I). The Immaculate Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary (Saturday after the Sacred Heart) and St Boniface, bishop and martyr, are both obligatory memorials; because they fall on the same day in 2027, by the rule for coinciding memorials both become optional this year (follow your diocesan Ordo). This page gives the readings of the Immaculate Heart. The weekday readings are Tobit 12:1, 5–15, 20 (Raphael reveals himself); the canticle Tobit 13:2, 6, 7, 8 (“Blessed be God, who lives forever”); and Mark 12:38–44 (the widow's two small coins). Also World Environment Day. Liturgical colour: white (red for St Boniface; green for the weekday).
2027-06-05.verse: Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.
theo: Yesterday the Church contemplated the pierced Heart of the Son; today she turns to the Heart of his Mother, which was pierced too, as Simeon foretold: “a sword will pierce your own soul too” (Luke 2:35). The two feasts stand side by side because the two hearts were never apart. The first reading is a song of the restored Zion, the city God has rescued and adorned: “I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my whole being shall exult in my God; for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself with a garland, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.” The Church has always heard Mary's voice in these words. She is the first of the redeemed, clothed in salvation from the first moment of her existence: that is what Immaculate means. Her heart was never stained by sin, not because she did not need a Saviour, but because the Saviour reached her first, in view of the merits of her Son. And Isaiah ends with an image of growth: “For as the earth brings forth its shoots, and as a garden causes what is sown in it to spring up, so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.” Mary's heart is that garden: the Word was sown in it, and it brought forth the Saviour. The responsorial psalm is the song of Hannah, the mother of Samuel: “My heart exults in the Lord; my strength is exalted in my God.” Hannah's song is the elder sister of Mary's Magnificat: “The barren has borne seven … He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap.” God lifts up the lowly, and Mary is the lowly one he lifted highest.

The Gospel is the only story of Jesus' boyhood in the Gospels. Every year Joseph and Mary go up to Jerusalem for the Passover. When Jesus is twelve, he stays behind in the city without telling them. They travel a day's journey, assuming he is with relatives, and then begin the long search. “After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.” Mary speaks for both parents: “Child, why have you treated us like this? Look, your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety.” Here we see the heart of Mary, not calm and untroubled, but anxious, searching, loving. The Immaculate Heart is not a heart that feels nothing; it is a heart that feels everything without sin. Jesus answers with his first recorded words: “Why were you searching for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” And Luke adds honestly: “they did not understand what he said to them.” Mary does not understand, yet she does not stop believing. “Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and was obedient to them. His mother treasured all these things in her heart.” The Greek word means to keep carefully, to hold together, to ponder over time. Mary's heart is the place where the mysteries of Christ are kept and slowly understood. Before she conceived Christ in her womb, says St Augustine (in substance), she conceived him in her heart by faith. Devotion to her Immaculate Heart grew through St John Eudes in the seventeenth century and was given new urgency at Fatima in 1917; Pius XII consecrated the world to her Immaculate Heart in 1942 and in 1944 extended this feast to the whole Church. To honour her Heart is to learn from her how to keep the Word, how to search for Jesus when we have lost him, and how to stay faithful when we do not understand.

Today the Church could also keep the memorial of St Boniface, the apostle of Germany. Wynfrith, an English Benedictine monk, was sent by Pope Gregory II in 719 and given the name Boniface. He preached in Hesse and Thuringia, felled the sacred oak of Thor at Geismar to show that the old gods had no power, founded monasteries such as Fulda, and became archbishop of Mainz. In old age he went back to the Frisians, and on 5 June 754, near Dokkum, he and his companions were killed by a band of raiders; tradition says he raised a book of the Gospels over his head. The weekday readings, if they are used, end the story of Tobit: Raphael reveals himself, “I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand ready and enter before the glory of the Lord,” and teaches that “almsgiving saves from death and purges away every sin”; and in the Gospel Jesus praises the poor widow who gave “everything she had, all she had to live on.” Mary, the widow, and Boniface each gave God everything. And on this World Environment Day, Isaiah's garden reminds us that the earth that brings forth its shoots is God's gift, to be tended with care.
conn: “A sword will pierce your own soul too.”
Simeon's words to Mary (Luke 2:35) unite the two feasts of these days: the pierced Heart of the Son and the sorrowful Heart of the Mother.
“As a bride adorns herself with her jewels.”
Isaiah 61:10. The Church sees in the adorned bride both Zion and Mary, the first of the redeemed, clothed in salvation from her conception (Catechism 490–492).
“As a garden causes what is sown in it to spring up.”
Isaiah 61:11. The Fathers called Mary a garden enclosed (Song of Songs 4:12), in which the Word was sown and the Saviour sprang up.
Hannah's song.
1 Samuel 2:1–10 is the model of Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55): both praise the God who lifts the lowly and fills the hungry.
Twelve years old.
At about this age a Jewish boy began to take on the obligations of the Law. Jesus' first recorded words are about his Father: “I must be in my Father's house.”
“After three days.”
The three days of searching foreshadow the three days between the Cross and the Resurrection, when Mary would again lose and find her Son.
“They did not understand.”
Mary walked by faith, not by sight; she advanced in her “pilgrimage of faith” (Lumen Gentium 58), keeping what she did not yet understand.
“Treasured all these things in her heart.”
Luke says it twice (2:19 and 2:51). Mary is the first contemplative of the Gospel, the memory of the Church.
The widow's two coins.
The weekday Gospel (Mark 12:41–44): Jesus praises a poor widow who gave all she had. Mary too gave all, her Son, at the foot of the Cross.
The memorial.

St John Eudes promoted the liturgical honour of the Heart of Mary in the seventeenth century. Pius XII extended the feast to the whole Church in 1944; since 1969 it is kept on the Saturday after the Sacred Heart, and St John Paul II made it an obligatory memorial in 1996.
altar: Mary kept the words of Jesus in her heart; at Mass we receive the Word made flesh into our own hearts. She is the model of every good Communion: welcome him with faith, keep him with love, ponder him in silence.

In Eucharistic Prayer I the Church names first among the saints “the glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of our God and Lord, Jesus Christ.” At every altar the Mother stands where she stood on Calvary, beside the sacrifice of her Son, and teaches us to offer ourselves with him.
outline: Opening
Ask: where do you keep the things that matter most to you? Mary kept them in her heart.
Point 1 · A heart clothed with salvation
Isaiah's bride and Hannah's song: Mary, the first of the redeemed, the lowly one lifted up.
Point 2 · A heart that searches
Three days of anxiety: the Immaculate Heart feels everything, without sin.
Point 3 · A heart that keeps
Not understanding, she treasures and ponders.
Point 4 · A heart that gives everything
The widow's coins, Boniface's martyrdom, Mary's Son.
Closing image
A mother in Nazareth at night, the lamp burning low, turning over in her heart the words of her twelve-year-old son.
Take-home line
“His mother treasured all these things in her heart.”
live: Consecrate yourself
Make or renew an act of consecration to the Immaculate Heart of Mary today, alone or with your family.
First Saturday
Begin the five First Saturdays asked at Fatima: confession, Holy Communion, five decades of the Rosary and fifteen minutes meditating on its mysteries, in reparation to her Immaculate Heart.
Ponder one word
Choose one sentence from today's Gospel and carry it in your heart all day, as Mary did.
Care for the garden
On World Environment Day, do one practical thing for God's creation: plant a tree, refuse plastic, or save water as the monsoon begins.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

Mary is more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ than in conceiving the flesh of Christ. Her motherhood would have profited her nothing had she not borne Christ in her heart more happily than in her flesh (On Holy Virginity 3).
St Bede the Venerable (in substance)

Mary kept all the words in her heart, not only what she understood but also what she did not yet understand, comparing them with what she had read in the prophets, waiting for the time when they would be made clear (Homilies on the Gospels).
St John Eudes (in substance)
The Heart of Mary is wholly given to the Heart of Jesus; whoever honours her Heart honours the Heart of her Son, who lives and reigns in it.
magis: Catechism 534

The finding of Jesus in the Temple: Mary and Joseph did not understand, but accepted in faith; and Mary kept all these things in her heart during the years Jesus remained hidden in the silence of an ordinary life.
Catechism 2599
Jesus learned to pray in his human heart from his mother, who kept all the great things the Almighty had done and treasured them in her heart.
Catechism 2617
Mary's prayer is revealed at the dawning of the fullness of time: her Fiat and her Magnificat.
Lumen Gentium 57–58
The Mother's union with her Son: when he was found in the Temple his parents did not understand, and his mother kept all these things in her heart; she advanced in her pilgrimage of faith.
Pius XII (1942)
In the midst of the Second World War Pius XII consecrated the Church and the human race to the Immaculate Heart of Mary; in 1944 he extended this feast to the universal Church.
saints: St Boniface (c. 675–754)

Born Wynfrith in Wessex, England, he became a Benedictine monk. In 719 Pope Gregory II gave him the name Boniface and sent him to preach to the Germanic peoples. Ordained bishop in 722, he felled the sacred oak of Thor at Geismar, founded monasteries including Fulda (744), reformed the Frankish Church and became archbishop of Mainz. Returning in old age to Frisia, he was killed with his companions near Dokkum on 5 June 754. He is buried at Fulda and honoured as the Apostle of Germany.
This week

6 Jun: Tenth Sunday in Ordinary Time. 9 Jun: St Ephrem, deacon and doctor. 11 Jun: St Barnabas, apostle. The weekday readings of the coming week begin the Second Letter to the Corinthians and the Sermon on the Mount.
2027-06-05.prayer: O God, who prepared a fit dwelling place for the Holy Spirit in the Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary, graciously grant that through her intercession we may be a worthy temple of your glory. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Immaculate Heart of Mary, you kept every word of your Son and treasured what you did not yet understand; teach us to search for Jesus when we have lost him, to keep his word, and to give him everything. Through the prayers of St Boniface, make us brave witnesses to the Gospel. Amen.

2027-06-07.title: Monday of the Tenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction
Taste and see the goodness of the Lord
Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven
2027-06-07.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 10 (Year I). This week the first reading begins the Second Letter of Paul to the Corinthians, and the Gospel begins the Sermon on the Mount, which will be read on the weekdays of the next two weeks. The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary Psalm 34:2–9 = NRSV 34:1–8). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-07.verse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.
theo: The Second Letter to the Corinthians is the most personal of all Paul's letters. He wrote it around the year 55 or 56, probably from Macedonia, after a painful time with the church he had founded in Corinth: a visit that went badly, a letter written “with many tears,” rumours that he was unreliable, rivals who mocked his weak appearance. We will read it for the next two weeks, and we will meet a Paul who is tired, wounded and yet full of hope. He does not begin with a defence. He begins with a blessing: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction.” The Greek word for consolation, paraklesis, rings through these few verses again and again. It is the word from which the Holy Spirit gets his name, the Paraclete, the one called to stand beside us. Paul does not say that God keeps him out of trouble. He says that God meets him inside it, and that the comfort he receives is not meant to stop with him: “so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.” Suffering and comfort both flow outward. “For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ.” The Christian who has been comforted becomes a channel of comfort. The Psalm sings the same experience in the voice of a poor man rescued: “This poor soul cried, and was heard by the Lord, and was saved from every trouble.” And it ends with an invitation: “O taste and see that the Lord is good.”

In the Gospel Jesus sees the crowds, goes up the mountain and sits down, as a teacher sat in his day, and his disciples come close. Matthew wants us to remember Moses, who went up Sinai and brought down the Law. Here a greater than Moses gives the law of the kingdom, and he begins not with a command but with a blessing, eight times over. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.” The Beatitudes turn the world's idea of happiness upside down. The world calls happy the rich, the strong, the people who never cry and never lose. Jesus calls happy the poor in spirit, who know they need God; the meek; those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; the merciful; the pure in heart; the peacemakers; those persecuted for righteousness' sake. The Beatitudes are first of all a portrait of Jesus himself, the poor, meek, merciful, pure and persecuted Son. They are also a promise. “Those who mourn” are not told to stop crying; they are told “they will be comforted.” Paul and Matthew meet in the same word. The God of all consolation is the one who fulfils the Beatitude. In Kerala this is the week when schools reopen after the summer and the monsoon rain has arrived: new books, new uniforms, wet umbrellas at the gate. The Church opens her own school today, the Sermon on the Mount, and its first lesson is that happiness is a gift of God given to the humble.
outline: Opening
Ask: when you were sad or in trouble, who comforted you, and how?
Point 1 · The God of all consolation
Paul begins a hard letter with a blessing, because God meets us inside our affliction.
Point 2 · Comforted in order to comfort
The consolation we receive is meant to flow on to others.
Point 3 · The upside-down happiness
The Beatitudes: Jesus calls blessed the poor, the mourners, the meek and the merciful.
Take-home line
“Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”
live: Pass the comfort on (2 Corinthians 1:4)
Think of one comfort God gave you in a hard time, and today offer the same kindness to someone going through something similar.
Pray one Beatitude (Matthew 5:3–10)
Choose one Beatitude, write it on a slip of paper, and ask Jesus to grow it in you this week.
2027-06-07.prayer: Blessed are you, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Father of mercies and God of all consolation. You have comforted us in our troubles more times than we can count. Make us channels of your comfort to all who are afflicted: the sick, the grieving, the lonely, the poor. Lord Jesus, you taught on the mountain that the poor in spirit, the meek and the merciful are blessed; give us hearts like yours, emptied of pride and open to your kingdom. Bless the children and teachers beginning a new school year, and keep them safe in the rains. Amen.
altar: At every Mass, before Holy Communion, the priest prays that we may be kept “safe from all distress” as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour. Then he lifts the Host and says: “Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb.” The Beatitudes of the mountain end at the altar. Here the poor in spirit are fed, the mourners are comforted, and the pure in heart receive the One they long to see.

2027-06-08.title: Tuesday of the Tenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: For in him every one of God's promises is a “Yes.”
Lord, let your face shine on me
You are the salt of the earth … You are the light of the world
2027-06-08.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 10 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green. A Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary or another votive Mass may be chosen on a weekday without a memorial.
2027-06-08.verse: In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.
theo: Paul had promised the Corinthians a visit and then changed his plans. Some of them said at once: you see, he is a man who says yes and no in the same breath; how can we trust his gospel? Paul answers the accusation, but he lifts it to a much higher level. His own travel plans may change; God's word does not. “As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been ‘Yes and No.’ For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not ‘Yes and No’; but in him it is always ‘Yes.’” Then comes one of the great sentences of the New Testament: “For in him every one of God's promises is a ‘Yes.’ For this reason it is through him that we say the ‘Amen,’ to the glory of God.” Every promise God made to Abraham, to Moses, to David and to the prophets finds its fulfilment in Jesus. He is God's Yes to the world. And when the Church answers at the end of the Eucharistic Prayer with the great Amen, she is saying her own yes through him. Then Paul uses words that the Church has always heard as a description of Baptism and Confirmation: “But it is God who establishes us with you in Christ and has anointed us, by putting his seal on us and giving us his Spirit in our hearts as a first installment.” Anointed, sealed, given the Spirit as a first installment, a pledge of the full inheritance to come. The Catechism (1296) quotes exactly these words when it explains the seal of Confirmation. The Psalm, a verse from the long praise of God's law, prays like a disciple who has tasted that faithfulness: “The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple,” and “Make your face shine upon your servant.”

Yesterday Jesus spoke the Beatitudes. Today he tells the same people, the poor, the meek, the persecuted, who they are: “You are the salt of the earth.” “You are the light of the world.” He does not say: try to become salt, or one day you may be light. He says: you are. It is a gift before it is a task. Salt in the ancient world preserved food from going bad and gave it taste; it was also used with sacrifices and in making covenants. A little salt changes a whole dish. But “if salt has lost its taste, how can its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything.” Light is useless if it is hidden: “No one after lighting a lamp puts it under the bushel basket, but on the lampstand, and it gives light to all in the house.” Every Kerala home knows this. When the monsoon storms cut the electricity, someone lights the nilavilakku or a kerosene lamp and sets it in the middle of the room, not under the cot. Jesus' last word explains the purpose of the light: “so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven.” Our good works are not meant to make people admire us but to make them praise God. The disciple is like the moon, which has no light of its own but reflects the sun. Paul's “Yes” in Christ and Jesus' salt and light belong together: the Christian sealed by the Spirit is God's Yes made visible in a village, an office, a classroom.
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever made a promise and failed to keep it? How did it feel to the other person?
Point 1 · God's Yes in Christ
Every promise of God is fulfilled in Jesus, and through him we say Amen.
Point 2 · Anointed and sealed
Baptism and Confirmation give us the Spirit as a first installment of heaven.
Point 3 · Salt and light
Jesus tells his disciples what they are, and why the lamp must not be hidden.
Take-home line
“Let your light shine before others.”
live: Mean your Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20)
At your next Mass, say the great Amen at the end of the Eucharistic Prayer slowly and with your whole heart.
Put the lamp on the stand (Matthew 5:15)
Do one good work today openly and simply, not for praise, so that someone may thank God.
2027-06-08.prayer: Faithful God, in your Son Jesus Christ every one of your promises is Yes. We thank you for anointing us, for setting your seal upon us and giving us your Spirit in our hearts. Keep us from being people of yes and no, who promise and do not keep their word. Lord Jesus, you call us the salt of the earth and the light of the world; do not let us lose our taste or hide our light. Let our good works shine, so that all who see them may give glory to our Father in heaven. Amen.
altar: At the end of the Eucharistic Prayer the priest lifts the Body and Blood of Christ and sings: through him, and with him, and in him, all glory and honour is yours, almighty Father. The whole people answers: Amen. This is the Amen Paul speaks of, said through Christ to the glory of God. It is the most important Amen of the Mass: our yes to the Son who is God's Yes to us.

2027-06-09.title: Wednesday of the Tenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Ephrem, Deacon and Doctor of the Church
readings: not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life
Holy is the Lord our God
I have come not to abolish but to fulfill
2027-06-09.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 10 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Ephrem, deacon and doctor of the Church, may be kept today. He is dear to the Syriac Churches of Kerala as Mar Aprem, and the Syro-Malabar Church keeps his feast today too. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-06-09.verse: Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
theo: In the Second Letter to the Corinthians Paul has to defend his ministry against people who came to Corinth with impressive letters of recommendation. He answers: I need no letters; “You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts,” “written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.” Today's reading continues: “Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God, who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” Paul is thinking of Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant, when God would write his law on the heart, and of Ezekiel's promise of a new spirit. He compares the giving of the Law on Sinai, which came “in glory so that the people of Israel could not gaze at Moses' face because of the glory of his face,” with the ministry of the Spirit, and concludes: “how much more will the ministry of the Spirit come in glory?” We must read this carefully. Paul, a Jew who loved the Law, does not say the Law was bad. Elsewhere he writes: “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). He means that a law written outside us, on stone, can show us what is right but cannot give us the power to do it; it can only condemn the one who fails. The Spirit writes God's will within us and gives life. The glory of Sinai was real; the glory of the Spirit is greater and lasting. The Psalm sings the holiness of the God who spoke to Moses and Aaron and Samuel “in the pillar of cloud” and was “a forgiving God to them.”

The Gospel guards us against a wrong conclusion. If the Spirit gives life and the letter kills, should Christians throw away the commandments? Jesus answers clearly: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.” He respects even the smallest marks of the Scripture: “not one letter, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished.” The Ten Commandments still stand; Jesus will show in the coming days that he asks for more, not less: not only no murder, but no anger; not only no adultery, but a pure heart. Fulfilment means bringing the Law to its full meaning, as a flower fulfils the bud. Jesus fulfils the Law by living it perfectly, by revealing its heart, which is love, and by giving the Spirit who makes us able to keep it. St Ephrem the Syrian, whom we may remember today, was born around 306 in Nisibis, served the Church there as a deacon and teacher, and spent his last years in Edessa, where he died in 373. He put the whole faith into hymns and taught choirs to sing them; the Syriac Churches call him the Harp of the Spirit. He wrote (in substance) that no one who drinks from the spring of God's word should be sad that he cannot drink it all; let him rejoice that it is inexhaustible. In 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church. The Kerala Churches of the Syriac tradition still sing his words.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there a rule you once obeyed only because you had to, and later came to love because you understood why?
Point 1 · A letter written on hearts
Our competence is from God, who makes us ministers of a new covenant.
Point 2 · The letter and the Spirit
The Law is holy; the Spirit writes it within us and gives life.
Point 3 · Not to abolish but to fulfill
Jesus brings the Law to its full meaning, as St Ephrem sang it.
Take-home line
“I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.”
live: Let the Spirit write (2 Corinthians 3:3)
Choose one commandment you keep only outwardly, and ask the Holy Spirit today to write it on your heart.
Sing your faith (Psalm 99:5)
Following St Ephrem, sing or listen to one hymn today and let its words become your prayer.
2027-06-09.prayer: Holy God, you spoke to Moses in the cloud and gave your people the holy Law. Now through Jesus Christ you have made us ministers of a new covenant, not of letter but of Spirit. Write your will on our hearts, so that we keep your commandments not from fear but from love. Lord Jesus, you came not to abolish but to fulfill; bring our lives to their full meaning in you. Through the prayers of St Ephrem, Harp of the Spirit, may our words and songs give you glory. Amen.
altar: Just before the consecration the priest stretches his hands over the bread and wine and asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit upon them, so that they may become the Body and Blood of Christ. The Spirit who gives life is at work on the altar. St Ephrem loved to sing that in the bread there is fire and Spirit (in substance). After the consecration we pray that the same Spirit may gather us, who receive the Body and Blood of Christ, into one body, a letter of Christ written on human hearts.

2027-06-10.title: Thursday of the Tenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord … are being transformed into the same image
The glory of the Lord will dwell in our land
first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift
2027-06-10.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 10 (Year I). The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary Psalm 85:9–14 = NRSV 85:8–13). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-10.verse: For it is the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
theo: Yesterday Paul spoke of Moses coming down from Sinai with a face shining so brightly that the people could not look at him. Exodus tells us that Moses then put a veil over his face, taking it off only when he went in to speak with the Lord. Paul turns this into a picture of how anyone, then or now, can read the Scriptures without seeing their goal: “Indeed, to this very day whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their minds; but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.” We must hear this as Paul meant it. He is speaking with grief about his own people, whom he loved so much that he wished he could be cut off for their sake (Romans 9:3); the Church today, following the Second Vatican Council, rejects every blame laid on the Jewish people as a whole and honours them as the people of the covenant God has never revoked. And the veil is not only theirs. Every Christian who reads the Bible coldly, as a book of rules or old stories, has a veil over the heart. The veil falls when one turns to the Lord. Then comes the most beautiful sentence of the chapter: “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. And all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another.” Moses' face shone for a time; the Christian is being changed day by day into the likeness of Christ. The reading ends at the first page of the Bible: “For it is the God who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” The Psalm promises the same: “that his glory may dwell in our land,” where “righteousness and peace will kiss each other.”

In the Gospel Jesus begins to show what he meant by fulfilling the Law. “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.” The scribes and Pharisees were serious, devout men; Jesus asks his disciples to go deeper still, to the root. “You have heard that it was said to those of ancient times, ‘You shall not murder’ … But I say to you that if you are angry with a brother or sister, you will be liable to judgment.” Murder begins in the heart, with anger nursed, with insults like “You fool.” Then Jesus gives an astonishing instruction: “So when you are offering your gift at the altar, if you remember that your brother or sister has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.” God would rather wait for our offering than receive it from a heart at war with a brother. The face of Christ that Paul speaks of is turned towards each person we meet; we cannot see his glory and refuse to look at our neighbour. In these monsoon days the sky can be dark at noon and suddenly bright when the clouds open. So it is with a reconciled heart: the light of Christ breaks through as soon as the quarrel is ended.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there someone you have not spoken to properly for a long time because of a quarrel?
Point 1 · The veil removed
When anyone turns to the Lord, the Scriptures open and the heart sees.
Point 2 · From glory to glory
With unveiled faces we are being changed into the image of Christ.
Point 3 · First be reconciled
Jesus goes to the root of murder, anger, and asks for peace before the altar.
Take-home line
“First be reconciled to your brother or sister, and then come and offer your gift.”
live: Turn to the Lord (2 Corinthians 3:16)
Before reading the Bible today, pray: Lord, take away the veil from my heart.
Leave your gift and go (Matthew 5:24)
Before your next Mass, take one step towards reconciliation with someone: a call, a message, a word of apology.
2027-06-10.prayer: God of light, you said at the beginning, Let there be light, and now you have shone in our hearts in the face of Jesus Christ. Take away every veil from our minds when we read your word, and change us from glory to glory into the image of your Son. Lord Jesus, you see the anger we hide and the quarrels we do not end; give us courage to be reconciled before we bring our gifts to your altar. Let righteousness and peace kiss in our homes and in our land. Amen.
altar: Before Holy Communion the priest prays: Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles, Peace I leave you, my peace I give you, look not on our sins but on the faith of your Church. Then we offer one another a sign of peace. This is Jesus' command in today's Gospel built into every Mass: before we receive the Gift on the altar, we turn to our brothers and sisters in peace.

2027-06-11.title: Saint Barnabas, Apostle
readings: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith
The Lord has revealed to the nations his saving power
You received without payment; give without payment
2027-06-11.alt: Memorial. The first reading is proper to the memorial and replaces the weekday reading (2 Corinthians 4:7–15). The Gospel given is the proper Gospel of the memorial, Matthew 10:7–13; some ordos give the weekday Gospel of Friday of the Tenth Week, Matthew 5:27–32, which may also be used. Barnabas was not one of the Twelve, but the Acts of the Apostles calls him an apostle (Acts 14:14). Liturgical colour: red.
2027-06-11.verse: for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. And a great many people were brought to the Lord.
theo: The Acts of the Apostles first introduces Barnabas as a generous man: a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, “to whom the apostles gave the name Barnabas (which means ‘son of encouragement’),” who sold a field and laid the money at the apostles' feet (Acts 4:36–37). The name fits him perfectly. When Saul, the former persecutor, came to Jerusalem and the disciples were all afraid of him, it was Barnabas who “took him, brought him to the apostles,” and vouched for him (Acts 9:27). Today's reading shows him at his best. After the persecution that followed Stephen's death, believers from Cyprus and Cyrene went to Antioch, the great city of Syria, and began to preach the Lord Jesus to Greeks as well as Jews. “The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number became believers and turned to the Lord.” The church in Jerusalem sent Barnabas to look into this new thing. He did not come with suspicion or a list of rules: “When he came and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast devotion; for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.” Then, seeing that the work was too big for him, he did something humble and wise: “Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch.” For a whole year the two taught together, “and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called ‘Christians.’” The second part of the reading shows the Church of Antioch at prayer: “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’ Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.” The great missionary journeys of the Church begin with worship, fasting and the laying on of hands. The Psalm is the song of that mission: “All the ends of the earth have seen the victory of our God.”

The Gospel is part of the instructions Jesus gave the Twelve when he sent them out for the first time. “As you go, proclaim the good news, ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’ Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons.” And then a principle for every missionary: “You received without payment; give without payment.” The apostle travels light, with no gold or silver or copper in his belt, trusting that “laborers deserve their food.” He brings peace into every house he enters: “If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it.” Barnabas lived this. He gave away his field before he gave away his life. He was big enough to step aside so that Saul, the more gifted preacher, could shine; Acts soon begins to say “Paul and Barnabas” instead of “Barnabas and Saul.” And when Paul refused to take John Mark on a second journey because the young man had left them once before, Barnabas, his cousin, took Mark with him to Cyprus and gave him a second chance (Acts 15:37–39). Years later Paul himself wrote that Mark was useful to him in his ministry (2 Timothy 4:11). The son of encouragement had been right. Tradition says that Barnabas preached in Cyprus and died a martyr at Salamis; the Church of Cyprus honours him as its founder. Every parish needs a Barnabas: someone who sees the grace of God in others and rejoices, who brings the newcomer in, who gives the one who failed a second chance.
outline: Opening
Ask: who believed in you when others doubted you, and what difference did it make?
Point 1 · He saw the grace of God and rejoiced
Barnabas comes to Antioch without suspicion, and encourages the new believers.
Point 2 · He went to look for Saul
The humility that seeks out a more gifted partner and gives others a second chance.
Point 3 · Set apart and sent
Worship, fasting and the laying on of hands; give without payment.
Take-home line
“He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.”
live: Be a son or daughter of encouragement (Acts 4:36)
Today say a sincere word of encouragement to someone who is struggling or doubting themselves.
Give without payment (Matthew 10:8)
Do one service today for which you could expect something in return, and accept nothing for it.
saints: St Barnabas (1st century)

Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, was named Barnabas, son of encouragement, by the apostles; he sold a field and gave the money to the community (Acts 4:36–37). He introduced the converted Saul to the apostles (Acts 9:27), was sent by the Jerusalem church to Antioch, brought Saul there, and with him was set apart by the Holy Spirit for the first missionary journey, through Cyprus and Asia Minor (Acts 13–14). He took part in the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15). After parting from Paul over John Mark, his cousin (Colossians 4:10), he sailed with Mark to Cyprus (Acts 15:39). Acts calls him an apostle (Acts 14:14), though he was not one of the Twelve. Tradition holds that he was martyred at Salamis in Cyprus; the Church of Cyprus venerates him as its founder.
2027-06-11.prayer: Lord God, you chose St Barnabas, a good man full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, to strengthen your Church and to carry the Gospel to the nations. Give us his eyes, to see your grace in others and rejoice; his humility, to make room for gifts greater than our own; and his generous heart, to give without payment what we have received without payment. Bless all missionaries, especially those sent from India to other lands, and make us all sons and daughters of encouragement. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: In the Church at Antioch Barnabas and Saul were set apart while the community was “worshiping the Lord and fasting.” The Greek word for worship there is the root of our word liturgy. The mission of the Church is born at the altar. At the end of every Mass we too are sent: Go forth, the Mass is ended; go and announce the Gospel of the Lord. Like Barnabas, we leave the altar to bring Christ's peace into every house we enter.

2027-06-12.title: Saturday of the Tenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: So we are ambassadors for Christ … be reconciled to God
The Lord is kind and merciful
Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’
2027-06-12.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 10 (Year I). On a Saturday in Ordinary Time without an obligatory memorial, the optional memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary may be kept. Liturgical colour: green (white for the Saturday memorial of Our Lady).
2027-06-12.verse: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!
theo: Today's reading is the heart of the Second Letter to the Corinthians, and one of the deepest pages Paul ever wrote. Why does he work so hard, suffer so much, put up with misunderstanding? “For the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all; therefore all have died. And he died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them.” The love of Christ is not only the love we have for him; it is first his love for us, which presses on us and drives us forward. Because of it Paul looks at everyone differently: “From now on, therefore, we regard no one from a human point of view.” Not by caste, wealth, education or usefulness, but as someone for whom Christ died. Then the great announcement: “So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new!” Baptism is not a coat of paint on an old house; it is a new creation. And all of this comes from God, “who reconciled us to himself through Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation.” God was not waiting for us to make the first move: “in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them.” Paul sees himself as an ambassador, carrying a message from the King: “we entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” The reading ends with a mysterious and wonderful exchange: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” The sinless One took our place so that we could take his. The Psalm answers with pure gratitude: “as far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our transgressions from us.”

In the Gospel Jesus continues his teaching on the Law. The Law forbade false oaths and commanded that vows made to the Lord be kept. Jesus goes further: “But I say to you, Do not swear at all,” neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by Jerusalem, nor by your own head. People swore by these things to make their words sound more solid, and to leave themselves a way out. Jesus wants disciples whose every word can be trusted: “Let your word be ‘Yes, Yes’ or ‘No, No’; anything more than this comes from the evil one.” (The Church has always understood that this does not forbid a solemn oath for a grave reason, such as in a court of law; Jesus is condemning the habit of swearing, and the lies that make it necessary.) Paul's ambassador and Jesus' plain-spoken disciple belong together: the one who carries the message of reconciliation must be someone whose word is true. On this Saturday many parishes keep the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Her whole life is the perfect Yes: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord; let it be with me according to your word.” And Saturday evening is the time when many Catholics go to confession before Sunday. The sacrament of Reconciliation is exactly Paul's ministry: a priest, an ambassador for Christ, saying in his name, I absolve you, and the old passing away, and everything becoming new.
outline: Opening
Ask: when did you last feel completely new, as if you had been given a fresh start?
Point 1 · The love of Christ urges us on
One died for all, so that we may live no longer for ourselves.
Point 2 · A new creation, reconciled
God reconciles the world in Christ and makes us his ambassadors.
Point 3 · Yes, Yes; No, No
The disciple's word is simple and true, like Mary's Yes.
Take-home line
“If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation.”
live: Be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20)
If you have not been to confession recently, go this weekend; if you have, pray for someone who is afraid to go.
Speak plainly (Matthew 5:37)
For one whole day, avoid exaggerations and the phrase I swear; let your yes be yes and your no be no.
2027-06-12.prayer: Father of mercy, in Christ you reconciled the world to yourself, not counting our trespasses against us. You made him who knew no sin to be sin for our sake, so that in him we might become your righteousness. We thank you for the new creation that began in our Baptism, and for every time you have made us new in the sacrament of Reconciliation. Let the love of Christ urge us on, so that we live no longer for ourselves. Make our words simple and true, and teach us to say Yes to you as Mary did. Amen.
altar: At every Mass, over the chalice, the priest repeats the words of Jesus: this is the chalice of my Blood, poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Here is the source of the ministry of reconciliation Paul speaks of: the one who died for all is present on the altar, and his sacrifice is offered so that we who live may live for him. Before Communion we confess, Lord, I am not worthy, and he answers by giving himself.

2027-06-14.title: Monday of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time
readings: See, now is the acceptable time … as having nothing, and yet possessing everything
The Lord has made known his salvation
But I say to you, Do not resist an evildoer
2027-06-14.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 11 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-14.verse: But I say to you, Do not resist an evildoer. But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also;
theo: St Paul writes to the Corinthians as a co-worker of God, and he speaks with urgency: “As we work together with him, we urge you also not to accept the grace of God in vain.” He quotes the prophet Isaiah, “At an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you,” and then he adds his own commentary, like a man pointing at a clock: “See, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation!” Grace is not something to be saved for later. Today is the day. Then Paul describes what his ministry has cost him, so that no one can say he preached for gain: “through great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger.” But the list does not end in complaint. It turns into a string of glorious paradoxes: “We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet are well known; as dying, and see, we are alive; as punished, and yet not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything.” This is the life of someone who belongs to the crucified and risen Christ. The world sees weakness and loss; God sees a man who possesses everything. The Psalm gives the reason for this joy: “O sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done marvelous things.”

In the Gospel we continue the Sermon on the Mount, and Jesus quotes one of the oldest laws of the ancient world: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’” We often think of this law as cruel, but in its time (Exodus 21:24) it was a limit on revenge: no more than an eye for an eye, not a life for an eye, not a whole family for one insult. Jesus now goes much further. “But I say to you, Do not resist an evildoer. But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also.” A blow on the right cheek, given by a right hand, is a backhanded slap: an insult more than an injury. Jesus says: do not answer insult with insult. If someone sues you for your coat, give your cloak as well; “if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile.” Roman soldiers could force a local man to carry their baggage for a mile, as Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry the cross. Jesus says: surprise him by going further than he demands. These are not rules for being weak. They are a way of breaking the chain of revenge with a stronger force, the force of goodness. The Church does not read this as a command to let the innocent be harmed: protecting the weak and legitimate defence remain duties of love (Catechism 2263–2265), and no one should remain in a home where they are being abused. But in the daily insults, quarrels and injustices of family, office and neighbourhood, the disciple of Jesus refuses to pay back evil for evil.
outline: Opening
Ask: when someone hurts me, what is my first reaction? To hit back, to sulk, or to bless?
Point 1 · Now is the acceptable time
Do not receive the grace of God in vain; today is the day of salvation.
Point 2 · Having nothing, possessing everything
Paul's sufferings become a song of paradox and joy.
Point 3 · The second mile
Jesus breaks the chain of revenge with the stronger force of goodness.
Take-home line
“If anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile.”
live: Today, not tomorrow (2 Corinthians 6:2)
Do today the good thing you have been putting off: a confession, a reconciliation, a visit.
Go the second mile (Matthew 5:41)
When someone asks you for a small service today, do a little more than they ask, with a smile.
2027-06-14.prayer: Lord God, now is the acceptable time and today is the day of salvation: do not let us receive your grace in vain. Give us the spirit of St Paul, who was sorrowful yet always rejoicing, poor yet making many rich, having nothing and yet possessing everything. Lord Jesus, you did not answer insult with insult, and on the cross you prayed for those who struck you. Teach us not to pay back evil for evil, to turn the other cheek to the small insults of each day, and to go the second mile in love. Amen.
altar: At the altar we receive the one who did not resist the evildoer: he offered his back to those who struck him and gave his life for those who took it. In the Eucharist this self-giving love is made present, the one sacrifice of the cross offered for us, and from it we receive the strength to go the second mile.

2027-06-15.title: Tuesday of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor
Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you
2027-06-15.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 11 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-15.verse: But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father in heaven; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the righteous and on the unrighteous.
theo: For several years St Paul organised a collection among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (Romans 15:26; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). It mattered to him greatly: it was a sign that Jews and Gentiles in Christ were one family. In today's reading he tells the Corinthians, who were fairly prosperous, about the churches of Macedonia, Philippi and Thessalonica, who were not: “during a severe ordeal of affliction, their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.” Poverty and joy together produced generosity. “They voluntarily gave according to their means, and even beyond their means, begging us earnestly for the privilege of sharing in this ministry to the saints.” The poor begged for the privilege of giving! And Paul gives the secret: “they gave themselves first to the Lord.” When the heart is given, the purse follows. Paul does not command the Corinthians; he invites them to “excel also in this generous undertaking,” and then he points to the source of all giving: “For you know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.” The word Paul uses for this “generous act” is charis, grace. The Son of God emptied himself, was born in a manger and died on a cross, and by his poverty we receive the riches of God. The Psalm sings of the same God, “who executes justice for the oppressed; who gives food to the hungry.”

In the Gospel Jesus reaches the summit of the Sermon on the Mount. “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’” The Law of Moses commanded love of neighbour (Leviticus 19:18); nowhere did it command hatred of enemies, but many concluded that a neighbour meant only one's own people, and that enemies could be hated. Jesus breaks that boundary: “But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father in heaven.” And he gives the reason from the sky itself: the Father “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the righteous and on the unrighteous.” In these monsoon weeks we see it with our own eyes: the rain does not ask whose field it is falling on. To love only those who love us is no more than “the tax collectors” do; to greet only our own is what everyone does. Then comes the great command: “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect.” The Greek word, teleios, means complete, mature, whole. St Luke gives the same saying as “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke 6:36). The perfection of the Father is not a cold flawlessness; it is mercy without limits. Every Christian, and not only priests and religious, is called to this holiness (Lumen Gentium 40).
outline: Opening
Ask: who is the hardest person for me to pray for? Have I ever prayed for them by name?
Point 1 · Rich by his poverty
The poor Macedonians give beyond their means because they gave themselves first to the Lord.
Point 2 · Sun and rain for all
The Father's love does not choose; ours must not either.
Point 3 · Be perfect as your Father
The perfection of the Father is mercy; all are called to holiness.
Take-home line
“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.”
live: Give yourself first (2 Corinthians 8:5)
Before you give money or time today, give yourself to the Lord in a short prayer, and then give gladly.
Pray for an enemy (Matthew 5:44)
Pray today by name for one person who has hurt you, asking God to bless them.
2027-06-15.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, though you were rich, yet for our sakes you became poor, so that by your poverty we might become rich. Give us the joy of the churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means because they gave themselves first to you. Father in heaven, you make your sun rise on the evil and on the good and send your rain on all; teach us to love our enemies and to pray for those who persecute us, so that we may truly be your children, merciful as you are merciful. Amen.
altar: In the Eucharist the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ is made present: he who was rich became poor, and now he gives himself under the poor signs of bread and wine. At the altar he prays for those who persecuted him, “Father, forgive them,” and the sacrifice of the cross is offered for friend and enemy alike. Whoever receives him receives a heart that can love enemies.

2027-06-16.title: Wednesday of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Blessed the man who fears the Lord
Your Father who sees in secret will reward you
2027-06-16.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 11 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-16.verse: Each of you must give as you have made up your mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
theo: St Paul is still speaking about the collection for the poor of Jerusalem, and now he uses the language every farmer understands: “The point is this: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.” A farmer who keeps back most of his seed for fear of losing it will have a poor harvest. Giving to the poor is not throwing seed away; it is sowing. Then Paul adds a word about the heart of the giver: “Each of you must give as you have made up your mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” The Greek word for cheerful is hilaros, from which comes our word “hilarious.” God does not want gifts squeezed out of us by guilt or by public pressure; he wants the gift of a glad heart. And the one who gives in this way will never be the poorer: “God is able to provide you with every blessing in abundance, so that by always having enough of everything, you may share abundantly in every good work.” Paul quotes today's Psalm about the just man: “He scatters abroad, he gives to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” God, “who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food,” will multiply our seed. And the final fruit of all giving is not only bread for the poor but praise for God: our generosity “will produce thanksgiving to God.”

In the Gospel Jesus speaks of the three great works of Jewish piety, which the Church still practises: almsgiving, prayer and fasting. He does not question these practices; he takes for granted that his disciples will give, pray and fast. He asks only one question: for whom are you doing it? “Beware of practicing your piety before others in order to be seen by them; for then you have no reward from your Father in heaven.” The word “hypocrite” in Greek meant a stage actor, someone playing a part behind a mask. Jesus describes the actor's way: sounding a trumpet when giving alms, praying “at the street corners, so that they may be seen by others,” disfiguring the face while fasting. Three times he says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.” They wanted applause, and they got it, and that is all they will get. Then three times he describes the way of the child of God: “do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing”; “go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret”; “put oil on your head and wash your face.” And three times comes the same promise: “your Father who sees in secret will reward you.” This does not forbid public worship or good example; a few verses earlier Jesus said, “let your light shine before others” (Matthew 5:16). The difference is the direction of the heart: the light is to give glory to the Father, not to ourselves.
outline: Opening
Ask: if no one ever knew about my good deeds, would I still do them?
Point 1 · Sowing bountifully
Giving is sowing; God multiplies the seed of the generous.
Point 2 · A cheerful giver
God wants the gift of a glad heart, not of reluctance or pressure.
Point 3 · In secret
Alms, prayer and fasting done for the Father who sees in secret.
Take-home line
“Your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”
live: Give cheerfully (2 Corinthians 9:7)
Decide today, in your heart, a gift for someone in need, and give it gladly, without waiting to be asked.
Shut the door (Matthew 6:6)
Find ten minutes today to pray alone, in a quiet room with the door shut, to your Father who sees in secret.
2027-06-16.prayer: Generous Father, you supply seed to the sower and bread for food, and you love a cheerful giver. Release our hearts from fear and meanness, so that we may sow bountifully and share abundantly in every good work. Lord Jesus, you saw the hypocrisy of those who wanted to be seen; purify our alms, our prayer and our fasting, so that we may do them for the Father who sees in secret, and our generosity may produce thanksgiving to God. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the gifts of bread and wine are brought to the altar, and with them the collection for the needs of the Church and the poor. The Eucharist is the perfect gift: Christ offering himself to the Father, not to be seen by others, but in the hidden obedience of love. United with his sacrifice, our small gifts become a thanksgiving to God.

2027-06-17.title: Thursday of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ
Your works, O Lord, are justice and truth
Pray then in this way: Our Father in heaven
2027-06-17.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 11 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-17.verse: Pray then in this way: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
theo: In the last chapters of the Second Letter to the Corinthians St Paul defends his ministry against some visiting preachers whom he calls, with irony, “super-apostles.” They were eloquent, they demanded payment, and they belittled Paul. He hates to boast, so he asks the Corinthians to put up with “a little foolishness.” Then he opens his heart: “I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” In the customs of the time, a friend of the family arranged a betrothal and kept the bride safe until the wedding. Paul sees himself as that friend: he brought the Corinthians to Christ, and he wants to present them to their Bridegroom with an undivided heart. His fear is that “as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.” The danger is “another Jesus,” “a different spirit,” “a different gospel.” The Church has always loved this image of herself as the virgin bride of Christ, and the Fathers saw its perfect fulfilment in the Blessed Virgin Mary, whose heart was wholly given to God (Lumen Gentium 63–64).
