Paul also explains why he never took money from the Corinthians: he “proclaimed God's good news” to them without charge, supported by the brothers from Macedonia, so that no one could say he preached for profit. And why? “Because I do not love you? God knows I do!”

In the Gospel Jesus teaches his disciples how to pray. First he warns against a mistake: “When you are praying, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.” Prayer is not a machine in which more words produce more results. “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” Then why pray at all? Because prayer is not informing God; it is being with him as children with a Father, and letting our hearts be formed by his. So Jesus gives the prayer that has been on Christian lips ever since: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” The first three petitions are about God: his name, his kingdom, his will. Only then come our needs: “Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one.” Tertullian called this prayer “the summary of the whole Gospel” (Catechism 2761), and the early Christians prayed it three times a day (Didache 8). Jesus adds a comment on one petition only, the one about forgiveness: “For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you; but if you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” We cannot pray “Our Father” with a closed heart towards our brothers and sisters.
outline: Opening
Pray the Our Father very slowly together, pausing after each line. Ask: which line was hardest to mean?
Point 1 · A sincere and pure devotion
Paul's divine jealousy for a Church betrothed to Christ alone.
Point 2 · Not many words
Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
Point 3 · Our Father
His name, his kingdom, his will first; then bread, forgiveness and deliverance.
Take-home line
“Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.”
live: One heart for Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3)
Name one thing that draws your heart away from a sincere devotion to Christ, and give it to him today.
Pray the Our Father slowly (Matthew 6:9–13)
Once today, pray the Lord's Prayer as slowly as you can, giving a full breath to each petition.
2027-06-17.prayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Keep us, your Church, a chaste bride for your Son, faithful to the one Jesus, the one Spirit and the one Gospel we have received. Give us today the bread we need, the bread of the earth and the Bread of life. Forgive us as we forgive those who have wronged us, and do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At every Mass, just before Communion, the priest invites us: at the Saviour's command and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say: Our Father. The Lord's Prayer is the table grace of the Eucharist: we ask for our daily bread just before we receive the Bread of life, and we ask forgiveness before we give one another the sign of peace and approach the altar as reconciled children.

2027-06-18.title: Friday of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time
readings: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness
From all their afflictions God will deliver the just
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also
2027-06-18.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 11 (Year I). The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary 34:2–3, 4–5, 6–7 = NRSV 34:1–2, 3–4, 5–6). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-18.verse: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
theo: St Paul's rivals in Corinth boasted of their pedigree, their visions and their eloquence. Paul, who hates boasting, decides to answer them in their own language, but he warns that he is “speaking as a fool.” First, his roots: “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.” Paul never stopped being proud of his Jewish people. Then, “Are they ministers of Christ? I am talking like a madman, I am a better one.” But instead of listing successes, he lists sufferings: “far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless floggings, and often near death.” He received the synagogue's punishment of “forty lashes minus one” five times (Deuteronomy 25:3), a discipline he accepted because he remained a member of the synagogue and went on preaching Christ in it; it is no charge against the Jewish people, among whom Paul counted himself. He was beaten with rods by Roman magistrates three times, stoned once, shipwrecked three times, “adrift at sea” for a night and a day; he faced danger from rivers, bandits, his own people and Gentiles, in city and wilderness and sea; he knew “toil and hardship,” sleepless nights, hunger and thirst, “cold and naked.” And above all, “I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches.” This is the heart of a true pastor: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” Then the surprising conclusion: “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.” Paul's glory is not his strength but the power of Christ shining through his weakness. The Psalm is the prayer of such a man: “This poor soul cried, and was heard by the Lord, and was saved from every trouble.”

In the Gospel Jesus continues the Sermon on the Mount with two short sayings. The first is about treasure: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust consume and where thieves break in and steal.” In the ancient world wealth was kept in fine clothes, which moths eat, and in coins and metals, which rust and which thieves dig through mud walls to steal. Everything earthly passes. “But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven,” which nothing can destroy: love, mercy, faith, the good done for the poor. Then comes the line that unlocks the whole passage: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Our heart follows what we treasure. The second saying is about the eye: “The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light.” The Greek word for healthy, haplous, also means single, undivided, generous; and in Jewish speech an “evil eye” meant a greedy, stingy heart. An eye fixed on God and generous to others fills the whole life with light; an eye fixed on possessions darkens everything. In this month of June, dedicated by popular devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, today's Gospel invites a simple question: where is my heart? The heart of Jesus has only one treasure: the Father's will and our salvation. To love his Heart is to let our hearts be drawn to the same treasure.
outline: Opening
Ask: if a thief broke into my house tonight, what would I most fear to lose? And what can no thief ever take?
Point 1 · Boasting of weakness
Paul's sufferings and his anxiety for all the churches; Christ's power in weakness.
Point 2 · Treasure in heaven
Moth, rust and thieves; the riches that last.
Point 3 · The lamp of the body
A healthy, generous eye fills life with light; where is my heart?
Take-home line
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
live: Pray for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28)
Share Paul's anxiety for the churches: pray today for your parish priest, your bishop, and a persecuted Christian community.
Move one treasure (Matthew 6:20)
Give away today one thing you are too attached to, or spend one hour of your day on someone who cannot repay you.
2027-06-18.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, your apostle Paul boasted only of his weakness, so that your power might dwell in him. Strengthen all who labour and suffer for your Church, and give our pastors a heart full of care for all the churches. Lord, you have taught us that where our treasure is, there our heart will be also: deliver us from greed for what moth and rust consume, make our eye healthy and generous, and draw our hearts to your own Sacred Heart, where our true treasure is. Amen.
altar: The greatest treasure on earth is on the altar: the Body and Blood of Christ, the pledge of the treasure of heaven. Here is the Heart that was pierced for us, and here our hearts learn where to rest. Every Communion is a moment to move our treasure from earth to heaven.

2027-06-19.title: Saturday of the Eleventh Week in Ordinary Time · St Romuald
readings: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness
Taste and see the goodness of the Lord
Strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well
2027-06-19.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 11 (Year I). St Romuald, abbot, may be remembered (optional memorial); by the traditional reckoning he died on 19 June 1027, so this year marks a thousand years since his death. A Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary on Saturday may also be celebrated. The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary Psalm 34:8–13 = NRSV 34:7–12). Liturgical colour: green (white if a memorial is kept).
2027-06-19.verse: but he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” So, I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.
theo: For several days Paul has been answering people in Corinth who compared him with smooth, impressive preachers and found him wanting. Today he reaches the strangest part of his defence. If they want boasting, he will boast, but of what? First he speaks, almost shyly, in the third person: “I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven.” He was “caught up into Paradise and heard things that are not to be told, that no mortal is permitted to repeat.” Then he refuses to build anything on it: “On behalf of such a one I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses.” The revelation is real, but he will not let the Corinthians judge him by it. And now the heart of the passage: “to keep me from being too elated, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to torment me.” We do not know what the thorn was. Some of the Fathers thought of a sickness, others of persecution or of a temptation; Paul never tells us, and perhaps that is a mercy, because every reader can place his own thorn beside Paul's. “Three times I appealed to the Lord about this, that it would leave me.” Paul prayed, and prayed again, as Jesus prayed three times in Gethsemane. The answer was not the one he asked for: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.” The thorn stayed; the grace came. And Paul's whole way of seeing changed: “Therefore I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities for the sake of Christ; for whenever I am weak, then I am strong.” The Psalm is the song of a poor man who learned the same thing: “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them. O taste and see that the LORD is good; happy are those who take refuge in him.”

The Gospel continues the Sermon on the Mount, and Jesus speaks to people who knew what it was to worry about tomorrow's food. He begins with a choice: “No one can serve two masters … You cannot serve God and wealth.” Then he goes to the root of so much of our anxiety: “do not worry about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, or about your body, what you will wear.” He does not tell us to stop working. He tells us to look: “Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?” “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of these.” Worry adds nothing: “can any of you by worrying add a single hour to your span of life?” The answer is not carelessness but a new order of things: “But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.” And then a word of great kindness: “So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will bring worries of its own. Today's trouble is enough for today.” Paul and Jesus say the same thing from two sides: God's grace is enough for today's weakness, and today's bread is enough for today. St Romuald, remembered today, was a young nobleman of Ravenna who turned from a violent world to a life of prayer, and spent his long life founding hermitages and monasteries in Italy; the best known is Camaldoli, in the hills near Arezzo. His followers kept a short rule attributed to him which begins, in substance: sit in your cell as in paradise, and watch your thoughts as a good fisherman watches for fish. It is the Gospel of the lilies put into practice: a heart at rest in God, seeking first his kingdom.
outline: Opening
Ask: what is the one worry that woke you up most often this month?
Point 1 · The thorn that stayed
Paul prays three times and receives not removal but grace.
Point 2 · Power made perfect in weakness
Our weakness becomes the place where Christ's power lives.
Point 3 · Look at the birds, consider the lilies
Seek first the kingdom, and live one day at a time.
Take-home line
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
live: Name your thorn (2 Corinthians 12:8)
Bring to the Lord in prayer today one weakness you have asked him many times to remove, and ask instead for the grace to carry it.
One day at a time (Matthew 6:34)
Write down tonight the worries you have for tomorrow, place the paper under your Bible or a crucifix, and leave them there till morning.
saints: St Romuald (c. 951–1027)

Born in Ravenna of a noble family, he turned to God as a young man after his father killed a relative in a quarrel, and did penance as a monk at Sant'Apollinare in Classe. Drawn to solitude, he lived for a time under a hermit's guidance and then spent decades travelling through Italy, reforming monasteries and founding hermitages. The best known is Camaldoli, near Arezzo, from which came the Camaldolese Benedictines, who unite the common life of monks with the solitary life of hermits. He died, by the traditional account, on 19 June 1027 at Val di Castro.
2027-06-19.prayer: Lord God, you know the thorn each of us carries and the worries that keep us awake. When we ask you to take them away and you do not, give us the grace that is sufficient, and let the power of Christ dwell in our weakness. Teach us to look at the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, to seek first your kingdom and its righteousness, and to leave tomorrow in your hands. Through the prayers of St Romuald, give us hearts at rest in you. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: Before Communion the priest shows us the Host and we answer: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. We come to the altar not because we are strong but because we are weak, and the Bread of Life is the grace that is sufficient for this day. Each Mass is our daily bread, given one day at a time.

2027-06-21.title: Saint Aloysius Gonzaga, Religious
readings: Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you
Blessed the people the Lord has chosen to be his own
First take the log out of your own eye
2027-06-21.alt: Memorial. Monday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I): the readings of the weekday are used, and from today until Saturday the first readings follow Abraham in the Book of Genesis. St Aloysius Gonzaga, Jesuit, died in Rome at twenty-three while caring for the sick; he is the patron of young people and of students. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-06-21.verse: Now the Lord said to Abram, “Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.”
theo: This week the first readings take us back to the beginning of the story of salvation: the call of Abraham. The chapters before it are sad ones. Adam and Eve are sent out of the garden, Cain kills Abel, the flood covers the earth, and at Babel people try to build a tower to heaven and end up scattered and unable to understand one another. Humanity has broken into pieces. And then, quietly, God begins again with one man: “Now the LORD said to Abram, ‘Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.’” Three things to leave, in rising order of cost: the country, the clan, the father's house. And no address for the new land, only “the land that I will show you.” Then come the promises, five blessings in a row: “I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” Babel scattered the families of the earth; Abraham's call is God's plan to bless them all. St Paul will say that this was the Gospel preached in advance (Galatians 3:8), fulfilled in Christ, the son of Abraham. The answer is told in a single line: “So Abram went, as the LORD had told him.” He is seventy-five years old. He goes with Sarai his wife and Lot his nephew, and wherever he stops, at Shechem by the oak of Moreh and on the hill east of Bethel, he builds an altar and calls on the name of the Lord. Abraham lives in a tent but marks the land with altars: a pilgrim who worships. The Letter to the Hebrews sums it up: “he set out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). Jews, Christians and Muslims all look to Abraham; the Church calls him “our father in faith,” and the Second Vatican Council reminds us that the Church is spiritually bound to the stock of Abraham, the Jewish people, to whom the promises first belong (Nostra Aetate 4). The Psalm sings of that people: “Happy is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage.”

The Gospel continues the Sermon on the Mount with a word that touches every family, parish and office: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment you make you will be judged, and the measure you give will be the measure you get.” Jesus is not telling us to stop telling right from wrong; a few verses later he will tell us to beware of false prophets and to know a tree by its fruits. What he forbids is the harsh verdict on another person's heart, the condemning spirit that sees every fault in others and none in ourselves. And he paints it with a carpenter's humour: a man with a beam of wood sticking out of his eye, leaning over his brother to remove a speck of sawdust. “You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor's eye.” Notice that Jesus does not say the speck does not matter. He says that only a person who has first dealt honestly with his own sin can help his brother with mercy. St Aloysius Gonzaga, whose memory we keep today, is a good teacher of both readings. Born in 1568, the eldest son of a marquis in northern Italy, he was raised to be a soldier and a ruler, and served as a page at the courts of Florence and Madrid. Like Abraham he left his father's house: at seventeen, after a long struggle with his father, he gave up his right to inherit in favour of his younger brother and entered the Society of Jesus in Rome. He was very strict with himself, and his companions remembered him as gentle and humble with others. In 1591, when plague and famine struck Rome, he begged in the streets for the sick and carried them to the hospital himself; he caught the disease and died on 21 June 1591, at twenty-three. The Church gives him to young people as their patron. In June, when schools and colleges reopen across Kerala, he is a good friend for every student.
outline: Opening
Ask: what would you find hardest to leave if God said “Go”: your town, your family, or your plans?
Point 1 · Go, to the land I will show you
Abraham leaves everything with no map, only a promise.
Point 2 · In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed
God's answer to Babel, fulfilled in Christ.
Point 3 · The log and the speck
Judge yourself honestly first, then help your brother with mercy, like St Aloysius.
Take-home line
“So Abram went, as the Lord had told him.”
live: One step of obedience (Genesis 12:4)
Think of one thing God has been asking of you for some time, and take the first small step today, as Abram set out.
Look for the log (Matthew 7:5)
Before criticising anyone today, stop and name one fault of your own; then speak, if you must, with kindness.
saints: St Aloysius Gonzaga (1568–1591)

Born at Castiglione delle Stiviere in Lombardy, the eldest son of the Marquis Ferrante Gonzaga, he was trained for court and army and served as a page in Florence and at the Spanish court in Madrid. He received his First Communion from St Charles Borromeo. In 1585, after long opposition from his father, he renounced his inheritance in favour of his brother Rodolfo and entered the Jesuit novitiate in Rome; St Robert Bellarmine was his spiritual director. During the epidemic of 1591 he nursed the sick in Rome, caught the infection and died on 21 June 1591, aged twenty-three. Canonised in 1726, he was named patron of students and later of Catholic youth.
2027-06-21.prayer: O God, giver of heavenly gifts, who in Saint Aloysius Gonzaga joined penitence to a wonderful innocence of life, grant, through his merits and intercession, that, though we have failed to follow him in innocence, we may imitate him in penitence. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord God, you called Abraham to leave his father's house and go to the land you would show him. Give us his trust, so that we set out when you call; and give us the humility to look first at our own faults, so that we may help our brothers and sisters with mercy. Bless all students beginning a new year, and keep our young people pure, generous and brave. Amen.
altar: In the First Eucharistic Prayer the priest asks God to accept our offering as he once accepted the sacrifice of Abraham, our father in faith. Abraham built altars wherever he pitched his tent; the Church builds altars wherever she goes, and on them the one sacrifice of Christ, the true son of Abraham through whom all the families of the earth are blessed, is offered for the whole world.

2027-06-22.title: Tuesday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time · St Paulinus of Nola; Sts John Fisher and Thomas More
readings: Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kindred
He who does justice will live in the presence of the Lord
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you
2027-06-22.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 12 (Year I). Two optional memorials may be kept: St Paulinus of Nola, bishop; and Sts John Fisher, bishop, and Thomas More, martyrs. Liturgical colour: green (white if St Paulinus is remembered, red for the martyrs).
2027-06-22.verse: Then Abram said to Lot, “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.”
theo: Abram has come back from Egypt a rich man: “Now Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold.” His nephew Lot has also grown rich, with “flocks and herds and tents.” And riches bring their usual trouble: “the land could not support both of them living together,” and “there was strife between the herders of Abram's livestock and the herders of Lot's livestock.” Every Kerala family that has quarrelled over a boundary wall, a coconut tree on the dividing line or the share of an ancestral house will recognise the scene. Abram is the elder and the head of the clan; by custom the choice is his. But he speaks first for peace: “Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herders and my herders; for we are kindred.” And then he does something astonishing: he gives the choice to the younger man. “Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me. If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left.” Lot looks and sees with the eyes of the market: the plain of the Jordan, “well watered everywhere like the garden of the LORD.” He chooses it, and moves his tent “as far as Sodom.” The narrator adds a quiet warning: “Now the people of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.” What looks best to the eye is not always best for the soul. Then, when Lot has gone, God speaks to Abram, who has kept the poorer hill country: “Raise your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward; for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.” The man who let go receives everything. Abram moves to the oaks of Mamre at Hebron and, as always, builds an altar. The Psalm draws the portrait of such a man: “Those who walk blamelessly, and do what is right, and speak the truth from their heart,” who “stand by their oath even to their hurt” and “do not take a bribe against the innocent.” “Those who do these things shall never be moved.”

The Gospel gathers three sayings from the end of the Sermon on the Mount. The first is about reverence: “Do not give what is holy to dogs; and do not throw your pearls before swine.” Holy things must be treated as holy; the early Christians applied this word to the Eucharist, which, as the Didache says, is only for the baptised. The second is the saying the world calls the Golden Rule: “In everything do to others as you would have them do to you; for this is the law and the prophets.” Jewish teachers before Jesus had taught the same wisdom in its negative form, do not do to others what you hate (Tobit 4:15); Jesus puts it positively, and so turns it from a limit into a programme: do not only avoid harming, but go and do the good you would hope for. Abram did exactly this with Lot. The third saying is the hardest: “Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the road is easy that leads to destruction, and there are many who take it. For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and there are few who find it.” Today's optional memorials show three men who found the narrow gate. St Paulinus of Nola, a rich Roman senator and governor in the fourth century, was baptised, and with his wife Therasia gave away his great wealth to the poor; he settled at Nola near Naples beside the shrine of the martyr St Felix, became a priest and then bishop, and wrote Christian poetry and letters to friends such as Augustine and Jerome. St John Fisher, bishop of Rochester, and St Thomas More, Lord Chancellor of England, were the two most respected men of their country when King Henry VIII demanded an oath that went against their conscience and their communion with the Pope. Under great pressure, almost everyone swore. They stood by the truth “even to their hurt.” Fisher was beheaded on 22 June 1535, More on 6 July. More is reported to have said on the scaffold that he died the king's good servant, but God's first.
outline: Opening
Ask: has a quarrel over land, property or inheritance ever divided your family?
Point 1 · No strife, for we are kindred
Abram chooses peace over property and gives Lot the first choice.
Point 2 · Raise your eyes
The one who lets go receives from God; Lot's eyes lead him toward Sodom.
Point 3 · The golden rule and the narrow gate
Do to others what you would want, and walk the narrow road, like Fisher and More.
Take-home line
“Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kindred.”
live: Make peace over property (Genesis 13:8)
If there is a quarrel in your family or neighbourhood over land, money or an inheritance, take one step toward peace this week, even at some cost to yourself.
Practise the golden rule (Matthew 7:12)
Before speaking to or about anyone today, ask: how would I want to be spoken to or about? Then do that.
saints: St Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431)

Born near Bordeaux of a wealthy Roman family, he became a senator and governor of Campania. Baptised around 389, he and his wife Therasia sold their estates for the poor. He was ordained priest and settled at Nola near Naples beside the tomb of the martyr St Felix, where he cared for pilgrims and the poor; about 409 he became bishop of Nola. A gifted poet, he corresponded with Sts Augustine, Jerome and Martin of Tours.
Sts John Fisher (1469–1535) and Thomas More (1478–1535)

John Fisher, bishop of Rochester and chancellor of the University of Cambridge, was a scholar and a devoted pastor. Thomas More, lawyer, writer and father of a large household, became Lord Chancellor of England. Both refused to take the oath required by King Henry VIII that rejected the authority of the Pope over the Church in England. Fisher, created a cardinal while in prison, was beheaded on 22 June 1535; More on 6 July 1535. They were canonised by Pius XI in 1935; in 2000 St John Paul II named Thomas More patron of statesmen and politicians.
2027-06-22.prayer: O God, who in martyrdom have brought true faith to its highest expression, graciously grant that, strengthened through the intercession of Saint John Fisher and Saint Thomas More, we may confirm by the witness of our life the faith we profess with our lips. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord God, you blessed Abram when he chose peace with his kinsman over the best land. Heal the quarrels in our families over property and inheritance; teach us to do to others as we would have them do to us; and give us courage, like St Paulinus, St John Fisher and St Thomas More, to enter through the narrow gate that leads to life. Amen.
altar: Before Communion the priest prays: Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles, peace I leave you, my peace I give you, look not on our sins but on the faith of your Church, and graciously grant her peace and unity. Then we offer one another a sign of peace. Like Abram with Lot, we may not come to the altar holding on to strife with our kin; the Lord who gives himself to us asks us first to be reconciled (Matthew 5:23–24).

2027-06-23.title: Wednesday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: He believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness
The Lord remembers his covenant for ever (or: Alleluia)
You will know them by their fruits
2027-06-23.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 12 (Year I). Liturgical colour: green. This evening the Vigil Mass of the Nativity of St John the Baptist may be celebrated (white), with its own readings: Jeremiah 1:4–10 (“Before I formed you in the womb I knew you”); Psalm 71:1–2, 3–4a, 5–6ab, 15ab, 17; 1 Peter 1:8–12; Luke 1:5–17, the angel's announcement to Zechariah in the Temple.
2027-06-23.verse: He brought him outside and said, “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your descendants be.” And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.
theo: Some years have passed since Abram left Haran, and the great promise has not moved. He is rich, respected and still childless. Then “the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, ‘Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.’” And for the first time in the Bible we hear Abram answer God with a complaint: “O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?” What use is a reward if there is no son to inherit it? The Bible is not afraid of such honest prayers. God does not rebuke him. He takes him outside under the night sky of the desert: “Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” Then he said to him, “So shall your descendants be.” Nothing in Abram's tent has changed. Sarai is still old and childless. But Abram looks up from his problem to God's sky, and the most important sentence of the chapter follows: “And he believed the LORD; and the LORD reckoned it to him as righteousness.” St Paul will build his teaching on this verse: we are made right with God not by our own achievements but by trusting his promise (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6), a faith that, as St James adds, shows itself in works (James 2:22–23). Then God seals the promise with a strange ceremony. Abram brings a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove and a pigeon, cuts the animals in two and lays the halves opposite each other. In the ancient world the two parties to a treaty walked between such pieces, as if to say: may I be cut in two like these if I break my word (compare Jeremiah 34:18). Abram waits all day, driving away the birds of prey. At sunset a deep sleep falls on him, and a terrifying darkness. And then “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.” Only God passes through. Abram does not. God binds himself alone to his promise. “On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram.” The Psalm sings the same faithfulness: “He is mindful of his covenant forever, of the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham.” The Church teaches that this covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked, “for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; Catechism 121).

In the Gospel Jesus warns his disciples about a danger every generation meets: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” How can we tell them apart? Jesus gives one simple test, said twice: “You will know them by their fruits.” “Are grapes gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles? In the same way, every good tree bears good fruit, but the bad tree bears bad fruit.” A preacher may be eloquent, a video may draw millions of views, a healing service may be crowded; the question is still the fruit. Does this message lead to humility or to pride, to charity or to money, to unity with the Church or to division, to repentance or to excitement only? St Paul named the fruit of the Spirit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Abram's faith was not just a feeling under the stars; its fruit was a whole life of obedience. And tomorrow the Church celebrates the birth of the greatest of the prophets, St John the Baptist, a true prophet whose fruit was this: he pointed away from himself to Christ. This evening, in many parishes, the Vigil Mass of his Nativity is celebrated. Its first reading is the call of Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you,” and its Gospel is the angel's message to the old priest Zechariah in the Temple: your prayer has been heard, and Elizabeth will bear a son, “and you will name him John.” Abram looking at the stars and Zechariah hearing the angel are two old men to whom God says the same thing: nothing is impossible for him.
outline: Opening
Ask: when was the last time you told God honestly what disappointed you?
Point 1 · Count the stars
Abram's honest complaint and God's answer under the night sky.
Point 2 · He believed, and it was reckoned as righteousness
Faith that trusts the promise, and the covenant God alone signs.
Point 3 · By their fruits
How to tell true prophets from false, and the true prophet whose birth we celebrate tomorrow.
Take-home line
“He believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.”
live: Look up (Genesis 15:5)
Tonight, if the monsoon clouds allow, step outside for a minute and look at the sky; if not, look at a picture of it. Tell God the promise you are still waiting for, and say: I believe.
Check the fruit (Matthew 7:16)
Before forwarding a religious message or video this week, ask: does it lead to love, humility and unity with the Church? If not, do not pass it on.
2027-06-23.prayer: Lord God, you said to Abram: do not be afraid, I am your shield. When we are tired of waiting and the promise seems far away, lead us outside to look at your sky, and give us faith like his, which you reckoned as righteousness. You alone passed between the pieces and bound yourself to your covenant; keep us faithful to the new covenant in the blood of your Son. Protect us from false prophets, and make our lives bear the good fruit of your Spirit. As we prepare to celebrate the birth of St John the Baptist, prepare our hearts for Christ. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.
altar: At the consecration the priest says over the chalice: this is the chalice of my Blood, the Blood of the new and eternal covenant. The God who passed alone between the pieces to bind himself to Abram has in Christ bound himself to us for ever, not with the blood of animals but with the Blood of his Son. Every Mass is that covenant renewed and made present.

2027-06-24.title: The Nativity of Saint John the Baptist
readings: The Lord called me before I was born; I will give you as a light to the nations
I praise you, for I am wonderfully made
One is coming after me; I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet
2027-06-24.alt: Solemnity. Mass during the Day (the Vigil Mass, with its own readings, was celebrated yesterday evening). Gloria and Creed. Liturgical colour: white. Apart from the Lord himself, St John the Baptist is the only saint whose birth is kept as a solemnity in the Roman Calendar; the Blessed Virgin Mary's birth is a feast (8 September). The weekday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time is not celebrated today.
2027-06-24.verse: All who heard them pondered them and said, “What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him.
theo: The Church usually celebrates the saints on the day of their death, which she calls their birthday into heaven. Only three births are kept in the calendar: the birth of the Lord at Christmas, the birth of his Mother on 8 September, and today, the birth of John the Baptist. Why John? Because, as the angel told Zechariah, “even before his birth he will be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Luke 1:15). When Mary, carrying the Son of God, came to the house of Elizabeth, the child leapt for joy in his mother's womb (Luke 1:41–44). The Church's tradition has seen in that moment a sanctification of John before his birth; he was born already rejoicing in the Lord. The date itself preaches. The angel said that Elizabeth was in her sixth month when Mary conceived (Luke 1:36), so John's birth is kept six months before Christmas, close to the June solstice. St Augustine noticed that John is born when the days begin to grow shorter and Christ when they begin to grow longer, and he heard in it John's own words: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). The first reading is the second Song of the Servant of the Lord in Isaiah, and it fits John strikingly: “The LORD called me before I was born, while I was in my mother's womb he named me. He made my mouth like a sharp sword … he made me a polished arrow.” The Servant knows discouragement too: “I have labored in vain, I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity.” But God answers with a mission wider than Israel: “I will give you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.” The Servant is fulfilled in Christ, the light of the nations; John, called from the womb and named by God, is the polished arrow sent ahead of him.

Luke's Gospel tells the birth with the joy of a village. “Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown his great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.” Elizabeth had carried the shame of being childless for many years; now the whole hill country of Judea shares her joy. On the eighth day comes the circumcision, when the child receives his name, and the relatives have already decided: he will be Zechariah, like his father. Elizabeth says, “No; he is to be called John.” They protest: “None of your relatives has this name.” They turn to the father, who has been unable to speak since the day he doubted the angel in the Temple. Zechariah asks for a writing tablet and writes four words: “His name is John.” The name in Hebrew, Yohanan, means “the Lord has shown favour.” This child does not belong to the family's plans but to God's grace. And immediately, Luke says, Zechariah's mouth was opened and he began to speak, praising God. The silence of doubt ends in praise. The song he sings, the Benedictus, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked favorably on his people and redeemed them,” is prayed by the whole Church every morning at Lauds. Then Luke records the question of all who heard: “What then will this child become?” For, indeed, the hand of the Lord was with him. The Gospel closes with a single verse that covers some thirty years: “The child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day he appeared publicly to Israel.” Luke tells us that Mary stayed with Elizabeth about three months (Luke 1:56); many have pictured the Mother of the Lord still in that house to see the child born, though the Gospel does not say so. What is certain is that the two mothers, the two children and the two miracles belong together: the barren woman gives birth, and the Virgin conceives the Son of God.

The Psalm lets us pray John's story as our own: “For it was you who formed my inward parts; you knit me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Every child in the womb is known and loved by God before anyone else sees his face; the feast of John's birth is a feast of the dignity of every human life from conception. In the second reading, St Paul, preaching in the synagogue of Pisidian Antioch, tells the story of Israel from the kings to Christ and gives John a place of honour: “before his coming John had already proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.” And he quotes John's own words of humility: “What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but one is coming after me; I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet.” Untying sandals was the work of the lowest servant. The greatest of the prophets, of whom Jesus said that “among those born of women no one has arisen greater” (Matthew 11:11), measured his greatness by his littleness before Christ. St Augustine put it beautifully (in substance): John is the voice, Christ is the Word. The voice is heard for a moment and passes; the Word remains for ever. So today we pray for parents and for children not yet born, for all who are waiting for a child as Elizabeth and Zechariah waited, and for ourselves, that like John we may point away from ourselves to the Lamb of God.
conn: Three birthdays.

The Church keeps the birth of only three persons: Christ (25 December), the Blessed Virgin Mary (8 September) and John the Baptist (24 June). Saints are usually honoured on the day of their death; John's beheading is remembered on 29 August.
Six months before Christmas.
Luke 1:26 and 1:36 place the Annunciation in Elizabeth's sixth month; hence 24 June, six months before 25 December.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
St Augustine linked John 3:30 with the seasons: after John's birth near the June solstice the days shorten, after Christ's birth near the December solstice they lengthen.
The Servant Songs.
Isaiah 49:1–6 is the second of four Songs of the Servant (Isaiah 42; 49; 50; 52–53). The Church sees them fulfilled in Christ; today's liturgy applies the call from the womb to his forerunner.
“His name is John.”
Yohanan means “the Lord has shown favour” or “the Lord is gracious.” Naming a son after his father or a relative was the custom; the new name marks a new beginning from God.
The Benedictus.
Zechariah's song (Luke 1:68–79) is sung or recited every morning in the Liturgy of the Hours at Lauds, as Mary's Magnificat is at Vespers.
In the wilderness.
Luke 1:80 says John lived in the desert until his public mission. The desert was the place of Israel's first love for God (Hosea 2:14) and of preparation for the Lord's coming (Isaiah 40:3).
The sandal-strap.
Untying a master's sandals was work too low even for a disciple, in Jewish custom; John says he is not worthy of it (Acts 13:25; Mark 1:7).
Do, re, mi.

The eighth-century hymn for this feast, Ut queant laxis, attributed to Paul the Deacon, begins each line on a higher note. In the eleventh century Guido of Arezzo used its first syllables, ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la, to teach singing: the names of the musical scale come from a hymn to St John.
altar: At every Mass, just before Communion, the priest lifts the Host and repeats the words of John the Baptist at the Jordan: Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). We answer with the humility of the centurion, and the forerunner's finger still points us to the One who is truly present on the altar.

John prepared the way for Christ; the Eucharist is the Lord's own coming to us now. Like John leaping in Elizabeth's womb when Mary brought Jesus near, we receive with joy the same Lord, truly present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity.
outline: Opening
Ask: who chose your name, and what does it mean? John's name was chosen by God.
Point 1 · Called before I was born
Isaiah's Servant and John: known, named and sent by God from the womb.
Point 2 · His name is John
The family's plans give way to God's grace; Zechariah's silence turns into praise.
Point 3 · What then will this child become?
Every child is wonderfully made; we pray for parents, the unborn and those waiting for a child.
Point 4 · He must increase
The greatest of the prophets is the voice that points to the Word, the Lamb of God.
Closing image
An old priest bending over a writing tablet, writing in large letters: His name is John.
Take-home line
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
live: Thank God for your name and your life (Psalm 139:13–14)
Today, find out what your baptismal name means, and thank God that he knew you before you were born.
Pray for the unborn and for those longing for a child
Pray today for mothers who are expecting, for children in danger of abortion, and for couples who long for a child.
Pray the Benedictus
Pray Zechariah's song (Luke 1:68–79) tomorrow morning, and make it your morning prayer for a week.
Decrease so that he may increase (John 3:30)
Look for one occasion this week to let Christ, or someone else, take the credit you might have claimed.
fathers: St Augustine (in substance)

The Church celebrates the birth of John because it was holy; the birth of no other saint is celebrated so solemnly. John was born when the days begin to shorten, Christ when they begin to lengthen: so John said, He must increase, but I must decrease. John is the voice that passes; Christ is the Word that remains for ever.
St Ambrose (in substance)

Commenting on Luke, he says that the mother heard Mary's greeting first, but the child felt grace first: Elizabeth heard the voice, John perceived the Lord's presence, and leapt for joy before he was born.
St Bede the Venerable (in substance)

John was the forerunner of the Lord in everything: in his birth, in his preaching, in his baptising, and in his death, going before him even into the dark places of death to announce that the Lord was coming.
magis: Catechism 523
St John the Baptist is the Lord's immediate precursor, sent to prepare his way; “prophet of the Most High,” he surpasses all the prophets, of whom he is the last.
Catechism 717–720
John, filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother's womb, is the voice of the Consoler who is coming; in him the Holy Spirit completes the work of preparing a people for the Lord.
Catechism 719
John is “more than a prophet”: in him the Holy Spirit concludes his speaking through the prophets; he inaugurates the Gospel, already from his mother's womb welcoming the coming of Christ.
Catechism 2270

Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5); “you knit me together in my mother's womb” (Psalm 139).
saints: The feast in history

The birth of John was celebrated on 24 June at least from the fourth century: St Augustine preached on it at Hippo. In the Middle Ages it was one of the great feasts of the year, kept in many places with bonfires on the eve. John's beheading is remembered on 29 August.
The coming days

25–26 Jun: weekdays of the Twelfth Week, with the stories of Abraham. 27 Jun: Thirteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time. 28 Jun: St Irenaeus, bishop and martyr (memorial), and in the evening the Vigil of Sts Peter and Paul. 29 Jun: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles (solemnity).
2027-06-24.prayer: O God, who raised up Saint John the Baptist to make ready a nation fit for Christ the Lord, give your people, we pray, the grace of spiritual joys and direct the hearts of all the faithful into the way of salvation and peace. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord, you called John before he was born, filled him with your Spirit and named him for your grace. Thank you for knitting each of us together in our mother's womb. Bless all parents and all children not yet born, and comfort couples who long for a child. Open our mouths, as you opened Zechariah's, to praise you; and make us, like John, glad to decrease so that Christ may increase in us and in our world. Amen.

2027-06-25.title: Friday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless
See how the Lord blesses those who fear him
Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean
2027-06-25.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 12 (Year I). The first reading continues the story of Abraham, read on the weekdays of weeks 12 and 13. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion. Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-25.verse: There was a leper who came to him and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.” He stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I do choose. Be made clean!”
theo: Twenty-four years have passed since Abram left Haran at the word of the Lord. He is now ninety-nine years old, and the son he was promised has still not been born. Then God appears to him again and gives him a name for himself: “I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless.” The Hebrew is El Shaddai, the God who is enough. The command is simple and searching: live your whole life before my face. Then God renews the covenant and seals it in two ways. First, a new name: Abram, “exalted father,” becomes Abraham, “father of a multitude” (Genesis 17:5), and Sarai becomes Sarah, “princess.” In the Bible a new name means a new mission. Second, a sign in the flesh: “This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised.” The covenant is not only an idea in the mind; it is carried in the body, in the family, from generation to generation. Then comes the promise that seems impossible: “I will bless her, and moreover I will give you a son by her.” Abraham falls on his face, and laughs. “Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Can Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?” He even suggests an easier plan: “O that Ishmael might live in your sight!” God does not reject Ishmael; he blesses him and promises to make him a great nation. But the covenant will pass through the child of the impossible: “your wife Sarah shall bear you a son, and you shall name him Isaac.” Isaac means “he laughs.” Abraham's laugh of disbelief will become the laugh of joy at his son's birth. St Paul will say that Abraham “grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God, being fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised” (Romans 4:20–21). The Psalm paints the blessing of a home that walks before the Lord: “Happy is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways,” with children “like olive shoots around your table.”

The Sermon on the Mount is over. “When Jesus had come down from the mountain, great crowds followed him.” St Matthew now shows us that the one who taught with authority also acts with authority: chapters 8 and 9 are a chain of ten mighty works. The first is a meeting with a man nobody wanted to meet. The Law of Moses required a person with a leprous disease to wear torn clothes, cover his lip and cry out “Unclean, unclean,” and to “live alone” outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46). The disease was feared; the loneliness was perhaps worse. This man breaks the distance. He comes, kneels, and says one of the humblest prayers in the Gospel: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.” He does not doubt that Jesus can; he only leaves it to Jesus' will. And Jesus does what no one had done for years: “He stretched out his hand and touched him.” By the Law, touching a leper made a person unclean. Here the opposite happens: the clean hand of Jesus does not become unclean; the man becomes clean. “I do choose. Be made clean!” Then Jesus sends him to the priest, to offer “the gift that Moses commanded” (Leviticus 14). Jesus does not despise the Law; he fulfils it, and gives the man back his place in the worshipping community. Abraham laughed because the promise seemed too great; the leper knelt because he trusted it. Both show us the God who wants to bless: I will establish my covenant, says God to Abraham; I do choose, says Jesus to the leper. In this month of the Sacred Heart, the outstretched hand of Jesus is a picture of his heart: he wants us clean, whole and at home.
outline: Opening
Ask: is there a promise of God that you have stopped expecting because it seems too late?
Point 1 · Walk before me
God Almighty gives Abraham a new name and a covenant carried in his body and family.
Point 2 · The laugh of Abraham
The impossible son: Isaac, “he laughs,” and a faith that grows strong.
Point 3 · I do choose
Jesus touches the leper whom no one touched, and makes him clean.
Take-home line
“Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
live: Walk before God (Genesis 17:1)
At three moments today, morning, noon and night, stop and say: Lord, I am walking before you. Let that thought guide what you do next.
Touch the untouched (Matthew 8:3)
Visit, call or sit beside one person whom others avoid: the sick, the lonely, the one nobody greets.
2027-06-25.prayer: God Almighty, you called Abraham to walk before you and be blameless, and you kept your promise when it seemed too late. Give us a faith that does not waver, that grows strong as it gives you glory. Lord Jesus, you came down from the mountain and stretched out your hand to the leper whom everyone avoided; stretch out your hand to us today. Where we are unclean, make us clean; where we are lonely, bring us home; and make our hands like yours, ready to touch those whom others will not touch. Sacred Heart of Jesus, we trust in you. Amen.
altar: At every Mass, just before Communion, we pray with the words of another man who knelt before Jesus in this same chapter of St Matthew: Lord, I am not worthy. Like the leper, we come with our need and leave it to his will. And in the Eucharist Jesus does more than touch us: he gives himself to us, Body and Blood, and his holiness is not stained by our weakness; it heals it.

2027-06-26.title: Saturday of the Twelfth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
The Lord has remembered his mercy
Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word
2027-06-26.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 12 (Year I). The responsorial psalm is Mary's canticle, the Magnificat. As on other Saturdays in Ordinary Time with no obligatory memorial, the optional memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary on Saturday may be celebrated. Liturgical colour: green (white if the Saturday memorial of Mary is kept).
2027-06-26.verse: The centurion answered, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.”
theo: It is the hottest hour of the day at the oaks of Mamre, near Hebron. Old Abraham is sitting at the entrance of his tent, the time when no sensible traveller is on the road. “He looked up and saw three men standing near him.” What follows is the most famous picture of hospitality in the Bible, and it is full of movement: Abraham “ran from the tent entrance to meet them,” bowed to the ground, “hastened into the tent to Sarah,” “ran to the herd.” A man of ninety-nine is running. He offers “a little water” and “a little bread” and then lays out a feast: cakes from three measures of choice flour, a calf “tender and good,” curds and milk, and he himself stands by them under the tree while they eat, like a servant. The narrator has already told us the secret that Abraham does not yet know: “The LORD appeared to Abraham.” In welcoming three strangers, he is welcoming God. The Letter to the Hebrews remembers this scene: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). Many Fathers of the Church saw in the three visitors, addressed now as “my lord” and now as “they,” a first shadow of the mystery of the Holy Trinity, and the famous Russian icon of Andrei Rublev paints them at Abraham's table. Then the guests ask, “Where is your wife Sarah?” and the promise is repeated, this time in her hearing: “your wife Sarah shall have a son.” Sarah, listening behind the tent flap, laughs to herself, as Abraham had laughed. And the Lord asks the question that runs through the whole Bible: “Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?” Sarah, afraid, denies it: “I did not laugh.” God answers gently and firmly: “Oh yes, you did laugh.” God is not offended by her laugh; he simply will not let her pretend.

Today's psalm is the song of another woman who received a promise that seemed impossible. To Mary in Nazareth the angel Gabriel used almost the same words that were spoken at Mamre: “For nothing will be impossible with God” (Luke 1:37). Sarah laughed and hid; Mary asked her question and then said yes. And her Magnificat ends by reaching back to this very tent: God has helped his servant Israel, “according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever.” On Saturdays the Church likes to honour Mary, and the readings give us good reason today. In the Gospel Jesus enters Capernaum and meets a Roman centurion, an officer of the occupying army, a Gentile. He asks for help for his paralysed servant. Jesus offers to come, and the centurion answers with words that the Church has placed on our lips before every Communion: “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof; but only speak the word, and my servant will be healed.” He knows that Jesus' word is enough, as a soldier's command is enough. Jesus is amazed and promises that “many will come from east and west and will eat with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.” Abraham's table at Mamre has become a table for all nations. The warning that follows, that “the heirs of the kingdom” may be left outside, is addressed to anyone who presumes on God's gifts; it is not a judgment on the Jewish people (Catechism 597–598), and it speaks first of all to us who are already at the table. Then Jesus enters Peter's house and touches the hand of his mother-in-law; the fever leaves her, “and she got up and began to serve him.” By evening he heals all who are brought to him, and Matthew sees the Servant of Isaiah at work: “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.”
outline: Opening
Ask: when did a visitor to your home turn out to be a blessing you did not expect?
Point 1 · Abraham runs to serve
At Mamre, welcoming strangers means welcoming God.
Point 2 · Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
Sarah laughs and hides; Mary believes and sings.
Point 3 · Only speak the word
The centurion's faith, a table for all nations, and a healed woman who serves.
Take-home line
“Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?”
live: Welcome someone (Genesis 18:2)
Invite someone to your table this week, or welcome an unexpected visitor with a little water and a little bread, as Abraham did.
Pray the centurion's words (Matthew 8:8)
At your next Communion, say Lord, I am not worthy slowly and with faith, thinking of one person you are carrying to Jesus, as the centurion carried his servant.
2027-06-26.prayer: Lord God, you came to Abraham at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, and he ran to welcome you. Teach us to see you in the stranger and the guest. When we laugh at your promises or hide our doubts, ask us again: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord? Give us the faith of Mary, who believed that nothing is impossible with you, and the faith of the centurion, who trusted your word alone. Lord Jesus, you took our infirmities and bore our diseases; heal the sick we bring to you today, and raise us up to serve you. Amen.
altar: Before Communion we repeat the centurion's words, changing only one: Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. The roof is now our own heart, and the Guest is the Lord himself, who comes to us in his Body and Blood. Like Abraham at Mamre we do not prepare a feast for God; at the altar God prepares the feast for us.

2027-06-28.title: Saint Irenaeus, Bishop, Martyr and Doctor of the Church
readings: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
The Lord is kind and merciful
Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head
2027-06-28.alt: Memorial of St Irenaeus. Readings of Monday of the Thirteenth Week in Ordinary Time (Year I); proper readings from the Common of Pastors or of Doctors may be used. Liturgical colour: red. This evening the Vigil Mass of the Solemnity of Sts Peter and Paul is celebrated, with its own readings: Acts 3:1–10; Psalm 19:1–4 (Lectionary 19:2–5); Galatians 1:11–20; John 21:15–19.
2027-06-28.verse: Then Abraham came near and said, “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?
theo: The three visitors leave Abraham's tent and look toward Sodom, and the Lord shares a secret with his friend: “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?” Abraham has been chosen so that through him “all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,” and so that he may teach his children “to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice.” A man with such a calling must learn how God judges. “How great is the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah and how very grave their sin!” The word outcry is the cry of victims; the Bible later names the sins of Sodom as pride, excess of food, prosperous ease and neglect of the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49), together with the violence against strangers told in the next chapter. God says he will “go down and see,” like a just judge who examines before he sentences. Then comes one of the most remarkable prayers in the Old Testament. “Abraham remained standing before the LORD.” He comes near and asks: “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?” He does not ask only that the righteous be spared; he asks that the whole city be forgiven for their sake. Six times he presses, from fifty to forty-five, to forty, thirty, twenty, ten, each time with deep humility, “I who am but dust and ashes,” and with great boldness: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” Each time God agrees. The story teaches that the presence of a few righteous people can protect a whole community, and that God is more ready to forgive than we are to ask. Abraham stopped at ten. The prophets would go further (Jeremiah 5:1), and St Paul would see the fulfilment in one righteous man: “by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). The Psalm sings the heart of the God Abraham was speaking to: “He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.”

In the Gospel two men offer to follow Jesus, and he answers each with a hard saying. To an eager scribe who promises, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go,” Jesus says, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” Following him is not a comfortable career; it means sharing the life of a homeless wanderer. To a disciple who asks first to bury his father, Jesus says, “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” The words are shocking, for burying one's parents was a sacred duty in Israel. Jesus is not teaching contempt for parents; he is saying that the call of the kingdom comes before everything, even the holiest human duties, and that those who do not follow him are, in a sense, the dead. St Irenaeus, whom the Church honours today, followed Christ wherever he went. Born in Smyrna in Asia Minor around the year 130, he heard as a boy the preaching of St Polycarp, who had known St John the Apostle. He went to Gaul, became a priest of Lyons, and after the bishop Pothinus died in the persecution of 177 he became bishop there himself. Against the Gnostics, who claimed a secret knowledge and despised the body and the created world, he wrote his great work Against Heresies. He taught that the true faith is the one handed on publicly by the apostles through the bishops who succeeded them, above all in the Church of Rome, founded, he wrote, by the two most glorious apostles Peter and Paul. He loved the body God created and the flesh the Word took on; he wrote that the glory of God is a human being fully alive. Tradition honours him as a martyr, and in 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church with the title Doctor of Unity. Like Abraham, he stood before God for others; like the disciples, he left home to follow Christ to the ends of the known world. And tonight, with the Vigil of Sts Peter and Paul, the Church begins to celebrate the very apostles whose teaching he guarded.
outline: Opening
Ask: when you pray for others, do you give up quickly, or do you stand before God and keep asking?
Point 1 · Abraham stands before the Lord
God shares his plan with his friend, and Abraham intercedes for a sinful city.
Point 2 · For the sake of ten
A few righteous can protect many; one righteous man saves all.
Point 3 · Nowhere to lay his head
Following Jesus comes before comfort and before every other duty.
Point 4 · St Irenaeus, Doctor of Unity
A follower of Christ who guarded the apostles' faith and the goodness of creation.
Take-home line
“Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?”
live: Intercede boldly (Genesis 18:32)
Choose one place, your town, a broken family, a troubled country, and pray for it today with Abraham's humility and persistence.
Follow without delay (Matthew 8:22)
Name one thing you keep postponing that Jesus is asking of you, a confession, a reconciliation, a commitment, and do it this week.
saints: St Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–c. 202)

Born in Smyrna in Asia Minor, a disciple of St Polycarp, who had known St John the Apostle. A priest of Lyons in Gaul, and its bishop after the persecution of 177. In Against Heresies he defended the faith handed down by the apostles through the bishops in succession, especially the Church of Rome, against Gnostic teachers who despised the body. He taught that Christ sums up and renews all creation, and that Mary's obedience undid Eve's disobedience. Honoured as a martyr; declared a Doctor of the Church, the Doctor of Unity, by Pope Francis in 2022.
2027-06-28.prayer: O God, who called the Bishop Saint Irenaeus to confirm true doctrine and peace in the Church, grant, we pray, through his intercession, that, being renewed in faith and charity, we may always be intent on fostering unity and concord. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord God, Judge of all the earth, you are merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. Give us Abraham's courage to stand before you for our cities and our families, and the readiness of true disciples to follow your Son without delay. Through the prayers of St Irenaeus, keep us faithful to the faith of the apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.
altar: At every Mass the priest prays for the Church spread throughout the world, together with the Pope and the bishop, and for all the living and the dead. Like Abraham, the Church stands before the Lord for the whole world. But she does not plead with empty hands: she offers the one sacrifice of the one righteous Man, Jesus Christ, for whose sake God forgives not ten cities but all who turn to him. St Irenaeus wrote that the Church offers to God the first fruits of his creation, bread and wine, which become the Body and Blood of Christ.

2027-06-30.title: Wednesday of the Thirteenth Week in Ordinary Time · The First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church
readings: God has heard the voice of the boy where he is
The Lord hears the cry of the poor
When they saw him, they begged him to leave their neighborhood
2027-06-30.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 13 (Year I). The optional memorial of the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church may be kept: the Christians put to death in Rome under the emperor Nero, remembered on the day after the apostles Peter and Paul. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green (red if the memorial is kept).
2027-06-30.verse: And God heard the voice of the boy; and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven, and said to her, “What troubles you, Hagar? Do not be afraid; for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
theo: The promise is fulfilled at last: “Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.” Sarah's laugh of doubt has become a laugh of joy. But today's reading does not let us rest in the happy ending. At the feast for Isaac's weaning Sarah sees Ishmael, the son of the Egyptian slave woman Hagar, “playing with her son Isaac,” and she demands: “Cast out this slave woman with her son.” Scripture does not hide the hurt in this family. “The matter was very distressing to Abraham on account of his son,” for Ishmael too is his child. God tells Abraham to let them go, because the covenant line will pass through Isaac, but adds a promise for the other son: “As for the son of the slave woman, I will make a nation of him also, because he is your offspring.” Early in the morning Abraham gives Hagar bread and a skin of water and sends her away with the child. The scene in the wilderness of Beer-sheba is one of the most heartbreaking in the Bible. The water runs out. Hagar puts the boy under a bush and sits down “about the distance of a bowshot,” because she cannot bear to watch him die, and she weeps aloud. And then: “God heard the voice of the boy.” The name Ishmael means “God hears.” The angel calls from heaven: “What troubles you, Hagar? Do not be afraid.” Then “God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water.” The well was there all along; she could not see it through her tears. “God was with the boy, and he grew up.” This is the second time Hagar has met God in the desert (Genesis 16), and she is the only person in the Old Testament who gives God a name: “You are El-roi,” the God who sees (Genesis 16:13). The God of Abraham is not the God of one family only; he hears the cry of the outcast, the foreign slave woman, the thirsty child. Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions all remember Hagar and Ishmael. The Psalm sings the same truth: “This poor soul cried, and was heard by the LORD, and was saved from every trouble.”

In the Gospel Jesus crosses the lake to “the country of the Gadarenes,” Gentile territory east of the Sea of Galilee, where pigs were kept. Two men possessed by demons come out of the tombs to meet him, so violent that “no one could pass that way.” They live among the dead, cut off from every human community. The demons recognise Jesus at once and cry out: “What have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” They know that their time is short, that the Son of God has come to destroy their power. They beg to be sent into a herd of swine, and Jesus says one word: “Go!” The whole herd rushes down the steep bank into the sea and perishes. The two men are set at liberty. But the ending is sad and surprising: “the whole town came out to meet Jesus; and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their neighborhood.” They had lost their pigs; they did not want to lose anything more. Two human beings had been restored, but the town counted its losses. It is possible to prefer our comfort, our business and our habits to the Lord who sets people at liberty. Hagar's eyes were opened and she saw the well; the Gadarenes saw the Lord and asked him to go. Today the Church also remembers the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, the many Christians whom Nero blamed for the great fire of the city in the year 64. The Roman historian Tacitus records that they were mocked, torn by dogs, crucified, and burned as torches in the night. Some were probably among those to whom St Paul had written his Letter to the Romans. Their names are known to God alone. Unlike the Gadarenes, they did not ask Jesus to leave; they let everything go rather than lose him.
outline: Opening
Ask: have you ever been unable to see the help God had already placed in front of you, because of your tears?
Point 1 · God hears
Hagar and Ishmael cast out into the desert, and the God who hears the voice of the boy.
Point 2 · God opened her eyes
The well was already there; God gives sight to see his help.
Point 3 · Do not send him away
The Gadarenes ask Jesus to leave; the first martyrs of Rome would not let him go.
Take-home line
“God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.”
live: Hear the outcast (Genesis 21:17)
Notice today one person who is pushed aside, a domestic worker, a migrant, a child in a difficult home, and do something concrete for them.
Do not send Jesus away (Matthew 8:34)
Ask yourself what you are afraid to lose if Jesus enters a part of your life, your money, a habit, a relationship, and let him in.
2027-06-30.prayer: God of Abraham, you heard the voice of the boy Ishmael and opened Hagar's eyes to see the well. Hear the cry of the poor, the outcast and the thirsty in our land, and open our eyes to the help you have already placed before us. Lord Jesus, you crossed the sea to release captives, and some asked you to leave; never let us prefer our possessions to you. Through the prayers of the first martyrs of the Church of Rome, who gave up everything rather than lose you, make us faithful to the end. Amen.
altar: At every Mass we share the water of life that Hagar could not see: Christ himself, who gives himself as food and drink. The first martyrs of Rome received the Eucharist in homes and catacombs, and from it drew the strength to die for him. Before the Gospel, when we sign our forehead, lips and heart, we ask that the Word may open our eyes, as God opened Hagar's.

quick: God calls to Adam, Where are you? Adam and Eve hide and blame; God curses the serpent and promises that the offspring of the woman will strike its head.
Paul does not lose heart: though our outer nature wastes away, our inner nature is renewed day by day, and we have a building from God, eternal in the heavens.
Jesus is accused of being out of his mind and of casting out demons by Beelzebul; he binds the strong man and declares: Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.
2027-06-06.action: Answer God's question tonight, Where are you?, honestly and without excuses.
2027-06-06.question: Am I hiding from God in some part of my life, and blaming others for what is mine?
catechism: The Protoevangelium and the new Eve.
Who are the brothers and sisters of Jesus?
What is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit?
kidsaint: St Norbert

Norbert was a rich young man who loved fine clothes and parties and did not think much about God. One day, riding his horse in a storm, a lightning bolt struck near him and he was thrown to the ground. He heard in his heart: Turn away from evil and do good. Norbert changed his life. He gave away his riches, became a priest, and walked from village to village telling people about Jesus' love. He loved Jesus in the Eucharist very much. Lesson: when God calls you, do not hide; come out and follow him.
2027-06-06.special: Tenth Sunday in Ordinary Time (Year B). Gloria and Creed. The memorial of St Norbert is omitted.
term: Greek for “first Gospel.” The name the Church gives to Genesis 3:15, God's words to the serpent after the fall, the first announcement of the Redeemer: the offspring of the woman will strike the serpent's head. The Fathers and the Church see in it Christ's victory over sin and death and Mary, the new Eve, associated with her Son (Catechism 410–411).

family.explain: After Adam and Eve disobeyed God, they hid. God came looking for them and called: Where are you? God was not looking to punish them only; he was looking for them because he loved them. And he made a promise: one day a child of the woman would defeat the serpent. That child is Jesus! Jesus said that everyone who does God's will is his brother, sister and mother. We can be part of Jesus' family.
family.intention: We pray for children who are afraid or hiding something, and for families where people blame one another.
family.ask: Ask: “When we do something wrong, how can we come out of hiding and say sorry, instead of blaming someone else?”

illus: An illustration

On the first day of school after the summer holidays, in the pouring June rain of Kottayam, a seven-year-old boy who had broken his new slate hid behind the water tank instead of going to class. His father, coming to pick him up in the evening, was told he had never arrived. He searched for an hour, calling his name in the rain. When he found him, soaked and shivering, the boy began at once: it was not my fault, the other boy pushed me. The father did not ask about the slate. He only said: I was afraid I had lost you. Years later the son, now a father himself, said that was the day he understood Genesis 3. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you called to Adam, Where are you? Here we are, Lord, gathered in your presence. Out of the depths we cry to you; hear our voice. Amen.
share: Where are you? (Genesis 3:9). Where am I hiding from God, and why?
So we do not lose heart (2 Corinthians 4:16). What is wearing out in my outer life, and how is God renewing me within?
Whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35). How do I find out the will of God, and do I do it?
pm.resp: With the Lord there is steadfast love, and with him is great power to redeem.
interc: For the Church, the family of Jesus, that all her members may seek and do the will of God.
For those who are hiding from God out of shame or fear, that they may hear his voice calling them in love.
For families divided by blame and quarrels, that they may learn to say: I am sorry.
For the elderly and the sick whose strength is wasting away, that their inner nature may be renewed day by day.
For students and teachers as schools reopen in Kerala, and for all who suffer in the monsoon rains.
