2027-06-22.action: Take one step toward peace in a family or neighbourhood quarrel, even at some cost to yourself.
2027-06-22.question: Do I care more about my share than about peace with my brothers and sisters?
kidsaint: St John Fisher

John Fisher was a bishop in England about five hundred years ago. He was a very clever teacher at the university, but he also loved the poor people of his diocese and visited them often. When the king ordered everyone to say that the king, and not the Pope, was the head of the Church in England, Bishop John said no, gently but firmly. He was old and sick, but he was put in prison and then put to death. Before he died he read a verse from St John's Gospel: this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God. Lesson: even when everyone else does what is wrong, ask Jesus for courage to do what is right.

family.explain: Abram and his nephew Lot had so many sheep and cows that their shepherds began to fight about the grass. Abram said: let us not fight, we are family! You choose first which land you want. Lot took the best land, but God gave Abram an even bigger blessing. Jesus said: do to others what you would like them to do to you.
family.intention: We pray for families who are quarrelling about land or money, that they may make peace.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone in our family or among our neighbours we should make peace with? What can we do first?”

illus: An illustration

Two brothers in a village near Pala had not spoken for eleven years because of a dispute over three cents of land and a well on the boundary. The case went from one court to another, and the lawyers' fees were greater than the price of the land. One Sunday the elder brother heard Genesis 13 read at Mass and could not sleep that night. The next morning he walked to his brother's house, which he had not entered in eleven years, and said: take the well and the land; I want my brother back. The younger brother withdrew the case the same week. Their families now share the well. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are our peace. Heal our quarrels, teach us your golden rule, and give us courage for the narrow way. Amen.
share: Let there be no strife between you and me … for we are kindred (Genesis 13:8). Where is there strife in my family or community that I could help to heal?
Raise your eyes now, and look (Genesis 13:14). When I gave something up for peace, how did God bless me?
In everything do to others as you would have them do to you (Matthew 7:12). How would my words and actions change if I lived this rule today?
pm.resp: He who does justice will live in the presence of the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that her children may be peacemakers in families divided by property and inheritance.
For lawyers, judges and politicians, through the prayers of St Thomas More, that they may serve the common good and keep their conscience clean.
For bishops, through the prayers of St John Fisher and St Paulinus, that they may be faithful shepherds and lovers of the poor.
For Christians who suffer for refusing to act against their conscience.
For our group, that we may choose the narrow gate and practise the golden rule at home.
pm.close: Father, you blessed Abram for choosing peace. Make us peacemakers, and lead us by the narrow road to life. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Abram complains honestly that he is still childless; God takes him outside and tells him to count the stars: so shall your descendants be.
Abram believed the Lord, and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness; God seals the covenant by passing alone between the pieces as a smoking fire pot and flaming torch.
Jesus warns against false prophets in sheep's clothing: you will know them by their fruits.
2027-06-23.action: Tell God honestly about a promise you are still waiting for, and make an act of faith in him.
2027-06-23.question: What fruit does my faith bear in my daily life?

family.explain: Abram was sad because he had no children. One night God took him outside and said: look at the sky! Can you count the stars? Your family will be as many as the stars. Abram could not see how it could happen, but he believed God. And God was very pleased with his faith. Jesus also said: a good tree gives good fruit. When we believe in God, our lives should be full of good fruit, like kindness and patience.
family.intention: We pray for couples who long for children, and for all who are waiting for a promise of God to come true.
family.ask: Ask: “What good fruit can each of us show this week at home?” Then, if the sky is clear, go out together and count the stars.

illus: An illustration

A couple in Kannur waited eleven years for a child. Friends offered advice, relatives asked questions, and some well-meaning people gave them the numbers of preachers who promised a baby within a year for a donation. The wife said later that what kept her faith alive was not those promises but an old priest who told her to read Genesis 15 every night for a month and simply say, like Abram: I believe. Their son was born in the twelfth year. She says she would have kept believing even if he had not been, because she had learned to look at the stars and not only at her own tent. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you are our shield and our great reward. Increase our faith, keep us faithful to your covenant, and make our lives bear good fruit. Amen.
share: O Lord God, what will you give me? (Genesis 15:2). What disappointment do I need to bring honestly to God in prayer?
He believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). When has trusting God's promise changed the way I live?
You will know them by their fruits (Matthew 7:20). What fruit are others seeing in my life?
pm.resp: The Lord remembers his covenant for ever.
interc: For the Church, that her faith in God's promises may never grow tired.
For the Jewish people, the children of Abraham, to whom God's covenant and promises belong.
For couples longing for a child, and for all who wait for an answer from God.
For all preachers and teachers of the faith, that their words and lives may bear good fruit, and for those misled by false prophets.
For our group, that as we prepare for the birth of St John the Baptist, we may become heralds of Christ.
pm.close: Father, you remember your covenant for ever. Make us children of Abraham by faith, and fruitful trees in your garden. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Isaiah's Servant was called by the Lord before he was born and given as a light to the nations; the Church sees this fulfilled in Christ and applies it to John, his forerunner.
When John is born, Elizabeth and Zechariah, against the family's custom, name him John, “the Lord has shown favour”; Zechariah's mouth is opened and he praises God.
John, the greatest of the prophets, says: I am not worthy to untie his sandals; he must increase, but I must decrease.
2027-06-24.action: Thank God for your life and your name today, and pray for mothers expecting a child.
2027-06-24.question: Do I point others to Christ, or to myself?
catechism: How did the Holy Spirit work in John?
Why must human life be protected from conception?
kidsaint: St John the Baptist

Zechariah and Elizabeth were very old and had no children. Then God sent an angel to say: you will have a son, and you will call him John. Before John was even born, when Mary came to visit carrying baby Jesus inside her, little John jumped for joy inside his mother! When he grew up, he lived in the desert, wore clothes of camel's hair and ate locusts and wild honey. He told everyone: get ready, Jesus is coming! When he saw Jesus, he pointed and said: Look, the Lamb of God! He never wanted people to look at him, only at Jesus. Lesson: help your friends to know Jesus, and be happy when Jesus gets all the attention.
2027-06-24.special: Solemnity of the Nativity of St John the Baptist. Gloria and Creed. Mass during the Day; the Vigil Mass was celebrated on the evening of 23 June.
term: The title given to John the Baptist: the one who runs ahead to announce the coming of the Lord and prepare his way (Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 3:1; Luke 1:76). John was the precursor of Christ in his birth, his preaching, his baptising and his death (Catechism 523).

family.explain: Elizabeth and Zechariah were very old when God gave them a baby boy. Everyone wanted to call him Zechariah, like his father, but Elizabeth said: no, his name is John! Zechariah, who could not speak, wrote on a tablet: His name is John. At once he could speak again, and he praised God. Everyone wondered: what will this child become? John grew up to be the one who pointed to Jesus.
family.intention: We pray for mothers who are expecting a baby, for babies not yet born, and for couples who are waiting for a child.
family.ask: Ask: “Do we know what our names mean, and who our patron saints are?” Then let each person tell one thing they thank God for in their own life.

illus: An illustration

A grandmother in Aluva kept a small notebook in which she wrote the date and time of birth of each of her eleven grandchildren, and next to each name a verse from the Bible she had prayed for that child before he or she was born. When her eldest grandson went abroad to study, she gave him a photocopy of his page. On it was Psalm 139: you knit me together in my mother's womb. He told his friends years later that whenever he felt lost or unimportant in a big foreign city, he looked at that page and remembered that he had been known and loved before anyone had seen his face. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you called John the Baptist from his mother's womb to prepare the way of your Son. Open our hearts to praise you, and make us heralds of Christ. Amen.
share: The Lord called me before I was born (Isaiah 49:1). What difference does it make to me that God knew and called me before I was born?
His name is John (Luke 1:63). In what area of my life do I need to let God's plan take the place of what others expect of me?
I am not worthy to untie the thong of the sandals on his feet (Acts 13:25). Where do I need to decrease so that Christ may increase in me?
pm.resp: I praise you, for I am wonderfully made.
interc: For the Church, that like John the Baptist she may always point the world to Christ, the Lamb of God.
For mothers who are expecting a child, that they may give birth safely, and for every unborn child, that its life may be protected.
For couples who long for a child, that they may find comfort in the God who heard Zechariah and Elizabeth.
For all who prepare the way of the Lord: parents, catechists, teachers, priests and missionaries.
For our group, that our mouths may be opened, like Zechariah's, to praise God and to witness to Christ.
pm.close: Father, you gave John the Baptist to prepare a people for your Son. Fill us with the joy of the Holy Spirit, and make us ready for his coming. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: God appears to Abraham as God Almighty, changes his name and Sarai's, and gives circumcision as the sign of the covenant.
Abraham laughs at the promise of a son at a hundred years; God names the child Isaac and also blesses Ishmael.
Jesus comes down from the mountain, touches a leper and says: I do choose. Be made clean!
2027-06-25.action: Spend time today with one person others tend to avoid.
2027-06-25.question: Do I pray, “Lord, if you choose,” and then trust his will, or do I only tell him what to do?

family.explain: A man was very sick with a skin disease, and people were afraid to come near him. He had to live alone. He knelt in front of Jesus and said: Lord, if you want, you can make me clean. Jesus did not run away. He touched him! And the man was healed. Long before, God had promised old Abraham and Sarah a baby, and they laughed because they were so old. But God keeps his promises.
family.intention: We pray for people who are sick and lonely, and for families who are waiting for a child.
family.ask: Ask: “Who in our school, street or parish is left alone? How can we be kind to them this week?”

illus: An illustration

For many years a small leprosy hospital near the Kerala coast was cared for by religious sisters. A visitor once asked an old patient, whose fingers were long gone, what had helped him most in all his years there. He did not speak of the medicines. He said: the first day I came, sister held my hand while she dressed my wound. Nobody had held my hand for eleven years. Then I knew God had not left me. The touch came before the cure, and it was the touch he remembered. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: God Almighty, you are faithful to your promises. Lord Jesus, stretch out your hand over us and make us clean. Amen.
share: Walk before me, and be blameless (Genesis 17:1). What would change in my day if I remembered that I am always walking before God's face?
Abraham fell on his face and laughed (Genesis 17:17). Which of God's promises do I find hard to believe in my own life?
He stretched out his hand and touched him (Matthew 8:3). Whom am I keeping at a distance, and how could I reach out to them?
pm.resp: See how the Lord blesses those who fear him.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a home where the rejected find welcome and healing.
For people with leprosy and other diseases that bring shame and isolation, and for those who care for them.
For couples longing for a child, that they may trust in God's love and find comfort.
For good relations between Jews, Christians and Muslims, who all honour Abraham as father in faith.
For our group, that we may pray with the leper's humility: Lord, if you choose.
pm.close: Father, you made Abraham the father of many nations and in Jesus you touch and heal us. Keep us in your covenant and make our hands instruments of your mercy. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Abraham runs to welcome three strangers at Mamre, and in them the Lord himself visits him.
Sarah laughs at the promise of a son; the Lord asks: Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
A Gentile centurion trusts Jesus' word alone, and Jesus heals his servant, Peter's mother-in-law and many sick.
2027-06-26.action: Welcome someone into your home this week with simple hospitality.
2027-06-26.question: Do I trust that Jesus' word is enough, or do I always need to see before I believe?

family.explain: Abraham was sitting outside his tent on a very hot day. He saw three visitors and he ran to meet them! He gave them water to wash their feet, fresh bread, meat and milk, and he stood beside them like a servant. Abraham did not know it yet, but God was visiting him. When we welcome guests kindly, we welcome God too.
family.intention: We pray for travellers, for migrant workers far from home, and for families who welcome guests.
family.ask: Ask: “Whom can our family invite for a meal, or help with a kind welcome, this month?”

illus: An illustration

In many old Syrian Christian and Hindu homes of Kerala there was a custom: a kindi of water stood at the front step so that any visitor could wash his feet before entering, and no one who came at mealtime was sent away without rice. A grandmother in Thrissur used to say to her grandchildren: never ask who it is before you put the water out; you do not know whom God is sending. One monsoon evening a drenched young priest, newly posted to the parish and lost on the way, knocked at that door. He was welcomed, fed and dried before anyone knew who he was. Years later, at her funeral, he preached on Genesis 18. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you visited Abraham at Mamre. Visit us now, and make us a people who welcome you in every guest. Amen.
share: He ran from the tent entrance to meet them (Genesis 18:2). How do I receive unexpected guests, at home, in the parish, in my plans?
Is anything too wonderful for the Lord? (Genesis 18:14). In which situation of my life do I need to hear this question today?
Only speak the word, and my servant will be healed (Matthew 8:8). Whom am I carrying to Jesus in prayer, as the centurion carried his servant?
pm.resp: The Lord has remembered his mercy.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a house of welcome for strangers, migrants and the poor.
For families who are waiting for a child, and for all who wait for a promise of God that seems impossible.
For soldiers, police officers and all who hold authority, that they may use it with humility and faith like the centurion.
For the sick of our parish, and for those who serve them as Peter's mother-in-law served the Lord.
For our group, that through the prayers of Mary we may believe that nothing is impossible with God.
pm.close: Father, you remembered your promise to Abraham and fulfilled it in Christ. Welcome us at your table with all the nations. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: The Lord shares his plan with Abraham, and Abraham pleads for Sodom: will God sweep away the righteous with the wicked?
Abraham bargains from fifty righteous down to ten, and God agrees each time to forgive the city for their sake.
Jesus warns would-be followers that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head and that the call of the kingdom comes first.
2027-06-28.action: Pray for your town or village today with Abraham's persistence.
2027-06-28.question: Do I give up quickly when I pray for others, or do I stand before the Lord?
kidsaint: St Irenaeus

When Irenaeus was a boy in a city called Smyrna, he listened to a holy old bishop named Polycarp, who had known St John, the friend of Jesus. Irenaeus never forgot what he heard. He travelled far away to France and became bishop of Lyons. Some people were teaching strange secret ideas and saying that our bodies and God's world are bad. Irenaeus wrote big books to explain the true faith of the apostles: God made the world good, and Jesus became a real man to save us. Lesson: hold on to the faith handed down to you, and share it clearly and kindly.

family.explain: Abraham was God's friend. When God said that the city of Sodom was very wicked, Abraham prayed for the city. He asked: if there are fifty good people there, will you save it? God said yes. Then he asked for forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and even ten! Each time God said yes. God loves it when we pray for others and keep on asking.
family.intention: We pray for our town or village, for our country, and for anyone we know who is far from God.
family.ask: Ask: “For which place or which person shall our family pray every night this week, like Abraham?”

illus: An illustration

In a small town in central Kerala, an elderly widow was known in the parish for one thing: every evening at six she knelt on her veranda facing the road and prayed the rosary aloud for the whole street, house by house, naming each family, Christian, Hindu and Muslim alike. When she died, a Muslim neighbour came to the funeral and told the priest: we always knew someone was praying for us at six o'clock; now who will stand before God for our street? The priest thought of Abraham: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, merciful and gracious, teach us to stand before you for others, and to follow your Son wherever he goes. Amen.
share: Abraham remained standing before the Lord (Genesis 18:22). For whom is God asking me to stand before him in prayer?
Let me take it upon myself to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes (Genesis 18:27). How do humility and boldness come together in my prayer?
Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead (Matthew 8:22). What am I putting before the call of Jesus?
pm.resp: The Lord is kind and merciful.
interc: For the Church, that following St Irenaeus she may guard the faith of the apostles in unity and peace.
For our towns and cities, especially places of violence and injustice against the poor and the stranger, that God may spare them and convert hearts.
For bishops and theologians, that they may teach the truth clearly and lovingly.
For all who are discerning a call to the priesthood or religious life, that they may follow Christ without delay.
For our group, that we may become persistent intercessors for our neighbourhood.
pm.close: Father, for the sake of your righteous Son you forgive the many. Hear the prayers we make for others, and keep us faithful to the faith of Peter and Paul. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

quick: Sarah asks Abraham to send away Hagar and Ishmael; in the desert, when the water runs out, God hears the boy's voice and opens Hagar's eyes to see a well.
God promises to make Ishmael too a great nation, for he is Abraham's son.
Jesus delivers two possessed men in the land of the Gadarenes, but the town begs him to leave.
2027-06-30.action: Do one concrete good thing today for someone who is pushed aside.
2027-06-30.question: Is there a part of my life where I am asking Jesus to leave because I am afraid of what it will cost?
kidsaint: The First Martyrs of Rome

Not long after Jesus rose from the dead, there were many Christians in the big city of Rome. In the year 64 a terrible fire burned much of the city, and the cruel emperor Nero blamed the Christians. Many of them, men, women and young people, were killed because they would not stop believing in Jesus. We do not know their names, but God knows every one of them. Lesson: even if nobody knows your name, God sees your faithfulness and loves you.

family.explain: Hagar and her little boy Ishmael were sent away into the desert. When their water was finished, Hagar was so sad that she sat down and cried. But God heard the voice of the boy! An angel said: do not be afraid. Then God opened Hagar's eyes and she saw a well of water. God hears children when they cry, and he cares for people whom others push away.
family.intention: We pray for children who are thirsty, hungry or abandoned, and for mothers who struggle alone.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone our family can help this week, someone who feels left out or alone?”

illus: An illustration

A social worker in Kochi tells of a young mother from a northern state who was left without money or papers when the contractor her husband worked for disappeared. For two days she sat with her small son outside the railway station, too frightened and ashamed to ask anyone for help. On the third morning a parish volunteer who sold tea nearby noticed the boy crying and asked what was wrong. Within a day the parish's migrant help desk had found them food, shelter and a way home. The mother said later: the help was in the same street all along; I could not see it until someone heard my son. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: God who sees and hears, open our eyes to see your help and our ears to hear the cry of the poor. Amen.
share: God heard the voice of the boy (Genesis 21:17). Whose cry around me am I being asked to hear today?
God opened her eyes and she saw a well of water (Genesis 21:19). Where has God's help been near me while I could see only my troubles?
They begged him to leave their neighborhood (Matthew 8:34). What am I afraid to lose if I let Jesus fully into my life?
pm.resp: The Lord hears the cry of the poor.
interc: For the Church, that she may always hear the cry of the outcast and the stranger, as God heard Hagar and Ishmael.
For migrant workers and their families in Kerala and across India, especially those without help or papers.
For all who are possessed by addiction, violence or despair, that Christ may deliver them.
For Christians persecuted today, through the prayers of the first martyrs of Rome.
For our group, that we may never prefer our comfort or possessions to the Lord.
pm.close: Father, you hear the poor and release captives in your Son. Open our eyes to see your gifts and keep us faithful to Christ. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, after the great feasts of Pentecost, the Holy Trinity and the Body and Blood of Christ, we come back today to the green Sundays of Ordinary Time. And the first reading takes us back to the very beginning, to a garden, and to a question. Adam and Eve have disobeyed. They hear God walking in the garden, and they hide. And God calls: where are you? (Genesis 3:9).

It is the first question God asks in the whole Bible, and he is still asking it. Not as a policeman, but as a father whose child has run away. God knows where Adam is. But Adam needs to say it. And notice what Adam says: I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid. Sin always does this. It makes us afraid of the God who loves us. And then comes the blame: the woman you gave me, she gave me the fruit. The woman says: the serpent tricked me. Nobody says, I did it. How often in our families do we do the same: it is his fault, it is her fault, it is the government's fault.

But God does not give up on them. Speaking to the serpent, he makes a promise: I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head (Genesis 3:15). This is the first Good News in the Bible. One day a child of the woman will crush the serpent. That child is Jesus, and the woman, in the fullest sense, is Mary, the new Eve, who said yes where Eve said no.

In the Gospel we see that promise coming true. The scribes say Jesus is working with the devil. Jesus answers: no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his property without first tying up the strong man (Mark 3:27). Satan is the strong man who has held us captive since the garden. Jesus is the stronger one who has come to tie him up and set us loose. Every exorcism, every confession, every Baptism is a sign that the strong man is bound.

Jesus also warns about the sin against the Holy Spirit, which cannot be forgiven. Do not be frightened by this. It does not mean that God's mercy has a limit. It means that if someone refuses God's mercy to the very end, saying that God's goodness is evil, he shuts the door from the inside. Anyone who is worried that he has committed this sin has not committed it, because he still wants God's mercy.

Finally, his mother and his relatives stand outside, and Jesus says: whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:35). He is not pushing his mother away. He is praising her! No one did the will of God like Mary: here am I, the servant of the Lord. And he opens the door to us. You and I can be the family of Jesus. So let us answer God's question today: where are you? Here I am, Lord. I come out of hiding. I want to do your will. And as St Paul says, let us not lose heart, for God is preparing for us a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever broken something and then hidden so that nobody would find you? That is what Adam and Eve did after they disobeyed God. They hid in the garden. But God came looking for them and called: where are you? God was not coming to shout at them. He came because he loved them and wanted them back.

Jesus is God's answer to Adam and Eve. He came to beat the devil and bring us back home. And he said that everyone who does what God wants is part of his family. So when you do something wrong, do not hide. Say sorry to God and to your parents, and you will feel his love.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, in these monsoon weeks we know what a storm is. The rain beats on the roof, the rivers rise, and on our coasts the fishing boats lie on the sand while the sea roars. Today the Word of God takes us out onto the water, into a storm, and asks us a simple question: who is in the boat with you?

In the first reading God answers Job out of the whirlwind. Job had suffered terribly and asked God why. God does not give him an explanation. He speaks of the sea. Who shut in the sea with doors when it burst out from the womb? (Job 38:8). To us the sea is huge and frightening. To God it is like a newborn baby wrapped in cloth. And God says to it: thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stopped (Job 38:11). Every storm has a limit, and God sets it.

In the Gospel the disciples are on the lake at night. A great windstorm comes, the waves fill the boat, and these strong fishermen are terrified. And Jesus is asleep on a cushion in the stern. They wake him: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). Have we not prayed like that? Lord, my child is sick, my husband has no work, my family is breaking: do you not care?

Jesus gets up. He rebukes the wind and says to the sea: Peace! Be still! And there is a dead calm (Mark 4:39). Then he asks them: why are you afraid? Have you still no faith? And they ask each other: who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? The answer is in the first reading. Only God can command the sea. The man sleeping on the cushion is the Lord of creation. He is truly man, tired enough to sleep in a storm, and truly God, able to calm it with a word.

St Paul tells us what this Lord has done for us: the love of Christ urges us on, because we are convinced that one has died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14). He went down into the greatest storm, death itself, and came out victorious. So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation. Jesus does not promise that our boat will never meet a storm. He promises that he is in the boat, and that the storm will not have the last word.

Today many of us remember our fathers. A good father is not a man who never faces storms. He is a man who stays in the boat with his family and keeps calling on the Lord. Let us pray for our fathers, for our fishermen at sea, and for everyone in a storm today. And when we are afraid, let us not be ashamed to wake the Lord with our prayer. He hears, and he says to us: Peace! Be still! Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever been frightened by thunder and lightning at night? Jesus' friends were in a boat when a huge storm came, and the waves splashed in. They were very scared. But Jesus was asleep! They woke him up, and Jesus stood up and said to the wind: Peace! Be still! And the storm stopped.

Jesus is stronger than every storm. So when you hear thunder, or when something at school or at home makes you afraid, you can say: Jesus, you are with me. I am not afraid. And today, give your Papa a big hug and say thank you to him.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, every one of us has stood beside a sickbed or a coffin. Every one of us knows the fear of a phone call at night. Today's readings speak straight into that fear. The Book of Wisdom says: God did not make death, and he does not delight in the death of the living (Wisdom 1:13). God created us for incorruption, in the image of his own eternity. Death was not his plan. It entered through the devil's envy. God is on the side of life.

In the Gospel two people come to Jesus. One is important: Jairus, a leader of the synagogue. He falls at Jesus' feet: my little daughter is at the point of death. The other is nobody: a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, has spent all her money on doctors and has only grown worse. Her illness made her unclean, so she should not even be in the crowd. She does not dare to speak. She only thinks: if I but touch his clothes, I will be made well (Mark 5:28).

Many people are pressing against Jesus. But only one touches him with faith. And Jesus stops everything: who touched my clothes? He will not let her slip away healed in body but still hiding in shame. He wants to look at her. And when she tells him the whole truth, he calls her Daughter. Your faith has made you well; go in peace. Dear friends, we come to Mass every Sunday, we press around Jesus. But do we touch him? At Communion today, let us touch him with faith.

While Jesus is still speaking, the terrible news comes for Jairus: your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any further? It is too late. And Jesus says to that father the words he says to every one of us: do not fear, only believe (Mark 5:36). He goes into the house where people are already wailing. He says: the child is not dead but sleeping, and they laugh at him. Then he takes the girl by the hand and says: Talitha cum, little girl, get up. And she gets up and walks.

Jesus has not yet abolished death in this story; the girl will one day die again. But he shows us that for him death is like sleep, and he can wake us with a word. That is why on Easter morning he rose, and why we bury our dead in the hope of the resurrection. And until then he takes our sick by the hand through the Church, in the Anointing of the Sick and in Holy Communion, the medicine of immortality.

St Paul adds one more thing. You know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). The one who raises us to life asks us to lift others up: the poor, the sick, the grieving. Today, as many parishes collect Peter's Pence for the Holy Father's works of charity, let us give generously. And whatever darkness we carry this week, let us hear his voice: do not fear, only believe. Amen.
kids: Children, a little girl twelve years old was very sick, and her daddy Jairus ran to Jesus for help. But before they reached home, people came and said: she has died. Jesus said to her daddy: do not be afraid, just believe! Then Jesus went into her room, held her hand, and said: Talitha cum, which means little girl, get up! And she got up and walked! Then Jesus said: give her something to eat.

Jesus is stronger than every sickness and even stronger than death. When someone you love is sick, hold your hands together and say: Jesus, I believe in you. And when you go to sleep tonight, remember that Jesus holds your hand too.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today the Church celebrates two great men together, Peter and Paul. They were very different. Peter was a fisherman from Galilee, with rough hands and a quick tongue. Paul was a learned man from Tarsus, a Pharisee who once persecuted the Church. They even argued with each other. But Christ made them the two pillars of his Church, and both gave their lives for him in Rome. Over their tombs stand today two great basilicas, and from every nation pilgrims come to pray there.

In the Gospel Jesus asks his disciples: who do people say that the Son of Man is? That is an easy question. We can all report what others say about Jesus: a good teacher, a prophet, a great man. Then comes the hard question: but who do you say that I am? (Matthew 16:15). Nobody can answer that for us, not our parents, not the priest. Peter answers: you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. And Jesus says: flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven. Faith is a gift. Let us ask for it today.

Then Jesus says to Peter: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:18–19). A rock that holds firm, keys that open and close. Jesus knew that his Church would need a visible shepherd to keep it together. That ministry did not end with Peter. Today it is carried by Pope Leo XIV. We do not follow the Pope because he is clever or because we like him; we follow him because Christ built his Church on Peter and his successors. And we pray for him, because his burden is heavy.

Do not forget: this rock was a weak man. Peter sank in the water. He denied Jesus three times. But the Lord prayed for him that his faith might not fail, and after the Resurrection asked him three times: do you love me? Feed my sheep. The Church is not built on Peter's strength but on Christ's mercy to Peter. That gives hope to all of us who are weak.

In the first reading Peter is in prison, chained between two soldiers, waiting for death. And what does the Church do? While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him (Acts 12:5). And the chains fell off. Dear friends, there are Christians in prison today, in many countries, also in our own. There are priests and bishops under pressure. Do we pray for them fervently? Peter was rescued by the prayer of the Church.

And Paul, at the end of his life, writes from prison: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). Could we say that at the end of our lives? Let us ask Peter to give us his faith, and Paul to give us his courage. And let us leave this church today with Peter's answer in our hearts and on our lips: you are the Messiah, the Son of the living God. Amen.
kids: Children, today we celebrate two of Jesus' best friends, Peter and Paul. Peter was a fisherman. Jesus asked him: who do you say that I am? Peter said: you are the Son of God! Jesus said: you are Peter, the rock! I will build my Church on you, and I will give you the keys of heaven. Today the Pope takes Peter's place, and we pray for him.

Paul travelled far, far away, on ships and on foot, to tell people about Jesus. At the end of his life he said: I ran the race and I kept the faith! Let us ask Peter and Paul to help us love Jesus and tell others about him. And tonight, say one Hail Mary for the Pope.

homily: Dear friends, in these weeks of June the monsoon arrives in Kerala, and anyone who has lived in a village knows what happens after the first rains. The dry red earth turns green almost overnight. Seeds that lay hidden in the soil for months suddenly push up their small shoots. Nobody pulled them up; nobody told them to grow. Today's readings are full of this mystery of growth.

In the first reading Ezekiel speaks to a people in exile. Their king has been taken to Babylon, the royal tree of David seems cut down. And God says: I myself will take a sprig from the lofty top of a cedar; I will set it out (Ezekiel 17:22). What the great empires broke, God replants. And the small, tender shoot becomes a noble cedar where every kind of bird finds shelter. God's way is always the same: I bring low the high tree, I make high the low tree (Ezekiel 17:24). It is the song of Mary in the Magnificat: he has brought down the powerful and lifted up the lowly.

In the Gospel Jesus tells of a farmer who scatters seed and then goes to sleep. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed would sprout and grow, he does not know how (Mark 4:27). This is a great comfort for parents, teachers, catechists and priests. We sow, and often we see nothing. A child seems to forget everything we taught. A husband does not come back to the sacraments. A parish seems to sleep. Jesus says: do your part, and trust the seed. The power of growth is not in you; it is in the word of God.

Then he speaks of the mustard seed, the smallest of all the seeds on earth (Mark 4:31). The kingdom of God did not begin with armies or palaces. It began in a stable in Bethlehem, in a carpenter's house in Nazareth, with twelve ordinary men. It began, in our own land, with a few families on the coast who received the faith long ago. Today it is a great tree. Never despise small beginnings: a small prayer group, a small act of kindness, a small Sunday school class.

St Paul tells us what kind of life this growth asks of us: we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). We cannot see the growth, but we make it our aim to please him. And Paul reminds us that there will be a harvest: all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10). What we sow now, we will reap then.

Today is also the day of St Antony of Padua, though this year the Sunday takes its place. Many of you will go to his shrine or keep his Tuesday devotions. He was a great sower of the word, and he loved the poor. Let us ask his prayers, and let us go home today to sow one small seed: a word of faith, an act of forgiveness, a gift to someone in need. Then let us go to sleep in peace. God will give the growth. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever planted a seed? You put it in the soil, you water it, and then you wait. You cannot see anything happening! But one day a little green shoot comes up. Jesus says God's kingdom is like that. When you pray, when you share, when you say sorry, you are planting little seeds. You cannot see them grow, but God makes them grow.

Jesus also talked about the mustard seed. It is so tiny, smaller than a grain of rice! But it grows into a big plant, and birds come and make their nests in it. So never think: I am too small to do anything for Jesus. Small seeds become big trees. Today, plant one seed of love at home: help your mother, share your toys, or say a prayer for someone who is sad.

homily: Dear friends, today we meet Tobit, a man everyone praised. He gave alms, he fed the hungry, he buried the dead at the risk of his life. And then one night, sleeping by a wall, droppings from some sparrows fell into his eyes. The doctors made it worse, and he became completely blind (Tobit 2:10). In one moment the generous man became the man who must be helped.

Suffering can make us holy, but it can also make us hard. Tobit's wife Anna goes out to work to keep the family. One day she comes home with a young goat, a gift from her employers. Tobit, sitting in his darkness, does not believe her: it is surely stolen, return it. He is ashamed of being poor and dependent, so he suspects the one who is carrying him. And Anna answers: where are your acts of charity? Where are your righteous deeds? (Tobit 2:14). The man who was kind to strangers had become unkind at home. Many of us know that temptation.

In the Gospel Jesus is trapped by a question about taxes. He asks for a coin and says: whose head is this? The emperor's. Then give to the emperor the things that are the emperor's, and to God the things that are God's (Mark 12:17). The coin has Caesar's face, so let it go back to him. But you, my friend, have God's image stamped on you. Caesar may have your coin. God wants you, all of you.

St Justin understood this. He was a philosopher, a seeker of truth, who found Christ. He told the emperor: we Christians pay our taxes more willingly than anyone, because Christ taught us; but we worship God alone. When he was ordered to sacrifice to idols, he refused, and gave his life. Today let us give God what bears his image: our heart, our thoughts, our home, our kindness to those closest to us. And when suffering comes, let us pray with the Psalm that our hearts be firm, secure in the Lord. Amen.
kids: Children, take a coin and look at it. Whose picture is on it? Jesus once held a coin like that and said: give the coin to the king whose picture is on it. Then he said: give to God what belongs to God. And what belongs to God? You do! God made you to look a little like him, inside your heart. So give God your heart, your prayers, your kindness. You are God's treasure!

homily: Dear friends, today we hear two prayers prayed on the same day in two different cities. In Nineveh old Tobit, blind and insulted, weeps and prays: command my spirit to be taken from me; it is better for me to die than to live (Tobit 3:6). In Ecbatana young Sarah, mocked because seven husbands have died, goes upstairs meaning to hang herself. But she thinks of her father's grief, and instead she stretches out her hands toward the window and prays.

Notice how both of them pray. They do not hide their pain. They tell God exactly how they feel. But they also begin with praise: you are righteous, O Lord; blessed are you, merciful God. Even at the bottom they still call God merciful. That is real faith. Faith is not pretending to be happy; it is turning to God even in the dark.

And then the Bible says: at that very moment, the prayers of both of them were heard in the glorious presence of God, and Raphael was sent to heal both of them (Tobit 3:16–17). God did not give them death. He gave them healing, a marriage, a future. Sometimes God says no to what we ask because he is preparing something far better.

In the Gospel Jesus tells the Sadducees that God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God not of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:27). Death does not have the last word. If you are carrying a heavy sorrow today, lift up your soul to the Lord, as the Psalm says. He hears you at this very moment. And pray for your beloved dead, because for God they are alive. Amen.
kids: Children, did you know that God hears every prayer, even a prayer whispered with tears? Long ago a blind old man called Tobit and a sad young woman called Sarah lived in different cities. On the same day both prayed. And God heard both of them at the very same moment and sent an angel to help! So when you are sad, tell God. He is listening right now.

homily: Dear friends, today's first reading is a wedding story. Young Tobias comes to the house of his kinsman Raguel and asks to marry Sarah. Everyone knows the danger: seven husbands have died on their wedding night. But the angel Raphael has told Tobias: do not be afraid, she was set apart for you before the world was made. So Raguel gives his daughter with a blessing, and a marriage contract is written.

Then comes the wedding night, and what does Tobias do first? He says to Sarah: sister, get up, and let us pray (Tobit 8:4). Before anything else, the two of them stand before God. They praise him, they remember how he made man and woman, and Tobias says: I take her not because of lust, but with sincerity; grant that she and I may grow old together (Tobit 8:7). And Sarah answers: Amen. What a beautiful beginning for a marriage! Love that begins in prayer is protected from evil.

In the Gospel Jesus tells us that the first commandment is to love God with all our heart, soul, mind and strength, and the second is to love our neighbour as ourselves (Mark 12:30–31). Tobias and Sarah did exactly that. First God, then each other. Our families too need this order. When God is first, love between husband and wife, parents and children, is pure and strong.

Today we also remember St Charles Lwanga and his companions, young Christians in Uganda. The king demanded of the palace boys what was sinful, and Charles protected them. When they refused to give up their faith, they were burned alive at Namugongo in 1886. Some of them were only fourteen. They loved God with all their strength, more than their own lives. Let us ask them to give our young people pure and brave hearts, and let us ask Tobias and Sarah to teach our families to pray together. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know the most important rule in the whole world? Jesus told us: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as much as you love yourself. Long ago in Uganda some boys your age loved Jesus so much that they would not do something wrong even when the king ordered them. They were very brave. Today, show your love for God by saying a prayer, and your love for others by being kind.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, in many of our homes there is a picture of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, with a small lamp burning before it. We have seen it so often that we may not notice it anymore. Today the Church asks us to look at it again, with new eyes, and to understand what it tells us: that God loves us with a heart, and that this Heart was pierced for us.

The first reading shows us God as a father, or a mother, with a little child. It was I who taught Ephraim to walk, I took them up in my arms … I was to them like those who lift infants to their cheeks. I bent down to them and fed them (Hosea 11:3–4). Think of a parent holding a baby's hands as it takes its first steps, or lifting it up to kiss its cheek. That is how God sees you. But the child grows up and runs away. And what does God say? Not, I will destroy you. He says: my heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (Hosea 11:8). God's heart is overturned, not against us, but in our favour.

In the second reading St Paul kneels before the Father and prays that we may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19). We cannot measure it. It is broad enough to embrace every person, long enough to last for ever, high enough to lift us to heaven, deep enough to reach the lowest sinner. We cannot measure it, but we can know it, the way a child knows its mother's love, by being held.

Then the Gospel takes us to the Cross. Jesus is already dead. A soldier pierces his side with a spear, and at once blood and water come out (John 19:34). John, who stood there with the Mother of Jesus, says: I saw it, and I tell you so that you may believe. From that wound the Church is born. The water reminds us of our Baptism; the blood, of the Eucharist. Every sacrament we receive flows from the open Heart of Jesus.

This Heart asks something of us. It asks for our love in return. When Jesus showed his Heart to St Margaret Mary, he complained gently that so many people treat his love with coldness and indifference. He asked for reparation: that we console him with our love, receive him in Holy Communion on the First Fridays, and spend time with him in adoration. He also said: learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29). Our homes need hearts like that.

Today is also the day of prayer for priests. A priest is a gift from the Heart of Jesus. Pray for your parish priest today. And tonight, gather your family before the picture of the Sacred Heart, light the lamp, and say together: Sacred Heart of Jesus, we trust in you. Let the lamp remind you that his love never goes out. Amen.
kids: Children, have you seen the picture of Jesus pointing to his heart, with a fire and a crown of thorns around it? That is the Sacred Heart. It tells us that Jesus loves us with a real heart, just like ours, but bigger than the whole world! When Jesus died on the cross, a soldier made a hole in his side, and blood and water came out. Jesus gave everything for us.
Today, when you see the Sacred Heart picture at home, stop and say: Jesus, I love you too! And pray for your parish priest, because today is a special day to pray for priests.

homily: Dear friends, yesterday we looked at the Heart of Jesus, pierced on the Cross. Today the Church invites us to look at the Heart of his Mother. These two feasts sit side by side because these two hearts were never separated. Simeon told Mary: a sword will pierce your own soul too (Luke 2:35). When the Son's Heart was pierced, the Mother's Heart was pierced with him.

Isaiah gives us a joyful picture: I will greatly rejoice in the Lord … for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation … as a bride adorns herself with her jewels (Isaiah 61:10). We hear Mary in these words. From the first moment of her life God clothed her with salvation and kept her heart pure from every sin. That is why we call her Heart Immaculate. And Hannah's song, which we prayed as the Psalm, is the mother of Mary's own Magnificat: my heart exults in the Lord.

But the Gospel shows us that an Immaculate Heart is not a heart without feelings. Mary loses her twelve-year-old son. For three days she searches, with Joseph, through the crowded city. When they find him, she says: Child, why have you treated us like this? Your father and I have been searching for you in great anxiety (Luke 2:48). Every mother who has waited at night for a child who did not come home knows that anxiety. Mary's Heart feels everything we feel, but without sin, without bitterness, without despair.

Then Jesus says something she does not understand: did you not know that I must be in my Father's house? And Luke says simply: his mother treasured all these things in her heart (Luke 2:51). She did not understand, but she did not throw the words away. She kept them, carried them, turned them over for years, until on Calvary and on Easter morning she understood. That is faith: keeping God's word even when we cannot see where it leads.

Today we could also remember St Boniface, who left England to bring the Gospel to Germany, cut down the oak that people worshipped, and was killed in his old age, raising the Gospel book over his head. And the weekday Gospel tells of a poor widow who gave everything she had. Mary, Boniface and the widow have one thing in common: they kept nothing back from God.

So let us consecrate ourselves today to the Immaculate Heart of Mary. When you lose Jesus, through sin or through busyness, search for him as she did, and you will find him in his Father's house, in the Church and in the Eucharist. When you do not understand what God is doing, keep his word in your heart as she did. And ask her to give you a heart like hers, wholly given to God. Amen.
kids: Children, when Jesus was twelve years old, he got lost! Mary and Joseph searched for him for three whole days. Can you imagine how worried they were? At last they found him in the Temple, talking with the teachers about God.

Mary did not understand everything Jesus said, but she kept it all in her heart like a treasure. Our Mother Mary has a heart full of love. If you ever feel lost or sad, you can talk to her. She will always lead you back to Jesus.

homily: Dear friends, today we begin to read St Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians. Paul had been through a very difficult time with this church. People were saying bad things about him; he had been hurt, and he had hurt them with a strong letter. You might expect him to begin with complaints. Instead he begins with praise: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation (2 Corinthians 1:3).

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say that God took away all his problems. He says that God consoles us in all our affliction. God does not always take us out of the storm; he comes and sits with us in the boat. And Paul says why: so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction (2 Corinthians 1:4). The comfort God gives us is not a private treasure. It is meant to be passed on.

Think of the people who comforted you best when you were in pain. Very often they were people who had suffered something similar. A mother who had lost a child, a man who had lost his job, a friend who had been sick. Their own wounds, healed by God, made them gentle with yours. That is what Paul means. Our sufferings, united with the sufferings of Christ, can become a source of comfort for others.

In the Gospel Jesus begins the Sermon on the Mount with a list of surprising blessings. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted (Matthew 5:4). The world does not call these people happy. Jesus does, because God is close to them. This week, as children go back to school, let us go back to the school of Jesus. Let us be humble, merciful, peacemaking. And let us pass on the comfort we have received. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever fallen down and hurt your knee? Who came running to help you? Maybe your mother, or a friend. St Paul says God is the God of all comfort: he comforts us when we are sad, so that we can comfort others. And Jesus told his friends on a mountain who the truly happy people are: people who are kind, gentle, who make peace and who have clean hearts. This week at school, look for a child who is sad or alone, and be a comforter for Jesus!

homily: Dear friends, St Paul had told the Corinthians he would visit them, and then he changed his plans. Some people immediately said: this man cannot be trusted; he says yes and no at the same time. Paul answers: my travel plans may change, but the message I preached never changes, because it is Jesus Christ, and in him it is always Yes (2 Corinthians 1:19).

For in him every one of God's promises is a Yes (2 Corinthians 1:20). Think of all God's promises in the Old Testament: a land, a descendant, a king, a new covenant, a new heart. In Jesus they are all fulfilled. He is God's great Yes to humanity. And at every Mass, when the priest lifts up the Body and Blood of Christ, we answer Amen. That Amen is our yes to God's Yes.

Paul also says that God has anointed us, put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts (2 Corinthians 1:21–22). At Baptism and Confirmation we were anointed with holy chrism and sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit. A seal is a mark of ownership. We belong to God. The Spirit in us is like an advance payment, a first installment of the joy of heaven.

And Jesus tells us what that means in daily life: you are the salt of the earth; you are the light of the world (Matthew 5:13–14). Not: you should become. You are. A Christian who hides his faith is like a lamp under a basket. In these monsoon nights, when the power goes off, we know how precious one small lamp is. Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16). Amen.
kids: Children, what happens if you forget to put salt in the curry? It tastes flat! And what happens when the electricity goes off at night? Everyone looks for a lamp. Jesus said to his friends: you are salt, and you are light. That means a Christian child makes things better, like salt in food, and helps others see God's goodness, like a lamp in the dark. When you share, help, and speak kindly, you are shining Jesus' light!

homily: Dear friends, some preachers in Corinth carried impressive letters of recommendation, and they asked: where are Paul's letters? Paul answers: you are my letter. You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts (2 Corinthians 3:2), written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. The best proof of a minister's work is not a certificate but a changed life.

Then Paul says: the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6). He does not mean that God's Law is bad. Paul loved the Law. He means that a law written only on stone, outside us, can tell us what is right, but it cannot give us the strength to do it. When we fail, it can only condemn us. The Holy Spirit writes God's will inside us, in our hearts, and gives us the power to live it. That is the new covenant God promised through the prophet Jeremiah.

But the Gospel warns us not to go to the other extreme. Jesus says: do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill (Matthew 5:17). The commandments are not thrown away. Jesus shows their full meaning and gives us his Spirit to keep them with love. A child obeys his mother first because he must, and later because he loves her. That is the journey from letter to Spirit.

Today the Church remembers St Ephrem, a deacon of the fourth century, whom our Syriac sister Churches in Kerala call Mar Aprem. He turned the faith into songs and taught people to sing it. He is called the Harp of the Holy Spirit. Let us ask him to help us sing God's commandments in our hearts, and to become letters of Christ that our families and neighbours can read. Amen.
kids: Children, imagine your mother writes on a paper: brush your teeth, say your prayers, help your little brother. You can obey the paper because you have to. But Jesus wants something better: he wants the Holy Spirit to write God's rules inside your heart, so that you do good because you love God. Jesus said: I did not come to throw away God's commandments, but to fulfill them. Today we remember St Ephrem, who wrote beautiful songs about Jesus. Sing a hymn to Jesus today!

homily: Dear friends, Moses came down from Mount Sinai with his face shining, and he covered it with a veil. Paul uses this story to speak about our hearts. Sometimes we read the Bible, we hear it at Mass, but it does not touch us. There is a veil over our hearts. Paul says: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed (2 Corinthians 3:16).

And then something wonderful happens. All of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). Every time we pray, every time we receive Holy Communion, every time we forgive, we become a little more like Jesus. Holiness is not a sudden jump. It is a slow change, from glory to glory.

But the Gospel tells us where this change must begin. Jesus says: you have heard that it was said, You shall not murder. But I say to you that if you are angry with a brother or sister, you will be liable to judgment (Matthew 5:21–22). Most of us have never killed anyone. But how many of us carry anger for years? How many insults have we spoken? Jesus goes to the root.

Then he says something that should make us stop: if you are offering your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there; first be reconciled, and then come and offer your gift (Matthew 5:24). God would rather wait for our gift than receive it from a heart at war. Before the next Mass, let us take one step towards peace. Then our faces too will shine with the light of Christ. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever had a fight with your brother, sister or friend, and then you did not want to look at them? Jesus says that God wants us to make peace quickly. If you come to church to pray and you remember that you hurt someone, go and say sorry first! St Paul says that when we turn to Jesus, our faces shine with his light, like a mirror in the sun. A face that has said sorry shines the brightest!

homily: Dear friends, today we celebrate St Barnabas. His real name was Joseph, but the apostles gave him a nickname: Barnabas, son of encouragement (Acts 4:36). Imagine being known in the whole Church for one thing: you make people stronger. What a beautiful reputation!

Look at what he did at Antioch. Something new was happening there: Greeks, not only Jews, were coming to believe in Jesus. Some people in Jerusalem may have been worried. Barnabas came, and when he saw the grace of God, he rejoiced (Acts 11:23). He did not look first for problems. He looked first for grace. Then he encouraged them to remain faithful. That is the first lesson of Barnabas: look for the good God is doing in others, and rejoice in it.

The second lesson is humility. The work at Antioch grew too big for Barnabas, so he went to Tarsus to look for Saul and brought him to Antioch (Acts 11:25–26). He knew Saul was a brilliant teacher, maybe more gifted than himself. He did not mind. Soon everyone was speaking of Paul and Barnabas, not Barnabas and Paul. Later, when Paul did not want to take young Mark on a journey because Mark had once left them, Barnabas gave Mark a second chance. That Mark became a great helper of the Church.

In the Gospel Jesus says to his apostles: you received without payment; give without payment (Matthew 10:8). Barnabas gave his field, his time, his trust, and finally, tradition says, his life in Cyprus. Today let us ask him for a heart like his. Let us look for the grace of God in others, make room for their gifts, give second chances, and be sons and daughters of encouragement. Amen.
kids: Children, do you know what an encourager is? It is someone who says: you can do it! Don't give up! St Barnabas was the best encourager in the Bible. When nobody trusted Saul, Barnabas trusted him, and Saul became St Paul. When young Mark made a mistake, Barnabas gave him another chance, and Mark wrote a Gospel! Today, say an encouraging word to a friend. You might be helping a future saint!

homily: Dear friends, why did St Paul work so hard? Why did he travel, suffer, write letters with tears? He tells us today: for the love of Christ urges us on (2 Corinthians 5:14). Christ died for all, so that those who live might live no longer for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them (2 Corinthians 5:15). When you really know that someone has died for you, you cannot go on living only for yourself.

Then Paul says one of the most hopeful sentences in the Bible: if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: everything old has passed away; see, everything has become new! (2 Corinthians 5:17). God does not just repair us. He makes us new. That happened at our Baptism, and it happens again every time we come back to him in the sacrament of Reconciliation.

And notice who makes the first move. Not us. In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them (2 Corinthians 5:19). God came looking for us. And he has given this message to the Church, so that Paul can say: we are ambassadors for Christ; be reconciled to God. Every priest in the confessional is such an ambassador. If you have been away from confession for a long time, this weekend is a good time to come home.

In the Gospel Jesus asks for honesty: let your word be Yes, Yes or No, No (Matthew 5:37). We do not need to swear by God or by our mother's head. A Christian's simple word should be enough. Today is Saturday, a day the Church often gives to Our Lady. Her Yes to God was simple and complete: let it be with me according to your word. May she help us to say Yes to God's reconciliation, and to be people whose word is true. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever broken something and wished you could have a brand-new one? St Paul says that when we belong to Jesus, God makes us new inside: the old is gone, the new has come! When we say sorry to God in confession, he makes our hearts new and clean again. Jesus also says: always tell the truth. When you say yes, mean yes; when you say no, mean no. Mother Mary said a big Yes to God. Let us say Yes to him too!

homily: Dear friends, St Paul says today: see, now is the acceptable time; see, now is the day of salvation! (2 Corinthians 6:2). We often say: later I will go to confession, later I will pray more, later I will make peace with my brother. Paul says: now. God's grace is offered today. Tomorrow is not promised to us.

Then Paul tells us what his life as an apostle was like: beatings, imprisonments, sleepless nights, hunger. And yet he says: we are sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything (2 Corinthians 6:10). How is this possible? Because Paul has Christ, and the one who has Christ has everything. Many of our grandparents lived this way: they had little money, but they had faith, and they were rich.

In the Gospel Jesus asks something very difficult: do not resist an evildoer. But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also (Matthew 5:39). Jesus does not mean that we should allow the weak to be harmed, or that a wife should stay with a husband who beats her. The Church teaches that we must protect the innocent. But in the small insults of daily life, the harsh word, the unfair blame, the rude neighbour, Jesus asks us not to hit back.

And he asks even more: if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile (Matthew 5:41). Do more good than is demanded. This is how a family, an office, a parish is healed. Revenge makes the circle of evil bigger; goodness breaks it. Let us ask Jesus today for this grace, and let us use it now, for now is the day of salvation. Amen.
kids: Children, what do you do when your brother or sister hits you? Many of us want to hit back! Jesus says: do not hit back. Be kind instead. And if someone asks you to help, help even more than they ask. If Amma asks you to carry one bag, carry two! This is called going the second mile. It makes Jesus very happy, and it makes your home a happier place.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul tells a beautiful story about the churches of Macedonia. They were poor and suffering, yet their abundant joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity (2 Corinthians 8:2). They even begged Paul for the privilege of giving! How is that possible? Paul says: they gave themselves first to the Lord (2 Corinthians 8:5). When we belong to God, giving becomes a joy.

And Paul shows us where this generosity comes from: you know the generous act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). Jesus left the glory of heaven, was born in a stable, and died with nothing. Everything we have of God, we have because he became poor for us.

In the Gospel Jesus asks the hardest thing of all: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matthew 5:44). Look at the monsoon rain. It falls on the field of the good farmer and of the lazy one, on the church and on the toddy shop. Jesus says: that is how your Father loves. He makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good. If we love only those who love us, what is special about that?

Our Church in India knows such love. Blessed Rani Maria was killed in 1995, and her family forgave her murderer and welcomed him as a brother. That is what Jesus means by: be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). Not a perfection of never making mistakes, but a perfection of mercy. Let us ask today for this grace: to pray, by name, for one person who has hurt us. Amen.
kids: Children, when it rains, does the rain fall only on good children's houses? No! It falls on everyone. Jesus says God loves everyone like that. And he asks us to love even people who are not nice to us. Is there someone at school who teases you? Tonight, say a little prayer for them: Jesus, bless my friend. That is a very brave and beautiful thing to do.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul speaks to us today like a farmer: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Corinthians 9:6). When we give to the poor, we are not losing; we are sowing. And God is the one who gives the harvest. He supplies seed to the sower and bread for food.

Paul also says: God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Not a giver who is forced, not a giver who complains, not a giver who gives only because his name will be read out in church. God loves the one who gives with a glad heart. Sometimes the poorest give most cheerfully, because they know what it is to be in need.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks about our good works: almsgiving, prayer and fasting. He says: do not do them to be seen by others. The hypocrites wanted to be praised, and Jesus says: they have received their reward (Matthew 6:2). If we give only to get a photograph in the newspaper, or pray only so that others think we are holy, we already have our reward: the praise of people, which lasts a moment.

Instead, Jesus invites us to a secret life with the Father: go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:6). Let us today do one good thing that nobody will ever know about. Let us give one gift with a cheerful heart. And let us find one quiet moment to pray behind a shut door. The Father sees, and that is enough. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: when you do something good, you do not have to show everyone. You can do it in secret! Maybe you can make your sister's bed when she is not looking, or put a coin in the box for the poor without telling anyone. Jesus says God sees everything, even secret good deeds, and he is very happy with them. Try one secret good deed today!

homily: Dear friends, St Paul speaks today like a loving father of the bride: I feel a divine jealousy for you, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). The Church is the bride of Christ. Each of us, by Baptism, belongs to him. Paul's fear is that our hearts may be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:3), by another gospel, by false teachers, by the attractions of the world.

How do we keep our hearts for Christ? Above all, by prayer. And in the Gospel Jesus teaches us how to pray. He says: do not heap up empty phrases, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him (Matthew 6:7–8). Sometimes we think that the longer our prayer, the more God will listen. But God is not tired by our words or impressed by them. He is our Father. He wants our hearts.

Then Jesus gives us the Our Father. Notice the order. First: hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done. Only after that: give us bread, forgive us, protect us. When we put God first, our own needs find their right place. And notice that we say our Father, not my Father. We never pray alone; we pray as one family.

Finally, Jesus explains only one line: the line about forgiveness. If you do not forgive others, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses (Matthew 6:15). Every time we pray the Our Father, we are asking God to forgive us in the same way we forgive. Today, let us pray it slowly, and let us mean it, especially those difficult words: as we forgive those who trespass against us. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus taught us a very special prayer: the Our Father. Do you know it by heart? Jesus said we do not need to use lots and lots of words, because God already knows what we need. In the Our Father we call God our Daddy in heaven! We ask him for food, we say sorry, and we promise to forgive others. Tonight, pray it slowly with your family, and think about each word.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul's rivals boasted of their gifts and successes. Paul answers them with a list of his sufferings: beatings, imprisonments, shipwrecks, dangers, hunger, cold. And then he adds: besides other things, I am under daily pressure because of my anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). This is the heart of a true shepherd. Let us remember today our priests and bishops, who carry so many burdens we do not see.

And Paul ends with words that turn the world upside down: if I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness (2 Corinthians 11:30). The world admires the strong, the rich, the successful. Paul says: my glory is my weakness, because there the power of Christ is seen. When we are weak, sick, poor or tired, God is not far from us. He is closest.

In the Gospel Jesus says: do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust consume and where thieves break in and steal (Matthew 6:19). We all know how quickly things pass: the new phone is old in a year, the gold can be stolen, the house needs repair. But there is a treasure no thief can take: the love we give, the prayers we pray, the good we do.

Then Jesus says the key word: for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:21). In this month of the Sacred Heart, let us ask ourselves: where is my heart? With my money, my property, my worries? Or with Jesus? His Heart was pierced for us; his only treasure is our salvation. Let us give him our hearts today, and our hearts will be full of light. Amen.
kids: Children, what is your favourite treasure? A toy, a bicycle, a game? Jesus says toys get old and break, and things can get lost. But there are treasures that last forever: when you are kind, when you pray, when you share. These go into your treasure box in heaven! And Jesus says: where your treasure is, there your heart will be. Let us keep our hearts with Jesus.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul was a great apostle. He had seen visions, he had been caught up into Paradise, as he tells us today. But when the Corinthians asked him for proof that he was a true apostle, he did not show them his visions. He showed them his weakness. On my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses (2 Corinthians 12:5).

He speaks of a thorn in the flesh. We do not know what it was: an illness, a persecution, a temptation. Paul prayed three times that it would leave him. And the Lord answered: My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). The thorn did not go. But grace came. Sometimes God answers our prayer not by taking away the burden but by giving us the strength to carry it.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks to people who worried, just as we do, about food and clothes and the future. Look at the birds of the air, he says; consider the lilies of the field (Matthew 6:26, 28). He does not say: do not work. He says: do not let worry be your master. You cannot serve God and wealth. Worry cannot add a single hour to our life. It can only steal the peace of today.

So Jesus gives us an order of life: strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well (Matthew 6:33). And he gives us a measure: today's trouble is enough for today. St Romuald, whom we remember today, taught his monks to sit with God as if they were already in paradise. Let us also find a quiet minute today, give God our thorn and our worries, and receive the grace that is enough. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever watched the crows and sparrows outside your window? They do not go to the market and they do not cook food, but God feeds them every day. Jesus said: if God takes care of the birds, he will take care of you too, because you are much more precious to him! So when you feel worried about an exam or a new class, say: Jesus, I trust you. Then do your best, and let him take care of the rest.

homily: Dear friends, today the first reading takes us to one of the great turning points of the Bible. After the stories of sin and division, of the flood and the tower of Babel, God begins again with one man. Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you (Genesis 12:1). No map, no address, only a promise.

And the promise is enormous: I will bless you, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:2–3). At Babel the families of the earth were scattered. Through Abraham God wants to bless them all. Christians believe this blessing reached its fullness in Jesus Christ, the son of Abraham, who died for all. Abram's answer is very short: So Abram went, as the Lord had told him (Genesis 12:4). He was seventy-five years old. It is never too late to obey God.

In the Gospel Jesus gives us a word for daily life: Do not judge, so that you may not be judged (Matthew 7:1). He does not mean that we cannot say what is right and wrong. He means that we must not condemn others while ignoring our own sins. He uses a funny picture: a man with a log in his eye trying to take a speck out of his brother's eye. First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly (Matthew 7:5).

St Aloysius Gonzaga lived both readings. Like Abraham he left his father's house: he gave up a princely inheritance to follow Christ as a Jesuit. He was strict with himself and gentle with others. And he died at twenty-three caring for the sick of Rome. In these weeks when schools reopen, let us entrust our children and young people to him, and let us ask for two graces: to go when God calls, and to look at the log in our own eye before we look at the speck in our neighbour's. Amen.
kids: Children, God once said to a man called Abram: pack your things and go to a new place that I will show you. Abram did not know where he was going, but he trusted God and went! Today we also remember St Aloysius, a young prince who left his palace to follow Jesus and to help sick people. You are starting a new school year. Ask Jesus to go with you, and ask St Aloysius to help you study well and be kind to everyone.

homily: Dear friends, today's first reading could have happened in any village in Kerala. Abram and his nephew Lot have become rich, and their herdsmen start fighting over the grass and the water. How many families have been broken by fights over land, a boundary or an inheritance? Brothers who do not speak, cases that go on for twenty years.

Abram, the elder, could have taken the best land for himself. Instead he says: let there be no strife between you and me, for we are kindred (Genesis 13:8). And he lets Lot choose first.
